speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Good evening.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: On behalf of the Commission on Presidential Debates I am pleased to welcome you to this first presidential debate of the 1988 campaign.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I’m Jim Lehrer of the McNeil-Lehrer News Hour.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: My colleagues on the panel are John Mashek of The Atlanta Journal-Constitution; Ann Groer of The Orlando Sentinel; and Peter Jennings of ABC News.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: For the next 90 minutes we will be questioning the candidates for president of the United States following a format designed and agreed to by representatives of the two candidates.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The candidates are Vice President George Bush, the Republican nominee; Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic nominee.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Our questions this evening will be about equally divided between foreign and domestic policy matters.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The first question by agreement between the two candidates goes to Vice President Bush.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It is a domestic question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You have two minutes for an answer, sir.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The polls say the number one domestic issue to a majority of voters is drugs.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: What is there about these times that drives or draws so many Americans to use drugs?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we’ve seen a deterioration of values.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think for a while as a nation we condoned those things we should have condemned.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: For a while, as I recall, it even seems to me that there was talk of legalizing or decriminalizing marijuana and other drugs, and I think that’s all wrong.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So we’ve seen a deterioration in values, and one of the things that I think we should do about it in terms of cause is to instill values into the young people in our schools.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We got away, we got into this feeling that value- free education was the thing.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I don’t believe that at all I do believe there are fundamental rights and wrongs as far as use.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And, of course, as far as the how we make it better, yes, we can do better on interdiction.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But we’ve got to do a lot better on education, and we have to do, be tougher on those who commit crimes.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve got to get after the users more.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We have to change this whole culture.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You know, I saw a movie – “Crocodile Dundee.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: ” And I saw the cocaine scene treated with humor, as though this was a humorous little incident.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And it’s bad.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Everybody ought to be in this thing.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Entertainment industry, people involved in the schools, education.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And it isn’t a Republican or a Democrat or a liberal problem.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But we have got to instill values in these young people.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I have put forward a many-point drug program that includes what I would do as president of the United States; in terms of doing better on interdiction; and in terms of better in the neighborhoods.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I think we’re all in this together, and my plea to the American people is values in the schools.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, you have one minute to respond.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I agree with Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush that values are important.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But it’s important that our leaders demonstrate those values from the top.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: That means those of us who are elected to positions of political leadership have to reflect those values ourselves.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Here we are with a government that’s been dealing with a drug-running Panamanian dictator.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’ve been dealing with him; he’s been dealing drugs to our kids.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Governors like me and others have been trying to deal with the consequences.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I remember being in a high school in my own state as we were organizing something we call the Governor’s Alliance Against Drugs, and a young 16 year old girl coming up to me, desperate, addicted, dependent, saying, Governor, I need help.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’re providing that young woman with help.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But I want to be a president of the United States who makes sure that we never again do business with a drug-running Panamanian dictator, that we never again funnel aid to the contras through convicted drug dealers.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Values begin at the top, in the White House.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Those are the values I want to bring to the presidency and to the White House beginning in January of 1989.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, a follow-up question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You have two minutes to answer it.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Are you suggesting, sir, that President Reagan is one of the causes of the drug problem in this country?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I’m saying that those of us who are elected to positions of political leadership, Jim, have a special responsibility, not only to come up with programs, and I have outlined in detail the very important, very strong program of enforcement as well as drug education prevention.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush is right – the two go hand in hand.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But if our government itself is doing business with people who we know are engaged in drug profiteering and drug trafficking, if we don’t understand that that sends out a very, very bad message to our young people, it’s a little difficult for me to understand just how we can reach out to that youngster that I talked about and to young people like her all over the country, and say to them we want to help you.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Now, I’ve outlined in great detail a program for being tough on enforcement at home and abroad, doubling the number of drug enforcement agents, having a hemispheric summit soon after the 20th of January when we bring our democratic neighbors and allies together here in this hemisphere and go to work together.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But we also have to take demand seriously.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: You know, we have five percent of the world’s population in this country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’re consuming 50 percent of the world’s cocaine.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Doing better in the neighborhoods.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But I think we’re all in this together, and my plea to the American people is values in the schools.

sentence_text: Governor, you have one minute to respond.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I agree with Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush that values are important.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But it’s important that our leaders demonstrate those values from the top.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: That means those of us who are elected to positions of political leadership have to reflect those values ourselves.

speaker: Lehrer

sentence_text: And Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And in my state I’m proud to say we’ve organized a drug education and prevention program which the Federal Drug Enforcement Administration says is a model for the country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’re helping youngsters; we’re reaching out to them.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And we’re beginning with drug education and prevention beginning in the early elementary grades in every elementary school in our state, and that’s the kind of effort we need in every elementary school in the United States of America.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And we’ve got to begin early, in the first, second and third grade, before our youngsters begin to experiment with these very, very dangerous substances.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I guess the question I would ask of Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush is how we instill those values, how we create this environment for the drug free schools that we want in this country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: If he or representatives of the administration are either with or involving people like Noriega in our foreign policy, or don’t pursue that connection in a way that makes it possible for us to cut it off and to be an example to our kids all over the country.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: A minute to rebut, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Vice President.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, the other day my opponent was given a briefing by the CIA.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I asked for and received the same briefing.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I am very careful in public life about dealing with classified information.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And what I’m about to say is unclassified.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Seven administrations were dealing with Mr.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Noriega.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It was the Reagan-Bush administration that brought this man to justice.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And as the governor of Massachusetts knows, there was no evidence that governor – that Mr.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Noriega was involved in drugs, no hard evidence until we indicted him.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so I think it’s about time we get this Noriega matter in perspective.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Panama is a friendly country.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I went down there and talked to the president of Panama about cleaning up their money laundering, and Mr.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Noriega was there, but there was no evidence at that time, and when the evidence was there, we indicted him.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we want to bring him to justice.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so call off all those pickets out there that are trying to tear down seven different administrations.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, the next question will be asked by John Mashek.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It goes to Governor Dukakis, and you’ll have two minutes to answer.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Governor Dukakis, another troublesome issue for voters this year is the bulging federal deficit.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: In a Dukakis administration, you say taxes will be raised only as a last resort.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Would you identify for us then please three specific programs that you are willing to cut to bring that deficit down?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Yes, I’ve been very specific about those, John.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And let me lay out for you my own strategy for bring that deficit down, because as a chief executive that’s balanced ten budgets in a row, I’ve had to make those tough decisions and those tough choices.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: First, I’ve suggested that there are certain weapons systems which we don’t need and we can’t afford.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush has been critical of me for that, but I think those are the kinds of tough choices you have to make.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I’ve also suggested that there are weapons systems that we should proceed on, and I’ve outlined those in detail.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Secondly, we’ve got to invest in economic growth in this country, in every part of this country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Building that kind of growth expands revenues and helps to bring down that deficit.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Thirdly, we have to bring interest rates down, and we will as we come up with a good, solid plan with the Congress for bringing that deficit down.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And, finally, we’ve got to go out there and collect billions and billions of dollars in taxes owed that aren’t being paid to this country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It’s very unfair to the average taxpayer who pays his taxes and pays them on time to permit these monies to go uncollected.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I’ve also suggested that on the domestic side there are areas where we can make some cuts.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We ought to be able to come up with an agricultural policy in this country that gives our farm families a fair price and a decent future without spending $20-25 billion a year, which is what we’ve been doing under this administration.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We can help people to live better lives, and at the same time save money by helping hundreds of thousands of families on welfare to get off or welfare, and to become productive citizens again.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The thing I don’t understand about Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush’s approach to this is how he could possibly be serious about bringing that deficit down given what he says he wants to do.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: He seems to want to spend a great deal of money on just about every weapon system; he says he’s against new taxes, although he’s broken that pledge at least times in the last year that I know of; he wants to give the wealthiest taxpayers in this country a five year, $40 billion tax break.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: He also wants to spend a lot of money on additional programs.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: If he keeps this up, he’s going to be the Joe Isuzu of American politics.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But I hope you won’t take my five seconds away from me.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I will say this –

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Your two minutes is up, Governor.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: If he’s serious about what he’s saying, then the only place he can go to balance that budget is to raid the Social Security Trust Fund, and he tried that in 1985, and I think he’s going to try it again.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You have a minute to rebut.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Is this the time to unleash our one-liners?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That answer was about as clear as Boston harbor.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me help the governor.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: There are so many things there, I don’t quite know where to begin.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: When you cut capital gains, you put people to work.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: John Kennedy proposed cutting capital gains.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Paul Tsongas, a liberal senator from Massachusetts said the dumbest thing I did was to oppose the capital gains cut.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s not going to cost the government money.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s going to increase revenues to the federal government, and it’s going to create jobs.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So that’s one of the things that I think makes a big difference between us.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Massachusetts doesn’t have an enormous defense budget, but nevertheless, the governor raised taxes five different times.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That happens to be a fact.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so let’s kind of stay on the issue, and I have made a specific proposal for what I call a flexible freeze.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And it permits – economists on the East Coast and West think it’s good – it permits the president to sort out the priorities, and we continue to grow because I will not raise taxes.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Your time is up, too.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: A follow-up, John.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Vice President, you have vowed not to raise taxes of any kind during your administration and at the same time you’ve proposed this capital gains cut, you’ve proposed more incentive breaks for the oil industry.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: You’ve suggested new spending programs and even some Republicans say the flexible freeze you just spoke about will hardly make a dent in the deficit.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Is the deficit no longer really a concern of yours, the Republican Party or the taxpayers?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think it’s the Republican Party and my concern to bring it down.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And presidential leadership that I want to provide in this area will bring it down, but we’ve got to get the Democrats – Congress under control.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They do all the spending, they appropriate every dime and tell us how to spend every dime.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’d like to ask the Governor to join in getting for the president what 43 governors have, the line-item veto.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He has to operate in Massachusetts under a balanced budget proviso.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I would like a balanced budget amendment.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But the dynamics of the economy – we cut the taxes and revenues are up by 25 percent in three years.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So the problem is – it’s not that the working is being taxed too little or the person working out – the woman working in some factory being taxed too little.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It is that we are continuing to spend too much.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So, my formula says grow at the rate of inflation.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Permit the president to set the priorities on where we do the spending.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And remember the Federal deficit has come down $70 billion in one year, in 1987.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And if we – and the – actually this year Congress is doing a little better in controlling the growth of spending.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Spending was only up something like 4 percent.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So, it isn’t that we’re taking too little – from taxpayer – we’re spending too much still.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And the formula I’ve given you works, we’ve put it through a good economic model, we’ve got good economists on the West Coast, Michael Boskin and Marty Feldstein up there who’s a very respected economist in the – Massachusetts.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And they agree, that if we can do what I’ve said, we can get it down without going and socking the American taxpayer once again.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Capital gains, one more point on that, please let’s learn from history.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: A capital gains differential will increase jobs, increase risk taking, increase revenues to the Federal Government.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, you have a minute to rebut.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, I hope all of those Americans out there who are watching us, listening to us and trying to make up their mind about which one of us ought to be president of the United States listen to the Vice President very carefully.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: What he’s proposing after over a trillion in new debt which has been added in the Federal debt in the course of the past eight years, an IOU our children and grandchildren will be paying for years, is a tax cut for the wealthiest one percent of the people in this country, an average of about $30,000 that we’re going to give to people making $200,000 a year.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Why that’s more than the average teacher makes.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’ve had enough of that, ladies and gentlemen.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’ve run up more debt in the last eight years than under all the presidents from George Washington to Jimmy Carter combined.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It’s time for a chief executive who can make tough choices, can work with the Congress, can get that deficit down and begin to build a strong fiscal foundation under this country.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, the next question will be asked by Anne Groer and it will go the Vice President.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You have two minutes to answer, sir.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: Vice President, you’ve said you want a kinder, gentler presidency, one that helps the less fortunate.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: Today, 37 million Americans including many working families with aging parents and young children cannot afford any health insurance, but earn too much to qualify for Medicaid.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: What will you do to provide protection for them and how will you pay for it?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: One thing I will not do is sock every business in the country and, thus, throw some people out of work.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to keep this economic recovery going.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: More Americans at work today than any time in history, a greater percentage of the work force.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What I will do is permit people to buy into Medicaid.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe that’s the answer.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I am proud to have been part of an administration that past the first catastrophic health bill.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And in that there are some Medicaid provisions that will be very helpful to the very kind of people we’re talking about here.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But we’ve got to keep going forward without killing off the engine and throwing people out of work.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So, the answer lies, it seems to me, in full enforcement of the catastrophic program.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It lies to me in flexibility in Medicaid so people at the lowest end can buy in there and get their needs covered and then it also – I do not want to see us mandate across the board that every company has to do this, because I really think that marginal operators are going to go say, “We can’t make it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: ” And I think then you’re going to see that people are put out of work.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: All these programs – and this cost on his – is – was – I saw an estimate, I’d love to know what he thinks, $35 – $40 billion – and it seems to me that somebody pays that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: There isn’t any such thing as something free out there.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It either gets passed along as increased prices or it gets passed along by people being put out of work so the business can continue to compete.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So, I think we ought to do it in the Medicaid system.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we ought to do it by full enforcement of the catastrophic health insurance.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we ought to do it by everybody doing what they can do out of conscience.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s a terrible problems in terms of flexibility on private insurance.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I just don’t want to mandate it and risk putting this – setting the recovery back.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: A rebuttal, Governor?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But, George, that’s no answer.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You don’t like the answer, but it’s an answer.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, no, it’s no answer to those 37 million people, most of them members of working families who don’t have a dime of health insurance and don’t know how to pay the bills if their kids get sick at night.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I was in Houston on Tuesday meeting with a group of good citizens, working citizens.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: All of them with little or no health insurance.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: One of them was a father who had been laid off a few months ago and lost his health insurance.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Has an 11 year old son and can’t let that son compete in sports and Little League, because he’s afraid he’s going to get hurt and he won’t be able to provide health insurance to pay those bills.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: My state just became the only state in the nation to provide for universal health care and we did it with the support of the business community and labor and the health care community and with virtually everybody in the state.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The fact of the matter is that employers who today are insuring their employees are paying the freight, because they’re paying for those who aren’t.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And I think it’s time that when you got a job in this country it came with health insurance.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: That’s the way we’re going to provide basic health security for all of the citizens of this country of ours.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Follow-up, Anne?

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: Yes.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: Since your Massachusetts health plan has been attacked by the Vice President and you have defended it in this way, I would like to move on to perhaps one of the most costly medical catastrophes facing Americans today and that is AIDS.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: In – at the end of September, the thousands of AIDS patients will lose their access to AZT, which is the only Federally approved drug for treatment of the disease.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: Now, I’d like to now, sir, if – what your position is on extending that and what it is you think the government ought to be doing about making AZT and other drugs available to people who are suffering from this disease.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, Anne, let me just say before I answer your question that I didn’t know that the Vice President attacked our program in Massachusetts.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I hope he hasn’t.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Because has won the support of a great many people all over the state and I think it’s a model for what I hope we can do across the country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But when I proposed my plan this past Tuesday, he or one of his spokesmen called it socialized medicine.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The last time the Vice President used that phrase, I suspect he remembers it, don’t you?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It was in 1964 and that’s what he called Medicare.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, he was wrong then and he’s wrong now.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: If I may interrupt at this point and caution the audience as I did before we went on the air, please hold it down.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You’re only taking time away from your candidate when you do that.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, continue, please.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Let me say this about AIDS.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It’s the single most important public health crisis, single most important public health emergency we’ve had in our lifetimes and I think there are a number of things we have to do including supporting legislation which is now moving through the Congress, which will commit this nation to the resources to find a cure which will provide broad education and prevention, which will provide sensitive and caring treatment for the victims of AIDS.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I think we have to demonstrate some flexibility and I think the FDA is attempting to do so now in trying to make it possible for new and experimental drugs to be available to people who are at risk at AIDS and I would hope that we could bring that kind of a policy to bear beginning in January.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And I would encourage the current administration to proceed with that kind of flexibility where it’s appropriate and where it’s done carefully and responsibly.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But we have not had the kind of leadership we should have had.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: In this particular area, I think the Vice President and I are in general agreement on what we have to do.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The special Federal commission made good solid recommendations.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I think we’re both supportive of them and I would strongly lead in that area as I have in my state as Governor.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Vice President, a minute of rebuttal.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, we’re on the right track.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The NIH is doing a good job in research.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The Surgeon General is doing a good job in encouraging the proper kind of education.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I notice that the Governor did not mention any testing.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But we got to have a knowledge base.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Testing should be confidential, but we have to have a knowledge.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We can’t simply stick our heads in the sands in terms of testing.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m Chairman of the President’s Task Force on Regulatory Relief and we are working with the FDA and they have sped up bringing drugs to market that can help.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And you got to be careful here, because there’s a safety factor, but I think these things – and then also I am one who believes we’ve got to go the extra mile in clean – being sure that that blood supply is pure.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We cannot have a lack of confidence in the blood supply when it comes to operations and surgery and things of this nature.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So, research, speeding the drugs to market, testing, blood supply are very important elements of this.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Next question will be asked by Peter Jennings.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It goes to the Governor.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: Good evening, Mr.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: Vice President, Governor.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: Governor, one theme that keeps coming up about the way you govern – you’ve both mentioned leadership tonight, so I’d like to stay with that for a second.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: The theme that keeps coming up about the way you govern is passionless, technocratic –

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Passionless?

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: Passionless, technocratic, the smartest clerk in the world.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: Your critics maintain that in the 1960’s your public passion was not the war in Vietnam or civil rights, but no fault auto insurance.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: And they say in the 1970’s you played virtually no role in the painful busing crisis in Boston.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: Given the fact that a president must sometimes lead by sheer inspiration and passion.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: We need to know if this is a fair portrait of your governing or if it is a stereotype.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: And if it isn’t fair, give us an example of where you have had that passion and leadership that sometimes a president needs?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Vice President, a rebuttal.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I don’t question his passion.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I question – and I don’t question his concern about the war in Vietnam.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He introduced or supported legislation back then that suggested that kids of Massachusetts should be exempt from going overseas in that war.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, that’s a certain passion that in my view it’s misguided passion.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He – we have a big difference on issues.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You see, last year in the primary, he expressed his passion.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He said, “I am a strong liberal Democrat” – August, ’87.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Then he said, “I am a card-carrying member of the ACLU.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: ” That was what he said.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He is out there on out of the mainstream.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He is very passionate.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: My argument with the governor is, do we want this country to go that far left.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I wish we had time to let me explain.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I salute him for his passion.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We just have a big difference on where this country should be led, and in what direction it ought to go.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Peter, a question?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Question for the vice president, Peter.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: I’d actually like to follow up if I may on this mention you’ve made of his card carrying membership in the American Civil Liberties Union.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: You’ve used the phrase “card carrying” so many times since Governor Dukakis first acknowledged that he was a card carrying member of the ACLU that some people have come to believe that you’ve used it to brand him in some way, to identify him as people were identified in the 1950’s as less than patriotic.

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: I’d like to know why you keep repeating the phrase, and what’s the important issue here?

speaker: Jennings
sentence_text: What is so wrong with the governor being a member of an organization which has come to the defense of, among other people, Colonel Oliver North?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Nothings wrong with it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But just take a look at the positions of the ACLU.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But, Peter, please understand, the liberals do not like me talking about liberal They don’t like it when I say that he says he’s a card carrying member.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, if that quote was wrong, he can repudiate it, right here.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve seen it authoritatively written twice, and if I’ve done him an injustice, and he didn’t say it, I’m very, very sorry.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I don’t agree with a lot of – most of the positions of the ACLU.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I simply don’t want to see the ratings on movies.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t want my ten year old grandchild to go into an X-rated movie.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I like those ratings systems.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think they’re right to try to take the tax exemption away from the Catholic Church.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t want to see the kiddie pornographic laws repealed; I don’t want to see “under God” come out from our currency.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, these are all positions of the ACLU.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I don’t agree with them.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He has every right to exercise his passion, as what he said, a strong, progressive liberal.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t agree with that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I come from a different point.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think I’m more in touch with the mainstream of America.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They raised the same thing with me on the Pledge of Allegiance.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You see, I’d have found a way to sign that bill.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Governor Thompson of Illinois did.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m not questioning his patriotism.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He goes out and says the man is questioning my patriotism.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And then all the liberal columnists join in.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I am not.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I am questioning his judgment on these matters, or where he’s coming from He has every right to do it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I believe that’s not what the American people want, and when he said, when he said at the convention, ideology doesn’t matter, just competence, he was moving away from his own record, from what his passion has been over the years.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And that’s all I’m trying to do, is put it in focus.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I hope people don’t think that I’m questioning his patriotism when I say he used his words to describe his participation in that organization.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, a response.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, I hope this is the first and last time I have to say this.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Of course, the vice president is questioning my patriotism.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I don’t think there’s any question about that, and I resent it.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I resent it.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: My parents came to this country as immigrants.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: They taught me that this was the greatest country in the world.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I’m in public service because I love this country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I believe in it.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And nobody’s going to question my patriotism as the vice president has now repeatedly.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The fact of the matter is if the Pledge of Allegiance was the acid test of one’s patriotism–the vice president’s been the presiding officer in the United States Senate for the past seven and a half years.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: To the best of my knowledge he’s never once suggested that a session of the Senate begin with the Pledge of Allegiance.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush, I don’t question your patriotism.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: When you’re attacked for your military record, I immediately said it was inappropriate, it had no place in this campaign, and I rejected it.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I would hope that from this point on, we get to the issues that affect the vast majority of Americans, jobs, schools, health care, housing, the environment.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Those are the concerns of the people that are watching us tonight.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Not labels that we attach to each other, questions about each other’s patriotism and loyalty.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The time is up, governor.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Let’s go now to John Mashek, again.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: A question for the vice president.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Vice President, in a debate during the Republican primaries, you said most of the nation’s homeless are suffering from mental illness, an assertion immediately challenged by one of your rivals.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Estimates of the homeless range from a low of 250,000 by the government, to around three million, including working families and their children.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: What commitment are you willing to make tonight to this voiceless segment of our society?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to see the McKinney Act fully funded.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe that that would help in terms of shelter.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to see – when I talked at our convention about a thousand points of light, I was talking about the enormous numbers of shelters and organizations that help.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The governor’s wife has been very active in the homeless.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: My campaign chairman, Secretary Jim Baker’s wife.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: This isn’t government.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: These are people that care, that are trying to give of themselves.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The government has a role.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It is to fully fund the McKinney Act.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: There are certain army bases that the act calls for that can be used in certain cases to shelter people when it’s rough.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so I think that we’re on the right track.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t see this, incidentally, as a Democrat or a Republican or a liberal or conservative idea.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I see an involvement by a thousand points of light.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I see the funding that is required, and I hope the Congress will fully fund this bill.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They gave it a great deal of conscience and a great deal of work.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’re on the track on this one.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But – and I, look, mental – that was a little overstated it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’d say around 30 percent.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think maybe we could look back over our shoulders and wonder whether it was right to let all those mental patients out.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Maybe we need to do a better job in mental clinics to help them.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Because there is a major problem there.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: A lot of them are mentally sick.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’ve got to attend to them.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But fully, my short range answer is fully fund that McKinney Act.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, a response.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, this is another fundamental difference that I have with the vice president, just as I do in the case of health care for 37 million members of working families in this country who don’t have health insurance.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The problem, Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush, is that you’ve cut back by 90 percent on our commitment to affordable housing for families of low and moderate income.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And when you do that, you’ve have homeless families.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We didn’t have two and a half million, or three million homeless people living on streets and in doorways in this country ten years ago.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’ve got to begin to get back to the business of building and rehabilitating housing for families of low and moderate income in this country; housing for young families that they can look forward some day to buy.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’ve got communities in this country increasingly where our own kids can’t afford to live in the communities that they grew up in.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: That’s an essential commitment.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And I think the housing community is ready.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But it’s going to take a president who’s committed to housing, who’s had experience in building and rehabilitating housing who understands that affordable housing for families of low and moderate income, for young families, first time home buyers, is an essential part of the American dream.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And while I’m all for the McKinney bill, that, by itself, simply won’t do.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We’ve got to have a president that can lead on this issue, that can work with the Congress, and I’m prepared to do so.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: This is one of the most important priorities that faces this country.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: John, a question for the governor.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Governor, you’ve mentioned the American dream of home ownership, and it’s certainly become an impossible one for many of the young people of our nation who are caught up in this economic squeeze of the middle class, as you’ve said so frequently during the campaign.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: And yet in spite of your answer just a few minutes ago, what promise can you realistically hold out to these people that with the costs of housing going up, and with limited help available from Washington, are we destined to become a nation of renters?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, I certainly hope not.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And it’s all a question of what our priorities are.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush talked about values.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I agree with him.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: What are our values?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Isn’t providing housing for families of low and moderate income, isn’t it making possible for young families, first time home buyers to own their own home some day something that’s part of the American dream?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I think so.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: You know, back after World War II when we had hundreds of thousands of GIs who came back from the war, we didn’t sit around.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We went out and built housing.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The government was very much involved; so was the housing industry; so was the banking industry; so were housing advocates; so were non-profit agencies; so were governors and mayors and people all over this country who believe deeply in home ownership and affordable housing.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Now, that’s the kind of leadership that I want to provide as president of the United States.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: This isn’t a question of a little charity for the homeless.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: This is a question of organizing the housing community.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I’ve talked to bankers and builders and developers, the housing advocates, community development agencies, and they want leadership from Washington.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Washington, by itself, can’t do it all.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We shouldn’t expect that.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But governors are ready; mayors are ready.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Builders and community leaders are ready.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It will require some funds, John.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And we ought to be prepared to provide those funds.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: But that, too, will require some choices.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Bush wants to spend billions and trillions on Star Wars.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Well, that’s a choice we have to make, isn’t it?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Do we spend money on that weapon system in the billions and trillions, or is providing some decent and affordable housing for families of this country something that is at least as important and probably more so.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Because it’s so essential to our economic strength and to our future.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: Now, that’s the kind of presidency I believe in.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And simply to say, well, the McKinney bill will do it just doesn’t do.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: We need a president who will lead on this issue, who has had experience on this issue.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It’s the kind of priority that will be at the top of our list beginning in January of 1989.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: A response, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Vice President.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think the governor is blurring housing and the homeless.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Let’s talk about housing which the question was.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: When you talk to those bankers, did they discuss where interest rates were when your party controlled the White House?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Ten days before I took the oath of office as president they were 21 and a half percent.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, how does that grab you for increasing housing?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Housing is up.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We are serving a million more families now.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But we’re not going to do it in that old Democratic, liberal way of trying to build more bricks and mortars.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Go out and take a look at St.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Louis at some of that effort.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It is wrong.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I favor home ownership.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to see more vouchers.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to see control of some of these projects, and I want to keep the interest rates down.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They’re half, now of what they were when we came into office, and with my policy of getting this deficit under control, they’ll be a lot less.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But if we spend and spend and spend, that is going to wrap up the housing market, and we’ll go right back to the days of the misery index and malaise that President Reagan and I have overcome – thank God for the United States on that one.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, the next question is to the governor.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Ann Groer will ask it.

speaker: Groer
sentence_text: Governor Dukakis, is there a conflict between your opposition to the death penalty and your support for abortion on demand, even though in the minds of many people, that’s also killing?

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: No, I don’t think there is.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: There are two very different issues here, and they’ve got to be dealt with separately.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I’m opposed to the death penalty.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I think everybody knows that.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I’m also very tough on violent crime.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And that’s one of the reasons why my state has cut crime by more than any other industrial state in America.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It’s one of the reasons why we have the lowest murder rate of any industrial state in the country.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: It’s one of the reasons why we have a drug education and prevention program that is reaching out and helping youngsters all over our state, the kind of thing I want to do as president of the United States.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: You know, the vice president says he wants to impose the death penalty on drug traffickers, and yet his administration has a federal furlough program which is one of the most permissive in the country, which gave last year 7,000 furloughs to drug traffickers and drug pushers, the same people that he says he now wants to execute.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The issue of abortion is a very difficult issue, one that I think that we all have to wrestle with, we have to come to terms with.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I don’t favor abortion.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I don’t think it’s a good thing.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: I don’t think most people do.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: The question is who makes the decision.

speaker: Michael Dukakis
sentence_text: And I think it has to be the woman, in the exercise of her own conscience and religious beliefs, that makes that decision.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Response, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Vice President.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, the Massachusetts furlough program was unique.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It was the only one in the nation that furloughed murderers who had not served enough time to be eligible for parole.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The federal program doesn’t do that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: No other state programs do that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I favor the death penalty.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I know it’s tough and honest people can disagree.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But when a narcotics wrapped up guy goes in and murders a police officer, I think they ought to pay with their life.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I do believe it would be inhibiting.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so I am not going to furlough men like Willie Horton, and I would meet with their, the victims of his last escapade, the rape and the brutalization of the family down there in Maryland.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Maryland would not extradite Willie Horton, the man who was furloughed, the murderer, because they didn’t want him to be furloughed again.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so we have a fundamental difference on this one.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think most people know my position on the sanctity of life.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I favor adoption.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
