sentence_text: Now, I honor your service in World War II, I honor Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Perot’s service in uniform and the service of every man and woman who ever served, including Admiral Crowe, who was your Chairman of the joint Chiefs and who’s supporting me.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But when Joe McCarthy went around this country attacking people’s patriotism he was wrong.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: He was wrong.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And a senator from Connecticut stood up to him named Prescott Bush.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Your father was right to stand up to Joe McCarthy, you were wrong to attack my patriotism.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I was opposed to the war but I loved my country and we need a president who will bring this country together, not divide it.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’ve had enough division.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want to lead a unified country.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We move now to the subject of taxes and spending.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The question goes to Governor Clinton for a two minutes answer.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It will be asked by Ann Compton.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: ANN

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: Governor Clinton, can you lock in a level here tonight on where middle-income families can be guaranteed a tax cut or, at the very least, at what income level they can be guaranteed no tax increase?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The tax increase I have proposed triggers in at family incomes of $200,000 and above.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Those are the people who in the 1980s had their incomes go up while their taxes went down.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Middle-class people, defined as people with incomes of $52,000 and down, had their incomes go down while their taxes went up in the Reagan-Bush years because of 6 increases in the payroll taxes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So that is where my income limit would trigger.

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: There will be no tax increases–

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Right.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: My plan –

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: –notwithstanding my opponent’s ad, my plan triggers in at gross incomes, family incomes of $200,000 and above.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Then we want to give modest middle-class tax relief to restore some fairness, especially to middle- class people with families with incomes of under $60,000.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: In addition to that, the money that I raise from upper-income people and from asking foreign corporations just to pay the same income on their income earned in America that American corporations do will be used to give incentives back to upper-income people.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want to give people permanent incentives on investment tax credit, like President Kennedy and the Congress inaugurated in the early ’60s to get industry moving again; a research and development tax credit; a low-income housing tax credit; a long-term capital gains proposal for new business and business expansions.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’ve got to have no more trickle down.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We don’t need across-the-board tax cuts for the wealthy for nothing.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We need to say here’s your tax incentive: if you create American jobs, the old-fashioned way.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’d like to create more millionaires than were created under Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush and Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Reagan, but I don’t want to have 4 years where we have no growth in the private sector, and that’s what’s happened in the last 4 years.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’re down 35,000 jobs in the private sector.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We need to invest and grow, and that’s what I want to do.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President Bush, one minute, sir.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, let me–I have to correct one thing.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I didn’t question the man’s patriotism.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I questioned his judgment and his character.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What he did in Moscow, that’s fine.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Let him explain it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He did.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I accept that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What I don’t accept is demonstrating and organizing demonstrations in a foreign country when your country’s at war.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m sorry.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I cannot accept that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: In terms of this one on taxes spells out the biggest difference between us.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I do not believe we need to go back to the Mondale proposals or the Dukakis proposals of tax and spend.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Governor Clinton says $200,000 but he also says he wants to raise $150 billion.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Taxing people over $200,000 will not get you $150 billion.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And then when you add in his other spending proposals, regrettably you end up socking it to the working man.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That old adage they use–we’re going to soak the rich- -we’re going to soak the rich–it always ends up being the poor cab driver or the working man that ends up paying the bill.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so I just have a different approach.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe the way to get the deficit down is to control the growth of mandatory spending programs, and not raise taxes on the American people.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve got a big difference there.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, one minute.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve got to have a growing, expanding job base to give us a growing, expanding tax base.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Right now we have a flat to deteriorating job base and where it appears to be growing, it’s minimum-wage jobs.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: So we’ve got to really rebuild our job base.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s going to take money for infrastructure and investment to do that.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Our foreign competitors are doing it; we’re not.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We cannot pay off the $4 trillion debt, balance the budget and have the industries of the future and the high- paying jobs in this country without having the revenue.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’re going to go through a period of shared sacrifice.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: There’s one challenge.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s got to be fair.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve created a mess, don’t have much to show for it and we have got to fix it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And that’s about all I can say in a minute.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Okay.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Next question goes to President Bush for a 2-minute answer, and it will be asked by Sandy Vanocur.

speaker: Sander Vanocur
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Sander Vanocur
sentence_text: President, this past week your secretary of the Army, Michael Stone, said he had no plans to abide by a congressional mandate to cut US forces in Europe from 150 to 100 thousand by the end of September 1996.

speaker: Sander Vanocur
sentence_text: Now, why, almost 50 years after the end of World War II, and with the total collapse of the Soviet Union, should American taxpayers be taxed to support armies in Europe when the Europeans have plenty of money to do it for themselves?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, Sander, that’s a good question, and the answer is: for 40-some years we kept the peace.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: If you look at the cost of not keeping the peace in Europe, it would be exorbitant.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We have reduced the number of troops that are deployed and going to be deployed.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I have cut defense spending.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And the reason we could do that is because of our fantastic success in winning the Cold War.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We never would have got there if we had gone for the nuclear freeze crowd; we never would have got there if we had listened to those that wanted to cut defense spending.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think it is important that the US stay in Europe and continue to guarantee the peace.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We simply cannot pull back.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, when anybody has a spending program they want to spend money on at home, they say, well, let’s cut money out of the Defense Dept.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I will accept and have accepted the recommendations of 2 proven leaders, General Colin Powell and Secretary Dick Cheney.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They feel that the levels we’re operating at and the reductions that I have proposed are proper.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so I simply do not think we should go back to the isolation days and starting blaming foreigners.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We are the sole remaining superpower, and we should be that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we have a certain disproportionate responsibility.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I would ask the American people to understand that if we make imprudent cuts, if we go too far, we risk the peace.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I don’t want to do that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve seen what it is like to see a war, to see the burdens of a war, and I don’t want to see us make reckless cuts.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Because of our programs we have been able to significantly cut defense spending.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But let’s not cut into the muscle, and let’s not cut down our insurance policy, which is participation of American forces in NATO, the greatest peace- keeping organization ever made.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Today you’ve got problems in Europe, still bubbling along even though Europe’s gone democracy’s route.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But we are there, and I think this insurance policy is necessary.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think it goes with world leadership, and I think the levels we’ve come up with are just about right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, one minute, sir.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If I’m poor and you’re rich, and I can get you to defend me, that’s good.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: But when the tables get turned, I ought to do my share.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Right now we spend about $300 billion a year on defense, the Japanese spend around 30 billion in Asia, the Germans spend around 30 billion in Europe.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: For example, Germany will spend a trillion dollars building infrastructure over the next 10 years.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s kind of easy to do if you only have to pick up a $30-billion tab to defend your country.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: The European Community is in a position to pay a lot more than they have in the past.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I agree with the president: when they couldn’t, we should have; now that they can, they should.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We sort of seem to have a desire to try to stay over there and control it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They don’t want us to control it, very candidly.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: So it I think is very important for us to let them assume more and more of the burden and for us to bring that money back here and rebuild our infrastructure, because we can only be a superpower if we are an economic superpower; and we can only be an economic superpower if we have a growing, expanding job base.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor Clinton, one minute, sir.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I agree with the general statement Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush made.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I disagree that we need 150,000 troops to fulfill our role in Europe.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We certainly must maintain an engagement there.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: There are certainly dangers there, there are certainly other trouble spots in the world which are closer to Europe than to the US.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But 2 former defense secretaries recently issued a report saying that 100,000 or slightly fewer troops would be enough, including President Reagan’s former defense secretary, Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Carlucci.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Many of the military experts whom I consulted on this agreed.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’re going to have to spend more money in the future on military technology and on greater mobility, greater airlift, greater sealift, the B-22 airplane.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’re going to have to do some things that are quite costly.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I simply don’t believe we can afford nor do we need to keep 150,000 troops in Europe given how much the Red Army, now under the control of Russia, has been cut, the arms control agreement concluded between Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush and Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Yeltsin, something I have applauded.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I don’t think we need 150,000 troops.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let me make one other point.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush talked about taxes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: He didn’t tell you that he vetoed a middle class tax cut because it would be paid for by raising taxes on the wealthy and vetoed an investment tax credit paid for by raising taxes on the wealthy.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We go now to Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot for a 2-minute question, and it will be asked by John Mashek.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Mr Perot, you talked about fairness just a minute ago and sharing the pain.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: As part of your plan to reduce the ballooning federal deficit, you’ve suggested that we raise gasoline taxes 50 cents a gallon over 5 years.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Why punish the middle class consumer to such a degree?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s 10 cents a year cumulative.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It finally gets to 50 cents at the end of the 5th year.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I think “punish” is the wrong word.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Again, see, I didn’t create this problem.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’re trying to solve it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, if you study our international competitors, some of our international competitors collect up to $3.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: 50 a gallon in taxes, and they use that money to build infrastructure and to create jobs.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We collect 35 cents, and we don’t have it to spend.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I know it’s not popular, and I understand the nature of your question.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: But the people who will be helped the most by it are the working people who will get the jobs created because of this tax.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Why do we have to do it?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Because we have so mismanaged our country over the years, and it is now time to pay the fiddler.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And if we don’t, we will be spending our children’s money.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We have spent $4 trillion worth.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: An incredible number of young people are active in supporting my effort because they are deeply concerned that we have taken the American dream from them.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I think it’s fitting that we’re on the campus of a university tonight.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: These young people, when they get out of this wonderful university, will have difficulty finding a job.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve got to clean this mess up, leave this country in good shape, and pass on the American dream to them.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve got to collect the taxes to do it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If there’s a fairer way, I’m all ears –aah.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: But–but–see, let me make it very clear.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If people don’t have the stomach to fix these problems, I think it’s a good time to face it, November.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If they do, then they will have heard the harsh reality of what we have to do.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’m not playing Lawrence Welk music tonight.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, Governor Clinton, you have a minute, sir.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Perot has confronted this deficit issue, but I think it’s important to point out that we really have 2 deficits in America, not one.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We have a budget deficit in the federal government, but we also have an investment, a jobs, an income deficit.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: People are working harder for less money than they were making 10 years ago, 2- 3rds of our people–a $1600 drop in average income in just the last 2 years.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The problem I have with the Perot prescription is that almost all economists who’ve looked at it say that if you cut the deficit this much this quick it will increase unemployment, it will slow down the economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That’s why I think we shouldn’t do it that quickly.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We have a disciplined reduction in the deficit of 50 % over the next 4 years, but first get incentives to invest in this economy, put the American people back to work.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’ve got to invest and grow.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: 9 Nobel Prize-winning economists and 500 others, including numerous Republican and Democratic business executives, have endorsed this approach because it offers the best hope to put America back to work and get our incomes rising instead of falling.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President Bush, one minute, sir.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Your question was on fairness.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I just disagree with Mr.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Perot.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t believe it is fair to slap a 50-cent-a-gallon tax over whatever many years on the people that have to drive for a living, people that go long distances.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think we need to do it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You see, I have a fundamental difference.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I agree with what he’s talking about in trying to get this spending down and the discipline, although I think we ought to totally exempt Social Security.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But he’s talking tough medicine, and I think that’s good.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I disagree with the tax-and-spend philosophy.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You see, I don’t think we need to tax more and spend more, and then say that’s going to make the problem better.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I’m afraid that’s what I think I’m hearing from Governor Clinton.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe what you need to do is some of what Ross is talking about: control the growth of mandatory spending and get taxes down.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He’s mentioned some ways to do it–and I agree with those.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve been talking about getting a capital gains cut forever, and his friends in Congress have been telling me that’s a tax break for the rich.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It would stimulate investment.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m for an investment tax allowance; I’m for a tax break for first- time homebuyers.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And with this new Congress coming in, gridlock will be gone, and I’ll sit down with them and say let’s get this done.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I do not want to go the tax-and-spend route.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, let’s move on now to the subject of jobs.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The first question goes to President Bush for 2 minutes, and John will ask that question.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: President, last month you came to St.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: Louis to announce a very lucrative contract for McDonnell Douglas to build F-15s for Saudi Arabia.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: In today’s Post- Dispatch, a retired saleswoman, a 75-year-old woman named Marjorie Roberts, asked if she could ask a question of the candidates.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: She said she wanted to register her concern about the lack of a plan to convert our defense-oriented industries into other purposes.

speaker: Mashek
sentence_text: How would you answer her.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I assume she was supportive of the decision on McDonnell Douglas, I assume she was supporting me on the decision to sell those airplanes.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think it’s a good decision–took a little heat for it, but I think it was the correct decision to do.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we worked it out, and indeed we’re moving forward all around the world in a much more peaceful way.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So that one we came away with in creating jobs for the American people.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I would simply say to her, look, take a look at what the president has proposed on job retraining.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: When you cut back on defense spending, some people are going to be thrown out of work.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: If you throw another 50,000 kids on the street because of cutting recklessly in troop levels, you’re going to put a lot more out of work.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I would say to them, look at the job retraining programs that we’re proposing.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Therein is the best answer to her.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And another one is: stimulate investment and savings.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I mean, we’ve got big economic problems, but we are not coming apart at the seams; we’re ready for a recovery.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: With interest rates down and inflation down, the cruelest tax of all, caught up in a global slowdown right now, that that will change if you go with the programs I’ve talked about and if you help with job retraining and education.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I am a firm believer that our America 2000 education problem is the answer–a little longer run; it’s going to take awhile to educate.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But it is a good program.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So her best help for short term is job retraining, if she was thrown out of work at a defense plant.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But tell her it’s not all that gloomy; we’re the US, we faced tough problems before.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Look at the misery index when the Democrats had both the White House and the Congress.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It was just right through the roof.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, we can do better.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And the way to do better is not to tax and spend but to retrain, get that control of the mandatory spending programs.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m much more optimistic about this country than some.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, you have one minute, sir.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Defense industries are going to have to convert to civilian industries.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Many of them are.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And the sooner they start, the sooner they’ll finish.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And there will be a significant transition.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And it’s very important that we not continue to let our industrial base deteriorate.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We had someone who I’m sure regrets said it in the president’s staff said he didn’t care whether we made potato chips or computer chips.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Well, anybody that thinks about it cares a great deal.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Number one, you make more making computer chips than potato chips; and, number 2, 19 out of 20 computer chips that we have in this country now come from Japan.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve given away whole industries.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: So as we phase these industries over, there’s a whole of intellectual talent in these industries.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: A lot of these people in industries can be converted to the industries of tomorrow, and that’s where the high-paying jobs are.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We need to have a very carefully thought through phase-over.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, see, we practice 19th century capitalism.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: The rest of the world practices 21st century capitalism.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I can’t handle that in a minute, but I hope we can get back into it later.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: In the rest of the world, the countries and the businesses would be working together to make this transition in an intelligent way.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor Clinton, you have one minute, sir.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We must have a transition plan to plan to convert from a defense to a domestic economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: No other nation would have cut defense as much as we already have without that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: There are 200,000 people unemployed in California alone because we have cut defense without planning to retrain them and to reinvest in the technologies of the future here at home.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That is what I want to do.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: This administration may say they have a plan, but the truth is they have not even released all the money, the paltry sum of money, that Congress appropriated.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want to take very dollar by which we reduce defense and reinvest it in technologies for the 21st century–in new transportation, in communication, in environmental clean-up technologies.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let’s put the American people to work, and let’s build the kind of high-tech, high-wage, high-growth economy that the American people deserve.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The next question goes to Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot for a 2-minute answer.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It will be asked by Ann.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Ann?

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: Perot, you talked a minute ago about rebuilding the job base.

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: But is it true what Governor Clinton just said, that that means that unemployment will increase, that it will slow the economy?

speaker: Compton

sentence_text: I know it’s tough.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The reason Magic Johnson resigned from the AIDS Commission is because the statement you heard tonight from Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush is the longest and best statement he’s made about it in public.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I am proud of what we did at the Democratic Convention, putting 2 HIV-positive people on the platform, and I am proud of the leadership that I’m going to bring to this country in dealing with the AIDS crisis.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: New question for Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You have 2 minutes to answer, and Ann will ask it.

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: Perot, even if you’ve got what people say are the guts to take on changes in the most popular, the most sacred of the entitlements, Medicare, people say you haven’t a prayer of actually getting anything passed in Washington.

speaker: Compton
sentence_text: Since a president isn’t a lone ranger, how in the world can you make some of those unpopular changes?

sentence_text: Two ways.

sentence_text: Number one, if I get there, it will be a very unusual and historical event — –because the people, not the special interests, put me there.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I will have a unique mandate.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I have said again and again, and this really upsets the establishment in Washington, that we’re going to inform the people in detail on the issues through an electronic town hall so that they really know what’s going on.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They will want to do what’s good for our country.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, all these fellows with thousand-dollar suits and alligator shoes running up and down the halls of Congress that make policy now — the lobbyists, the PAC guys, the foreign lobbyists, and what-have-you, they’ll be over there in the Smithsonian, you know — — because we’re going to get rid of them, and the Congress will be listening to the people.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And the American people are willing to have fair, shared sacrifice.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They’re not as stupid as Washington thinks they are.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: The American people are bright, intelligent, caring, loving people who want a great country for their children and grandchildren.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And they will make those sacrifices.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: So I welcome that challenge, and just watch — — because if the American people send me there, we’ll get it done.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, everybody will faint in Washington.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They’ve never seen anything happen in that town.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: This is a town where the White House says, Congress did it; Congress says, the White House did it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And I’m sitting there and saying, well, who else could be around, you know?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Then when they get off by themselves, they say nobody did it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And yet the cash register’s empty and it used to have our money, the taxpayers’ money, in it, and we didn’t get the results.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: No, we’ll get it done.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, one minute.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Ross, that’s a great speech, but it’s not quite that simple.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I mean, look at the facts.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Both parties in Washington, the president and the Congress, have cut Medicare.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The average senior citizen is spending a higher percentage of income on health care today than they were in 1965, before Medicare came in.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The president’s got another proposal to require them to pay $400 a year more for the next 5 years.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But if you don’t have the guts to control costs by changing the insurance system and taking on the bureaucracies and the regulation of health care in the private and public sector, you can’t fix this problem.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Costs will continue to spiral.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And just remember this, folks.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: A lot of folks on Medicare are out there every day making the choice between food and medicine; not poor enough for Medicare-Medicaid, not wealthy enough to buy their medicine.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’ve met them, people like Mary Annie and Edward Davis in Nashua, New Hampshire.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: All over this country, they cannot even buy medicine.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So let’s be careful.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: When we talk about cutting health care costs, let’s start with the insurance companies and the people that are making a killing instead of making our people healthy.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: One minute, President Bush.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, first place, I’d like to clear up something because every 4 years, the Democrats go around and say, Republicans are going to cut Social Security and Medicare.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They started it again.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m the president that stood up and said, don’t mess with Social Security, and I’m not going to and we haven’t and we are not going to go after the Social Security recipient.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I have one difference with Mr.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Perot on that because I don’t think we need to touch Social Security.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What we do need to do, though, is control the growth of these mandatory programs.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And Ross properly says, okay, there’s some pain in that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But Governor Clinton refuses to touch that, simply refuses.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So what we’ve got to do is control it, let it grow for inflation, let it grow for the amount of new people added, population, and then hold the line.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I believe that is the way you get the deficit down, not by the tax-and-spend program that we hear every 4 years, whether it’s Mondale, Dukakis, whoever else it is.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I just don’t believe we ought to do that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So hold the line on Social Security and put a cap on the growth of the mandatory program.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: New question, it is for Governor Clinton, 2 -minute answer.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Sandy will ask it.

speaker: Vanocur
sentence_text: Governor Clinton, Ann Compton has brought up Medicare.

speaker: Vanocur
sentence_text: I remember in 1965, when Wilbur Mills of Arkansas, the chairman of Ways and Means, was pushing it through the Congress.

speaker: Vanocur
sentence_text: The charge against it was it’s socialized medicine.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush made that charge.

speaker: Vanocur
sentence_text: Well, he served with him 2 years later, in 1967, where I first met him.

sentence_text: The 2nd point, though, is that it is now skyrocketing out of control.

speaker: Vanocur
sentence_text: People want it.

speaker: Vanocur
sentence_text: We say it’s going bonkers.

sentence_text: Is not the Oregon plan applied to Medicaid rationing the proper way to go even though the federal government last August ruled that it violated the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I thought the Oregon plan should at least have been allowed to be tried because at least the people in Oregon were trying to do something.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let me go back to the main point, Sandy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush is trying to run against Lyndon Johnson and Jimmy Carter and everybody in the world but me in this race.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I have proposed a managed competition plan for health care.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I will say again: you cannot control health care costs simply by cutting Medicare.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Look what’s happened.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The federal government has cut Medicare and Medicaid in the last few years, states have cut Medicaid — we’ve done it in Arkansas under budget pressures.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But what happens?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: More and more people get on the rolls as poverty increases.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: If you don’t control the health care costs of the entire system, you cannot get control of it.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Look at our program.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We set up a national ceiling on health care costs tied to inflation and population growth set by health care providers, not by the government.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We provide for managed competition, not government models, in every states.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And we control private and public health care costs.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now, just a few days ago a bipartisan commission of Republicans and Democrats — more Republicans than Democrats — said my plan will save the average family $1200 a year more than the Bush plan will by the year 2000, $2.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: 2 trillion in the next 12 years, $400 billion a year by the end of this decade.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’ve got a plan to control health care costs.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But you can’t just do it by cutting Medicare; you have to take on the insurance companies, the bureaucracies.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And you have to have cost controls, yes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But keep in mind we are spending 30% more on health care than any country in the world, any country, and yet we have 35 million people uninsured, we have no preventing and primary care.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The Oregon plan is a good start if the federal government is going to continue to abandon its responsibilities.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I say if Germany can cover everybody and keep costs under inflation, if Hawaii can cover 98% of their people at lower health care costs than the rest of us, if Rochester, New York, can do it with two-thirds of the cost of the rest of it, America can do it, too.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’m tired of being told we can’t.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I say we can.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We can do better, and we must.

sentence_text: President Bush, one minute.

sentence_text: Well, I don’t have time in 30 seconds, or whatever — a minute — to talk about our health care reform plan.

sentence_text: The Oregon plan made some good sense, but it’s easy to dismiss the concerns of the disabled.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: As president I have to be sure that those waivers, which we’re approving all over the place, are covered under the law.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Maybe we can work it out.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But the Americans with Disabilities Act, speaking about sound and sensible civil rights legislation, was the most foremost piece of legislation passed in modern times, and so we do have something more than a technical problem.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Governor Clinton clicked off the things — he’s going to take on insurance companies and bureaucracies.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He failed to take on somebody else — the malpractice suit people, those that bring these lawsuits against — these frivolous trial lawyers’ lawsuits that are running the costs of medical care up 25 to 50 billion.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And he refuses to put anything, controls, on these crazy lawsuits.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: If you want to help somebody, don’t run the costs up by making doctors have to have 5 or 6 tests where one would do for fear of being sued, or have somebody along the highway not stop to pick up a guy and help him because he’s afraid a trial lawyer will come along and sue him.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’re suing each other too much and caring for each other too little.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, one minute.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We got the most expensive health care system in the world; it ranks behind 15 other nations when we come to life expectancy, and 22 other nations when we come to infant mortality.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: So we don’t have the best.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Pretty simple, folks — if you’re paying more and you don’t have the best, if all else fails go copy the people who have the best who spend less, right?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Well, we can do better than that.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Again, we’ve got plans lying all over the place in Washington.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Nobody ever implements them.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now I’m back to square one.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If you want to stop talking about it and do it, then I’ll be glad to go up there and we’ll get it done.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: But if you just want to keep the music going, just stay traditional this next time around, and 4 years from now you’ll have everybody blaming everybody else for a bad health care system.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Talk is cheap; words are plentiful, deeds are precious.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Let’s get on with it.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And that’s exactly what we’re going to do.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: That was, in fact, the final question and answer.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’re now going to move to closing statements.

sentence_text: Each candidate will have up to 2 minutes.

sentence_text: The order, remember, was determined by drawing, and Mr.

sentence_text: Perot, you are first.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Well, it’s been a privilege to be able to talk to the American people tonight.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I make no bones about it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I love this country.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I love the principle it’s founded on.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I love the people here.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I don’t like to see the country’s principles violated.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I don’t like to see the people in a deteriorating economy in a deteriorating country because our government has lost touch with the people.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: The people in Washington are good people.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We just have a bad system.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve got to change the system.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s time to do it because we have run up so much debt that time is no longer our friend.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve got to put our house in order.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: When you go to bed tonight, look at your children.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Think of their dreams.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Think of your dreams as a child and ask yourself, isn’t it time to stop talking about it?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Isn’t it time to stop creating images?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Isn’t it time to do it?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Aren’t you sick of being treated like an unprogrammed robot?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Every 4 years, they send you all kinds of messages to tell you how to vote and then go back to business as usual.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They told you at the tax and budget summit that if you agreed to a tax increase, we could balance the budget.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They didn’t tell you that that same year they increased spending $1.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: 83 for every dollar we increased taxes.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s Washington in a nutshell right there.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: In the final analysis, I’m doing this for your children when you look at them tonight.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: There’s another group that I feel very close to, and these at the men and women who fought on the battlefield, the children — the families — of the ones who died and the people who left parts of their bodies over there.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’d never ask you to do anything for me, but I owe you this, and I’m doing it for you.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And I can’t tell you what it means to me at these rallies when I see you and you come up and the look in your eyes — and I know how you feel and you know how I feel.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And then I think of the older people who are retired.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They grew up in the Depression.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They fought and won World War II.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We owe you a debt we can never repay you.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And the greatest repayment I can ever give is to recreate the American dream for your children and grandchildren.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’ll give you everything I have, if you want me to do it.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor Clinton, your closing statement.

sentence_text: I’d like to thank the people of St.

sentence_text: Louis and Washington University, the Presidential Debate Commission and all those who made this night possible.

sentence_text: And I’d like to thank those of you who are watching.

sentence_text: Most of all, I’d like to thank all of you who have touched me in some way over this last year, all the thousands of you whom I’ve seen.

sentence_text: I’d like to thank the computer executives and the electronics executives in Silicon Valley, two-thirds of whom are Republicans who said they wanted to sign on to a change in America.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’d like to thank the hundreds of executives who came to Chicago, a third of them Republicans, who said they wanted to change.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’d like to thank the people who’ve started with Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Perot who’ve come on to help our campaign.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’d like to thank all the folks around America that no one ever knows about — the woman that was holding the AIDS baby she adopted in Cedar Rapids, Iowa who asked me to do something more for adoption; the woman who stopped along the road in Wisconsin and wept because her husband had lost his job after 27 years; all the people who are having a tough time and the people who are winning but who know how desperately we need to change.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: This debate tonight has made crystal clear a challenge that is as old as America — the choice between hope and fear, change or more of the same, the courage to move into a new tomorrow or to listen to the crowd who says things could be worse.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush has said some very compelling things tonight that don’t quite square with the record.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: He was president for 3 years before he proposed a health care plan that still hasn’t been sent to Congress in total; three years before an economic plan, and he still didn’t say tonight that that tax bill he vetoed raised taxes only on the rich and gave the rest of you a break — but he vetoed it anyway.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I offer a new direction.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Invest in American jobs, American education, control health care costs, bring this country together again.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want the future of this country to be as bright and brilliant as its past, and it can be if we have the courage to change.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President Bush, your opposing statement.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me tell you a little what it’s like to be president.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: In the Oval Office, you can’t predict what kind of crisis is going to come up.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You have to make tough calls.

sentence_text: You can’t be on one hand this way and one hand another.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You can’t take different positions on these difficult issues.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And then you need a philosophical — I’d call it a philosophical underpinning.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Mine for foreign affairs is democracy and freedom, and look at the dramatic changes around the world.

sentence_text: The Cold War is over.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The Soviet Union is no more and we’re working with a democratic country.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, the Baltics are free.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Take a look at the Middle East.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We had to stand up against a tyrant.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The US came together as we haven’t in many, many years.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we kicked this man out of Kuwait.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And in the process, as a result of that will and that decision and that toughness, we now have ancient enemies talking peace in the Middle East.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Nobody would have dreamed it possible.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think the biggest dividend of making these tough calls is the fact that we are less afraid of nuclear war.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Every parent out there has much less worry that their kids are going to be faced with nuclear holocaust.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: All this is good.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: On the domestic side, what we must do is have change that empowers people — not change for the sake of change, tax and spend.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We don’t need to do that any more.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What we need to do is empower people.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We need to invest and save.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We need to do better in education.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We need to do better in job retraining.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We need to expand our exports, and they’re going very, very well, indeed.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we need to strengthen the American family.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I hope as president that I’ve earned your trust.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve admitted it when I make a mistake, but then I go on and help, try to solve the problems.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I hope I’ve earned your trust because a lot of being president is about trust and character.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I ask for your support for 4 more years to finish this job.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Thank you very, very much.

sentence_text: Don’t go away yet.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: Good evening and welcome to this second of three presidential debates between the major candidates for president of the US.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: The candidates are the Republican nominee, President George Bush, the independent Ross Perot and Governor Bill Clinton, the Democratic nominee.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: My name is Carole Simpson, and I will be the moderator for tonight’s 90-minute debate, which is coming to you from the campus of the University of Richmond in Richmond, Virginia.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: Now, tonight’s program is unlike any other presidential debate in history.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: We’re making history now and it’s pretty exciting.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: An independent polling firm has selected an audience of 209 uncommitted voters from this area.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: The candidates will be asked questions by these voters on a topic of their choosing — anything they want to ask about.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: My job as moderator is to, you know, take care of the questioning, ask questions myself if I think there needs to be continuity and balance, and sometimes I might ask the candidates to respond to what another candidate may have said.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: Now, the format has been agreed to by representatives of both the Republican and Democratic campaigns, and there is no subject matter that is restricted.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: Anything goes.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: We can ask anything.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: After the debate, the candidates will have an opportunity to make a closing statement.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: So, President Bush, I think you said it earlier — let’s get it on.

speaker: Carole Simpson
sentence_text: PRESIDENT GEORGE BUSH: Let’s go.

speaker: Simpson
sentence_text: And I think the first question is over here.

speaker: Audience Question
sentence_text: Yes.

speaker: Audience Question
sentence_text: I’d like to direct my question to Mr.

speaker: Audience Question
sentence_text: Perot.

speaker: Audience Question
sentence_text: What will you do as president to open foreign markets to fair competition from American business and to stop unfair competition here at home from foreign countries so that we can bring jobs back to the US?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s right at the top of my agenda.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve shipped millions of jobs overseas and we have a strange situation because we have a process in Washington where after you’ve served for a while you cash in, become a foreign lobbyist, make $30,000 a month, then take a leave, work on presidential campaigns, make sure you’ve got good contacts and then go back out.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, if you just want to get down to brass tacks, first thing you ought to do is get all these folks who’ve got these 1-way trade agreements that we’ve negotiated over the years and say fellas, we’ll take the same deal we gave you.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And they’ll gridlock right at that point because for example, we’ve got international competitors who simply could not unload their cars off the ships if they had to comply — you see, if it was a 2-way street, just couldn’t do it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We have got to stop sending jobs overseas.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: To those of you in the audience who are business people: pretty simple.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If you’re paying $12, $13, $14 an hour for a factory worker, and you can move your factory south of the border, pay $1 an hour for labor, hire a young — let’s assume you’ve been in business for a long time.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: You’ve got a mature workforce.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Pay $1 an hour for your labor, have no health care — that’s the most expensive single element in making the car.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Have no environmental controls, no pollution controls and no retirement.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And you don’t care about anything but making money.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: There will be a job-sucking sound going south.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If the people send me to Washington the first thing I’ll do is study that 2000-page agreement and make sure it’s a 2-way street.

speaker: Ross Perot

sentence_text: Well, we have come to that position.

sentence_text: Since I became president, 43, 44 countries have gone democratic, no longer totalitarian, no longer living under dictatorship or communist rule.

sentence_text: This is exciting.

sentence_text: New world order to me means freedom and democracy.

sentence_text: I think we will have a continuing responsibility, as the only remaining superpower, to stay involved.

sentence_text: If we pull back in some isolation and say we don’t have to do our share, or more than our share, anymore, I believe you are going to just ask for conflagration that we’ll get involved in the future.

sentence_text: NATO, for example, has kept the peace for many, many years, and I want to see us keep fully staffed in NATO so we’ll continue to guarantee the peace in Europe.

sentence_text: But the exciting thing is, the fear of nuclear war is down.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And you hear all the bad stuff that’s happened on my watch; I hope people will recognize that this is something pretty good for mankind.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I hope they’ll think it’s good that democracy and freedom is on the move.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’re going to stay engaged, as long as I’m president, working to improve things.

sentence_text: We’re doing this all around the world.

sentence_text: And I think I got a good plan to help fix those problems at home.

sentence_text: But because of our leadership, because we didn’t listen to the freeze — the nuclear-freeze group, do you remember — freeze it, back in the late 70s — freeze, don’t touch it; we’re going to lock it in now or else we’ll have war.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So the new world order to me means freedom and democracy, keep engaged, do not pull back into isolation.

sentence_text: And only the US could do this.

sentence_text: Coming out of World War II it made sense.

sentence_text: The mayor up there, on the program.

sentence_text: And the schools that are not chosen are improved — competition does that.

sentence_text: We know better how to do it in California or Texas or wherever it is.

sentence_text: Seventy percent of my state’s money goes to the public schools, and I was really honored when Time magazine said that our schools have shown more improvement than any other state in the country except one other — they named 2 states showing real strides forward in the 80s.

sentence_text: So I care a lot about this, and I’ve spent countless hours in schools.

sentence_text: We live in a world where what you earn depends on what you can learn, where the average 18- year-old will change jobs 8 times in a lifetime and where none of us can promise any of you that what you now do for a living is absolutely safe from now on.

sentence_text: So what should we do?

sentence_text: Number one, under my program we would provide matching funds to states to teach everybody with a job to read in the next 5 years and give everybody with a job the chance to get a high school diploma, in big places on the job.

sentence_text: Number 2, we would provide 2-year apprenticeship programs to high school graduates who don’t go to college.

sentence_text: And community colleges are on the job.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Number three, we’d open the doors to college education to high school graduates without regard to income.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: They could borrow the money and pay it back as a percentage of their income or with a couple of years of service to our nation here at home.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Number 4, we would fully fund the Head Start program to get little kids off to a good start.

sentence_text: And, 5, I would have an aggressive program of school reform, more choices — I favor public schools or these new charter schools — we can talk about that if you want.

sentence_text: I don’t think we should spend tax money on private schools.

sentence_text: But I favor public school choice, and I favor radical decentralization in giving more power to better-trained principals and teachers with parent councils to control their schools.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Those things would revolutionize American education and take us to the top economically.

sentence_text: The other stuff — all the other stuff I mentioned — costs much less than that.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: This is going to take fair, shared sacrifice.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: My plan balances the budget within 6 years.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We didn’t do it faster than that because we didn’t want to disrupt the economy.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We gave it off to a slow start and a fast finish to give the economy time to recover.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: But we faced it and we did it, and we believe it’s fair, shared sacrifice.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: The one thing I have done is lay it squarely on the table in front of the American people.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: You’ve had a number of occasions to see in detail what the plan is, and at least you’ll understand it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I think that’s fundamental in our country, that you know what you’re getting into.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, the word “pain” — one of the other leadership things that’s put on you is that you don’t speak of pain, that you speak of all things — nobody’s going to really have to suffer under your plan.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You’ve heard what Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot has said.

sentence_text: He’s said it’s got — to do the things that you want to do, you can’t do it by just taking the money from the rich.

sentence_text: That’s what the president says as well.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: How do you respond to that?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: They said the numbers don’t add up.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I disagree with both of them.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: For one thing, let me just follow up here.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I disagree with Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Perot that the answer is to raise — put a 50-cent gas tax on the middle class and raise more taxes on the middle class and the working poor than on the wealthy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: His own analysis says that unemployment will be slightly higher in 1995 under his plan than it is today.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And as far as what Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush says, he is the person who raised taxes on the middle class after saying he wouldn’t.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And just this year, Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush vetoed a tax increase on the wealthy that gave middle class tax relief.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: He vetoed middle class tax relief this year.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And furthermore, under this administration, spending has increased more than it has in the last 20 years and he asked Congress to spend more money than it actually spent.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now, it’s hard to out-spend Congress but he tried to for the last 3 years.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So my view is the middle class is the — they’ve been suffering, Jim.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now, should people pay more for Medicare if they can?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Yes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Should they pay more for Social Security if they get more out of it than they paid in, they’re upper income people?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Yes.

sentence_text: But look what’s happened to the middle class.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Middle class Americans are working harder for less money than they were making ten years ago and they’re paying higher taxes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The tax burden on them has not gone down.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It has gone up.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I don’t think the answer is to slow the economy down more, drive unemployment up more and undermine the health of the private sector.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The answer is to invest and grow this economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That’s what works in other countries and that’s what’ll work here.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: As a practical matter, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, do you agree with the governor when he says that the middle class, the taxes on the middle class — do your numbers agree that the taxes on the middle class have gone up during the last —

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think everybody’s paying too much taxes.

sentence_text: He refers to one tax increase.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me remind you it was a Democratic tax increase, and I didn’t want to do it and I went along with it.

sentence_text: And I said I make a mistake.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: If I make a mistake, I admit it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s quite different than some.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I think that’s the American way.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think everyone’s paying too much, but I think this idea that you can go out and — then he hits me for vetoing a tax bill.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Yes, I did.

sentence_text: And the American taxpayer ought to be glad they have a president to stand up to a spending Congress.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We remember what it was like when we had a spending president and a spending Congress, and interest rates — who remembers that?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They were at 21.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: 5% under Jimmy Carter, and inflation was 15.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We don’t want to go back to that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so yes, everybody’s taxed too much and I want to get the taxes down, but not by signing a tax bill that’s gonna raise taxes on people.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, when you said just then that you admit your mistakes and you looked at Governor Clinton and said — what mistake is it that you want him to admit to?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, the record in Arkansas.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I mean, look at it, and that’s what we’re asking America to have?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Now look, he says Arkansas’s a poor state.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They are.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But in almost every category they’re lagging.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ll give you an example.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He talks about all the jobs he’s created in one or 2 years.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Over the last ten years since he’s been governor, they’re 30% behind, 30% — they’re 30% of the national average.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: On pay for teachers, on all these categories, Arkansas is right near the very bottom.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You haven’t heard me mention this before, but we’re getting close now and I think it’s about time I start putting things in perspective.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I’m going to do that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s not dirty campaigning because he’s been talking about my record for a half a year here, 11 months here.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So we’ve got to do that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I gotta get it in perspective.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What’s his mistake?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Admit it, that Arkansas is doing very, very badly against any standard — environment, support for police officers, whatever it is.
