sentence_text: Governor, is that true?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush’s Bureau of Labor Statistics says that Arkansas ranks first in the country in the growth of new jobs this year, first.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: This year.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: 4th in manufacturing jobs, 4th in the reduction of poverty, 4th in income increase.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Over the last 10 years we’ve created manufacturing jobs much more rapidly than the national average.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Over the last 5 years our income has grown more rapidly than the national average.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We are 2nd in tax burden, the 2nd lowest tax burden in the country.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We have the lowest per capita state and local spending in the country.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’re low spending, low tax burden.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We dramatically increased investment and our jobs are growing.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I wish America had that kind of record and I think most people looking at us tonight would like it if we had more jobs and a lower spending burden on the government.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, if you were sitting at home now and just heard this exchange about Arkansas, who would you believe?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I grew up 5 blocks from Arkansas.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Let’s put it in perspective.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s a beautiful state.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s a fairly rural state.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It has a population less than Chicago or Los Angeles, about the size of Dallas and Forth Worth combined.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: So I think probably we’re making a mistake night after night after night to cast the nation’s future on a unit that small.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Why is that a mistake?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s irrelevant.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: What he did as governor of Arkansas is irrelevant?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: No, no, no, but I could say, you know, that I ran a small grocery store on the corner, therefore I extrapolate that into the fact that I can run Wal-Mart.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s not true.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I can’t protect an Arkansas company, you notice there, Governor.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Perot, with all respect, I think it is highly relevant, and I think that a 4-billion dollar budget of state and federal funds is not all that small, and I think the fact that I took a state that was one of the poorest states in the country and had been for 153 years and tried my best to modernize its economy and to make the kind of changes that have generated support from people like the presidents of Apple Computer and Hewlett-Packard and some of the biggest companies in this country, 24 retired generals and admirals and hundreds of business executives, are highly relevant.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And, you know, I’m frankly amazed that since you grew up 5 blocks from there you would think that what goes on in that state is irrelevant.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think it’s been pretty impressive.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: It’s not —

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And the people who have jobs — The people who have jobs and educations and opportunities that didn’t have them 10 years ago don’t think it’s irrelevant at all; they think it’s highly relevant and they wish the rest of the country had them.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t have a dog in this fight, but I’d like to get in on this.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Well, you think it’s relevant.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Governor Clinton has to operate under a balanced budget amendment — he has to do it, that is the law.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’d like to see a balanced budget amendment for America, to protect the American taxpayers, and then that would discipline not only the executive branch but the spending Congress, the Congress that’s been in control of one party, his party, for 38 years.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we almost had it done.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And that institution, the House of Representatives — everyone is yelling “Clean House!

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: ” One of the reasons is we almost had it done, and the speaker — a very, able, decent fellow, I might add — but he twisted the arms of some of the sponsors of that legislation and had them change their vote.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What’s relevant here is that tool, that discipline, that he has to live by in Arkansas, and I’d like it for the American people.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I want the line-item veto.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I want a check-off, so if the Congress can’t do it, let people check off their income tax, 10% of it, to compel the government to cut spending.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And if they can’t do it, if the Congress can’t do it, let them then have to do it across the board.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s what we call a sequester.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s the discipline we need, and I’m working for that — to protect the American taxpayer against the big spenders.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, let’s move to some of the leadership concerns that have been voiced about you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And they relate to something you said in your closing statement in Richmond the other night about the president being the manager of crises.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And that relates to an earlier criticism, that you began to focus on the economy, on health care, on racial divisions in this country, only after they became crises.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Is that a fair criticism?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Jim, I don’t think that’s a fair shot.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I hear it — I hear it echoed by political opponents.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I don’t think it’s fair.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we’ve been fighting from day one to do something about the inner cities.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m for enterprise zones.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I have had it in every single proposal I’ve sent to the Congress.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And now we hear a lot of talk, oh, well, we all want enterprise zones, and yet the House and the Senate can’t send it down without loading it up with a lot of, you know, these Christmas tree ornaments they put on the legislation.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think in racial harmony that I’m a laggard on that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve been speaking out since day 1.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve gotten the Americans for Disabilities Act, which I think is one of the foremost pieces of civil rights legislation.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And yes, it took me to veto 2 civil rights quota bills because I don’t believe in quotas, and I don’t think the American people believe in quotas.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I beat back the Congress on that, and then we passed a decent civil rights bill that offers guarantees against discrimination in employment.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And that is good.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve spoken out over and over again against antisemitism and racism, and I think my record as a member of Congress speaks for itself on that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What was the other part of it?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Well, it’s just that — you’ve spoken to it.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I mean, but the idea, not so much in specifics, but that it has to be a crisis before it gets your attention.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think that’s true at all.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think that’s true, but you know, let others fire away on it.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you think that’s true, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’d like to just talk about issues, and so —

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You don’t think this is an issue?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Well, no, but the point is that’s a subjective thing.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: See, the subjective thing is when does President Bush react?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And it would be very difficult for me to answer that in any short period of time.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Well, then, let’s phrase — I’ll phrase it differently, then.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: He said the other night in his closing words in Richmond that one of the key things that he believes the American people should decide between — among the 3 of you is who they want in charge if this country gets to a crisis.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Now, that’s what he said, and the rap on the president is that it’s only crisis time that he focuses on some of these things.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: So my question to you — we’re going to talk about you in a minute — — my question to you —

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I thought you’d forgotten I was here.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: No, no, no, no, no.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But my question to you is, so — if you have nothing to say about it, fine, I’ll go to Governor Clinton, but —

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I will let the American people decide that.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I would rather not critique the 2 candidates.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, what do you think?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The only thing I would say about that is, I think that on the economy, Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Bush said for a long time there was no recession, and then said it would be better to do nothing than to have a compromise effort with the Congress.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: He really didn’t have a new economic program until over 1300 days into his presidency, and not all of his health care initiative has been presented to the Congress even now.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think it’s important to elect a president who is committed to getting this economy going again, and who realizes we have to abandon trickle-down economics and put the American people first again, and who will send programs to the Congress in the first hundred days to deal with the critical issues that America is crying out for leadership on — jobs, incomes, the health care crisis, the need to control the economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Those things deserve to be dealt with from day one.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I will deal with them from day 1.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: They will be my first priority, not my election year concern.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I think you’re overlooking that we have had major accomplishments in the first term.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But if you’re talking about protecting the taxpayer against his friends in the US Congress, go back to what it was like when you had a Democratic president and a Democratic Congress.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You don’t have to go back to Herbert Hoover.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Go back to Jimmy Carter, and interest rates were 21%, inflation was 15%.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: The misery index — unemployment and inflation added together — it was invented by the Democrats — went right through the roof.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve cut it in half.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And all you hear about is how bad things are.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You know, remember the question, are you better off?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, is a homebuyer better off he can refinance the home, because interest rates are down?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Is the senior citizen better off because inflation is not wiping out their family’s savings?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I think they are.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Is the guy out of work better off?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Of course he’s not, but he’s not gonna be better off if we grow the government, if we invest, as Governor Clinton says, invest in more government.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You’ve got to free up the private sector.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: You’ve got to let small businesses have more incentives.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: For 3 months — quarters I’ve been fighting, 3 quarters been fighting to get the Congress to pass some incentives for small business.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Capital gains, investment tax allowance, credit for first- time homebuyers.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And it’s blocked by the Congress.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And then if a little of it comes my way, they load it up with Christmas trees and tax increases, and I have to stand up and favor the taxpayer.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I have to — we have to talk about Ross Perot now or he’ll get me, I’m sure.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, on this issue that I have raised at the very beginning and we’ve been talking about, which is leadership, as president of the US, it concerns — my reading of it, at least, my concerns about you, as expressed by folks in the polls and other places, it goes like this.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You had a problem with General Motors.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You took your $750 million and you left.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You had a problem in the spring and summer about some personal hits that you took as a potential candidate for president of the US and you walked out.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Does that say anything relevant to how you would function as president of the US?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I think the General Motors thing is very relevant.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I did everything I could to get General Motors to face its problems in the mid-’80s while it was still financially strong.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They just wouldn’t do it, and everybody now knows the terrible price they’re paying by waiting until it’s obvious to the brain-dead that they have problems.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, hundreds, thousands of good, decent people, whole cities up here in this state are adversely impacted because they would not move in a timely way.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Our government is that point now.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: The thing that I am in this race for is to tap the American people on the shoulder and to say to every single one of you, fix it while we’re still relatively strong.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If you have a heart problem, you don’t wait till a heart attack to address it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: So the General Motors experience is relevant.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: At the point when I could not get them to address those problems, I had created so much stress in the board, who wanted to just keep the Lawrence Welk music going, that they asked to buy my remaining shares.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I sold them my remaining shares.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They went their way.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I went my way because it was obvious we had a complete disagreement about what should be done with the company.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: But let’s take my life in perspective.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Again and again, on complex, difficult tasks, I have stayed the course.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: When I was asked by our government to do the POW project, within a year the Vietnamese had sent people into Canada to make arrangements to have me and my family killed.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And I had 5 small children, and my family and I decided we would stay the course, and we lived with that problem for 3 years.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Then I got into the Texas War on Drugs program and the big-time drug dealers got all upset.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Then when I had 2 people imprisoned in Iran, I could have left them there.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I could have rationalized it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We went over, we got them out, we brought them back home.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And since then, for years, I have lived with the burden of the Middle East, where it’s eye for an eye and tooth for a tooth country, in terms of their unhappiness with the fact that I was successful in that effort.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Again and again and again, in the middle of the night, at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, my government has called me to take extraordinary steps for Americans in distress, and again and again and again I have responded.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And I didn’t wilt and I didn’t quit.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, what happened in July we’ve covered again and again and again.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: But I think in terms of the American people’s concern about my commitment, I’m here tonight, folks; I never quit supporting you as you put me on the ballot in the other 26 states; and when you asked me to come back in, I came back in.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And talk about not quitting, I’m spending my money on this campaign; the 2 parties are spending your money, taxpayer money.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I put my wallet on the table for you and your children.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Over $60 million at least will go into this campaign to leave the American dream to you and your children, to get this country straightened out, because if anybody owes it to you, I do.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’ve lived the American dream; I’d like for your children to be able to live it, too.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, do you have a response to the staying- the-course question about Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I don’t have any criticism of Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Perot.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think what I’d like to talk about a minute, since you’re asking the question, is the General Motors issue.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I don’t think there’s any question that the automobile executives made some errors in the 1980s, but I also think we should look at how much productivity has increased lately, how much labor has done to increase productivity and how much management has done.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And we’re still losing a lot of auto jobs, in my judgment, because we don’t have a national economic strategy that will build the industrial base of this country.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Just today I met with the presidents and the vice presidents of the Willow Run union here, near here.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: They both said they were Vietnam veterans supporting me because I had an economic program to put them back to work.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We need an investment incentive to modernize plant and equipment; we’ve got to control the health care costs for those people — otherwise we can’t keep the manufacturing jobs here; and we need a tough trade policy that is fair, that insists on open markets in return for open markets.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We ought to have a strategy that will build the economic and industrial base.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So I think Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Perot was right in questioning the management practices.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But they didn’t have much of a partner in government here as compared with the policies the Germans and the Japanese followed, and I believe we can do better.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That’s one of the things I want to change.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I know that we can grow manufacturing jobs.

speaker: Bill Clinton

sentence_text: I felt very strongly about it, and I didn’t want to go at the time.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s easy to say in retrospect I would have done something differently.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: President Lincoln opposed the war and there were people who said maybe he shouldn’t be president, but I think he made us a pretty good president in wartime.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’ve had a lot of other presidents who didn’t wear their country’s uniform who had to order our young soldiers into battle, including President Wilson and President Roosevelt.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So the answer is I could do that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I wouldn’t relish doing it but I wouldn’t shrink from it.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think that the president has to be prepared to use the power of the nation when our vital interests are threatened, when our treaty commitments are at stake, when we know that something has to be done that is in the national interest, and that is a part of being president.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Could I do it?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Yes, I could.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: A reminder now.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’re back on the St.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Louis rules, which means that the governor had his answer and then each of you will have 1 minute to respond.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I’ve expressed my heartfelt difference with Governor Clinton on organizing demonstrations while in a foreign land against your country, when young ghetto kids have been drafted and are dying.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: My argument with him on — the question was about the draft — is that there’s this same pattern.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: In New Hampshire Senator Kerrey said you ought to level, you ought to tell the truth about it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: On April 17 he said he’d bring out all the records on the draft.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: They have not been forthcoming.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He got a deferment or he didn’t.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: He got a notice or he didn’t.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think it’s this pattern that troubles me, more than the draft.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: A lot of decent, honorable people felt as he did on the draft.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But it’s this pattern.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And again, you might be able to make amendments all the time, Governor, but you’ve got to, as president, you can’t be on all these different sides, and you can’t have this pattern of saying well, I did this or I didn’t, then the facts come out and you change it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s my big difference with him on the draft.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: It wasn’t failing to serve.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Your minute is up, sir.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Yes, sir.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Helen?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, 1 minute.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’ve spent my whole adult life very close to the military.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I feel very strongly about the people who go into battle for our country.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I appreciate their idealism, their sacrifices.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Appreciate the sacrifices their families make.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s been displayed again and again in a very tangible way.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I look on this as history.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I don’t look on it personally as relevant, and I consider it really a waste of time tonight, when you consider the issues that face our country right now.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

sentence_text: The next question goes to President Bush and Gene Gibbons will ask it.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Gene.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: GENE GIBBONS : Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, you keep saying that you made a mistake in agreeing to a tax increase to get the 1990 budget deal with Congress.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But if you hadn’t gotten that deal, you would have either had to get repeal of the Gramm-Rudman Deficit Control Act or cut defense spending drastically at a time when the country was building up for the gulf war, and decimate domestic discretionary spending, including such things as air traffic control.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: If you had it to do all over again, sir, which of those alternatives would you choose?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I wouldn’t have taken any of the alternatives.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe that — I believe I made a mistake.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I did it for the very reasons you say.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: There was one good thing that came out of that budget agreement, and that is we put a cap on discretionary spending.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: One-third of the president’s budget is at the president’s discretion, or really the Congress, since they appropriate every dime and tell a president how to spend every dime.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve put a cap on the growth of all that spending, and that’s good and that’s helped.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But I was wrong because I thought the tax compromise, going along with 1 Democratic tax increase, would help the economy.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I see no evidence that it has done it.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So what would I have done?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: What should I have done?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I should have held out for a better deal that would have protected the taxpayer and not ended up doing what we had to do, or what I thought at the time would help.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So I made a mistake, and I — you know, the difference, I think, is that I knew at the time I was going to take a lot of political flak.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I knew we’d have somebody out there yelling “read my lips”, and I did it because I thought it was right.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And I made a mistake.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s quite different than taking a position where you know it’s best for you.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: That wasn’t best for me and I knew it in the very beginning.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I thought it would be better for the country than it was.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So there we are.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Perot, 1 minute.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: 101 in leadership is be accountable for what you do.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Let’s go back to the tax and budget summit briefly.

sentence_text: Nobody ever told the American people that we increased spending $1.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: 83 for every dollar of taxes raised.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s absolutely unconscionable.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Both parties carry a huge blame for that on their shoulders.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: This was not a way to pay down the deficit.

sentence_text: This was a trick on the American people.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s not leadership.

sentence_text: Let’s go back in terms of accepting responsibility for your actions.

sentence_text: If you create Saddam Hussein, over a 10-year period, using billions of dollars of US taxpayer money, step up to the plate and say it was a mistake.

sentence_text: If you create Noriega, using taxpayer money, step up to the plate and say it was a mistake.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If you can’t get your act together to pick him up one day when a Panamanian major has kidnapped him and a special forces team is 400 yards away and it’s a stroll across the park to get him, and if you can’t get your act together, at least pick up the Panamanian major, who they then killed, step up to the plate and admit it was a mistake.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s leadership, folks.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, leaders will always make mistakes.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve created, and I’m not aiming at any one person here, I’m aiming at our government — nobody takes responsibility for anything.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: We’ve gotta change that.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I’m taking responsibility for saying your time’s up.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’m watching the lights.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

sentence_text: Governor Clinton, 1 minute, sir.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The mistake that was made was making the “read my lips” promise in the first place just to get elected, knowing what the size of the deficit was.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Knowing what the size of the deficit was, knowing there was no plan to control health care costs and knowing that we did not have a strategy to get real economic growth back into this economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The choices were not good then.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think at the time, the mistake that was made was signing off on the deal late on Saturday night in the middle of the night.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That’s just what the president did when he vetoed the Family Leave Act.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think what he should have done is gone before the American people on the front end and said listen, I made a commitment and it was wrong.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I made a mistake because I couldn’t have foreseen these circumstances and this is the best deal we can work out at the time.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: He said it was in the public interest at the time and most everybody who was involved in it, I guess, thought it was.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The real mistake was the “read my lips” promise in the first place.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: You just can’t promise something like that just to get elected if you know there’s a good chance that circumstances may overtake you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, Mr.

sentence_text: You have a 2-minute answer, and it will be asked by Susan Rook.

sentence_text: Perot, you’ve talked about going to Washington to do what the people who run this country want you to do.

sentence_text: But it is the president’s duty to lead, and often lead alone.

sentence_text: In order to lead, you first have to use the White House as a bully pulpit and lead; then you have to develop consensus or you can’t get anything done, and that’s where we are now.

sentence_text: How do you get anything done when you’ve got all of these political action committees, all of these thousands of registered lobbyists — 40,000 registered lobbyists, 23,000 special interest groups — and the list goes on and on and on.

sentence_text: And the average citizen out here is just working hard every day.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: You’ve got to go to the people.

sentence_text: I just love the fact that everybody, particularly in the media, goes bonkers over the town hall.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I guess it’s because you will lose your right to tell them what to think.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: The point is, they’ll get to decide what to think.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I love the fact that people will listen to a guy with a bad accent and a poor presentation manner talking about flip charts for 30 minutes, because they want the details.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: See, all the folks up there at the top said the attention span of the American people is no more than 5 minutes, they won’t watch it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They’re thirsty for it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: You want to have a new program in this country.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: If you get grassroots America excited about it, and if they tap Congress on the shoulder and say do it, Charlie, it’ll happen.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: And that’s a whole lot different from these fellows running up and down the halls whispering in their ears now and promising campaign funds for the next election if they do it.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Now, I think that’s going back to where we started.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: That’s having a government from the people.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I think that’s the essence of leadership, rather than cutting deals in dark rooms in Washington.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor Clinton, 1 minute.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Well, I believe in the town hall meetings; they started with my campaign in New Hampshire.

sentence_text: And I think Ross Perot has done a good job in having them.

sentence_text: And I, as you know, pushed for the debate to include the 209 American citizens who were part of it in Richmond a few days ago.

sentence_text: I’ve done a lot of them, and I’ll continue to do them as president.

sentence_text: But I’d also like to point out that I haven’t been part of what we’re criticizing in Washington tonight.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Of the 3 of us, I have balanced a government budget 12 times, I have offered and passed campaign finance reform, offered, pushed for and passed in public referendum lobbyist restrictions, done the kinds of things you have to do to get legislators together not only to establish consensus but to challenge them to change.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And in 12 years as governor I guess I’ve taken on every interest group there was in my state at one time or another to fight for change.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It can be done.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That’s why I tried to be so specific in this campaign to have a mandate, if elected, so that Congress will know what the American people have voted for.

sentence_text: President Bush, 1 minute.

sentence_text: My favorite bumper sticker, though, is: Annoy the Media.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Re-elect President Bush.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Sorry, Helen.

sentence_text: I’m going to pay for this later on.

sentence_text: Look, you have to build a consensus, but in some things — Ross mentioned Saddam Hussein.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Yes, we tried, and, yes, we failed to bring him into the family of nations; he had the 4th largest army.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But then when he moved against Kuwait, I said this will not stand.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And it’s hard to build a consensus.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We went to the UN, we made historic resolutions up there, the whole world was united, our Congress was dragging its feet.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Governor Clinton said, well, I might have been with the minority, let sanctions work — but I guess I would have voted with the majority.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: A president can’t do that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Sometimes he has to act.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And in this case I’m glad we did, because if we had let sanctions work and tried to build a consensus on that, Saddam Hussein today would be in Saudi Arabia controlling the world’s oil supply, and he would be there maybe with a nuclear weapon.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We busted the 4th largest army, and we did it through leadership.

sentence_text: All right, we’re going to go on to another subject now, and the subject is priorities.

sentence_text: I think the woman that works with me, Rose Zamaria, is about as tough as a boot out there and makes some discipline and protects the taxpayer.

sentence_text: Look at our Cabinet.

sentence_text: You talk about somebody strong.

sentence_text: Jim Baker’s a man.

sentence_text: Yeah, I plead guilty to that.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But look who’s around with him there.

sentence_text: I mean, this is a little defensive on your part, Susan, to be honest with you.

sentence_text: We’ve got a very good record appointing women to high positions and positions of trust, and I’m not defensive at all about it.

sentence_text: What we got to do is keep working, as the Labor Dept is doing a first-class job on, to break down discrimination, to break down the glass ceiling.

sentence_text: And I am not apologetic at all about our record with women.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve got, I think — you know, you think about women in government, I think about women in business.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: Why not try to help them with my small business program to build some incentives into the system?

sentence_text: I think we’re making progress here.

sentence_text: You got a lot of women running for office.

sentence_text: As I said the other night, I hope a lot of them lose because they’re liberal Democrats — — and we don’t need more of them in the Senate or more of them in the House.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: But nevertheless, they’re out there.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we got some very good Republican women running.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: So we’re making dramatic progress.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: Perot, 1 minute.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Well, I come from the computer business, and everybody knows the women are more talented than the men.

sentence_text: And the rest of my minute, I want to make a very brief comment here in terms of Saddam Hussein.

sentence_text: Well, where are the papers?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: Where are the papers?

sentence_text: And talk to any head of any of those key committees in the Senate.

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: They will not let them see the written instructions given to Ambassador Glaspie.

sentence_text: And I suggest that in a free society owned by the people, the American people ought to know what we told Ambassador Glaspie to tell Saddam Hussein, because we spent a lot of money and risked lives and lost lives in that effort, and did not accomplish most of our objectives.

sentence_text: We got Kuwait back to the emir but he’s still not his nuclear, his chemical, his bacteriological and he’s still over there, right?

speaker: Ross Perot
sentence_text: I’d like to see those written instructions.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: President, just to make sure that everybody knows what’s going on here, when you responded directly to Mr.

sentence_text: Now —

sentence_text: All right.

sentence_text: They went to extraordinary sick lengths, and I just found it amusing that they would take 2 or 3 cases where I was involved in lawsuits and would engage an investigator — the lawyers would engage an investigator, which is common.

sentence_text: Now, let’s go back to Saddam Hussein.

sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: Also I got a philosophical difference.

sentence_text: I got to watch the clock here.

sentence_text: I don’t think we’re a declining nation.

sentence_text: The whole world has had economic problems.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: We’re doing better than a lot of the countries in the world.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’re going to lead the way out of this economic recession across this world and economic slowdown here at home.

sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: It’s not trickle down economics.

sentence_text: It’s been tried for 12 years and it’s failed.

sentence_text: More people are working harder for less, 100,000 people a month losing their health insurance, unemployment going up, our economy slowing down.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We can do better.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And it’s not tax and spend economics.

sentence_text: It’s invest and grow, put our people first, control health care costs and provide basic health care to all Americans, have an education system 2nd to none and revitalize the private economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That is my commitment to you.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It is the kind of change that can open up a whole new world of opportunities to America as we enter the last decade of this century and move towards the 21st century.

sentence_text: I want a country where people who work hard and play by the rules are rewarded, not punished.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want a country where people are coming together across the lines of race and region and income.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I know we can do better.

sentence_text: Thank you very much.

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: And so the question is, who will safeguard this nation, who will safeguard our people and our children?

speaker: George H. W. Bush
sentence_text: I need your support, I ask for your vote.

speaker: George H. W. Bush

sentence_text: All right, thank you, Mr.

sentence_text: Good evening from the Bushnell Theatre in Hartford, Connecticut.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I’m Jim Lehrer of the News Hour on PBS.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Welcome to the first of the 1996 Presidential debates between President Bill Clinton, the Democratic nominee, and Senator Bob Dole, the Republican nominee.

sentence_text: Now, to the opening statements and to President Clinton.

sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

sentence_text: Thank you, Jim.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And thank you to the people of Hartford, our hosts.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want to begin by saying again how much I respect Senator Dole and his record of public service and how hard I will try to make this campaign and this debate one of ideas, not insults.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Four years ago I ran for president at a time of high unemployment and rising frustration.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I wanted to turn this country around with a program of opportunity for all, responsibility from all, and an American community where everybody has a role to play.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I wanted a government that was smaller and less bureaucratic to help people make the most of their own lives.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Four years ago you took me on faith.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now there’s a record: Ten and a half million more jobs, rising incomes, falling crime rates and welfare rolls, a strong America at peace.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We are better off than we were four years ago.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let’s keep it going.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We cut the deficit by 60 percent.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now, let’s balance the budget and protect Medicare, Medicaid, education and the environment.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We cut taxes for 15 million working Americans.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now let’s pass the tax cuts for education and child rearing, help with medical emergencies, and buying a home.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We passed family and medical leave.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now let’s expand it so more people can succeed as parents and in the work force.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We passed 100,000 police, the assault weapons ban, the Brady Bill.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now let’s keep going by finishing the work of putting the police on the street and tackling juvenile gangs.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We passed welfare reform.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now let’s move a million people from welfare to work.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And most important, let’s make education our highest priority so that every eight-year-old will be able to read, every 12-year-old can log onto the Internet, every 18-year-old can go to college.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We can build that bridge to the 21st Century.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I look forward to discussing exactly how we’re going to do it.

sentence_text: Senator Dole, two minutes.

sentence_text: Thank you.

sentence_text: Thank you, Mr.

sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: There is a major difference in your view of the role of the Federal government and that of Senator Dole.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: How would you define the difference?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Well, Jim, I believe that the Federal government should give people the tools and try to establish the conditions in which they can make the most of their own lives.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That, to me, is the key.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And that leads me to some different conclusions from Senator Dole.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: For example, we have reduced the size of the Federal government to its smallest size in 30 years.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We reduced more regulations, eliminated more programs than my two Republican predecessors.

sentence_text: But I have worked hard for things like the Family and Medical Leave Law, the Brady Bill, the assault weapons ban, the program to put 100,000 police on the street.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: All of these are programs that Senator Dole opposed that I supported, because I felt they were a legitimate effort to help people make the most of their own lives.

sentence_text: I’ve worked hard to help families impart values to their own children.

sentence_text: I supported the V-chip so that parents would be able to control what their kids watch on television when they’re young, along with the ratings systems for television and educational television.

sentence_text: I supported strong action against the tobacco companies to stop the marketing, advertising, and sale of tobacco to young people.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I supported a big increase in the safe and drug-free schools program.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: These were areas on which Senator Dole and I differed, but I believed they were the right areas for America to be acting together as one country to help individuals and families make the most of their own lives and raise their kids with good values and a good future.

sentence_text: Where possible, I want to give power back to the states and back to the people.

sentence_text: That’s my difference with the President.

sentence_text: He noted a few, but there are others.

sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: I trust the people.

sentence_text: Our government is smaller and less bureaucratic and has given more authority to the states than its two predecessors under Republican presidents.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But I do believe we have to help our people get ready to succeed in the 21st Century.

sentence_text: Senator Dole, the President said in his opening statement we are better off today than we were four years ago.

sentence_text: When Senator Dole made that remark about all the elitists, all the young elitists in the administration, one of the young men who works for me who grew up in a house trailer looked at me and said, Mr.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: President, I know how you grew up, who is he talking about.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And you know this liberal charge, that’s what their party always drags out when they get in a tight race.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s sort of their golden oldie, you know.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s a record they think they can play that everybody loves to hear.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I just don’t think that dog will hunt this time.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The American people should make up their own mind.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Here’s the record: We cut deficit four years in a row for the first time before the Civil War — I mean, before World War II, and maybe before the Civil War, too.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’ve got ten and a half million new jobs; we’ve got record numbers of those new small businesses.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’ve made every one of them eligible for a tax cut.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’ve got declining crime rates, two million fewer people on welfare rolls before welfare reform passed, and a 50 percent increase in child support and a crime bill with 60 death penalties and 100,000 police and the assault weapons ban.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The American people can make up their mind about whether that’s a liberal record or a record that’s good for America.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Liberal, conservative, you put whatever label you want on it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, I think it’s pretty liberal, I’ll put that label on it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You take a look at all the programs you’ve advocated, Mr.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Thank goodness we had a Republican Congress there.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The first thing you did when you came into office was set up the stimulus package, said we’ve got a little pork we want to scatter around America, $16 billion.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And even some in your own party couldn’t buy that.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I remember talking by the telephone.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’m not even certain you were too excited about that.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I won’t, I never repeat what I’ve talked to the President about.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: In any event, we saved the taxpayers $16 billion.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And then came some other program, and then came healthcare, and then came the tax increase and a lot of these things stopped in 1994 because then the Congress changed, and I think we’ve done a good job.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, if you’re not a liberal, describe your political philosophy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I believe that the purpose of politics is to give people the tools to make the most of their own lives; to reinforce the values of opportunity and responsibility, and to build a sense of community so we’re all working together.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I don’t believe in discrimination.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I believe you can protect the environment and grow the economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I believe that we have to do these things with a government that’s smaller and less bureaucratic, but that we have to do them nonetheless.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s inconvenient for Senator Dole, but the truth is I’ve reduced the size of government more than my Republican predecessors.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I did stop them, I admit that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I sure stopped their budget.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Their budget cut enforcement for the Environmental Protection Agency by a third.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It cut funds to clean up toxic waste dumps with 10 million of our kids still living within four miles of a toxic waste dump, by a third.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It ended the principle that the polluters should pay for those toxic waste dumps unless it was very recent.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Their budget weakened our support for education.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: $30 billion, even cut funds for scholarships and college loans.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Their budget cut $270 billion in Medicare and, finally, their budget withdrew the national guarantee of healthcare to poor children, families with children with handicaps, the elderly in nursing homes, poor pregnant women.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It was wrong for the country and calling it conservative won’t make it right.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It was a bad decision for America and would have been bad for our future if I hadn’t stopped it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, the President can define himself in any way he wants, but I think we have to look at the record.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Go back to the time he was, what, Texas director for George McGovern.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: George McGovern is a friend of mine, so I don’t mean, but he was a liberal, proud liberal.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’ve just finished reading a book, I think it’s called — what is it called, what is it, The Demise of the Democratic Party by Ronald Cardash or something talking about all the liberal influences in the administration.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Whether it’s organized labor or whether it’s the Hollywood elite or whether some of the media elite or whether it’s the labor unions or whatever.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And so I think you take a look at it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The bottom line is this: I think the American people, thought he’d recite all these bills and all these things, they want to know what’s going to happen to them.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: They’ve all got a lot of anxieties out there.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Did anybody complain when you raised taxes?

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Did anybody go out and ask the people, how are you going to pay the extra money?

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: That’s why we want an economic package.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We want the government to pinch their pennies for a change instead of the people pinching their pennies.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: That’s what our message is to the people watching.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Not all this back and forth, you voted this way, you voted that way, we want a better America as we go into the next century.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The way you get a better America is to balance the budget and protect Medicare, Medicaid, education and the environment; to give a targeted tax cut — and let me talk about the education tax cut — to let people have a $10,000 deduction for the cost of college tuition in any year, any kind of college tuition; to give families a tax credit, a dollar for dollar reduction in their taxes for the cost of a typical community college so we can open that to everybody.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And then to let people save in an IRA and withdraw from it without a tax penalty for education, home buying or medical expenses, that’s the right way to go into the 21st Century, balance the budget and cut taxes, not balloon with this $550 billion tax scheme.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator Dole, we’ve talked mostly now about differences between the two of you that relate to policy issues and that sort of thing.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Are there also significant differences in the more personal area that are relevant to this election?

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Let me say first, on the President’s promise for another tax cut.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I mean, I’ve told people as I’ve traveled around, all of you that got the tax cut he promised last time, vote for him in ’96 and not many hands go up.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So the question is, would you buy a used election promise from my opponent.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The people want economic reform.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: They’re having a hard time making ends meet.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You’ve got one parent working for the government, the other parent working for the family.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is important business.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is about getting the economy moving again.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is about American jobs and opportunities.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s about the government, as I said before, pinching its pennies for a change instead of the poor taxpayer.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: When they raise your taxes nobody runs around asking people where are you going to get the extra money.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I think the government can do better.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Are there personal differences?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: That are relevant to this.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, my blood pressure is lower, my weight, my cholesterol, but I will not make health an issue in this campaign.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So I think he’s a bit taller than I am.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But I think there are personal differences.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I mean, I’m not I don’t like to get into personal matters.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: As far as I’m concerned, this is a campaign about issues.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s about my vision for America and about his liberal vision for America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And not about personal things.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You know, I think his liberal vision is a thing of the past.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I know he wants to disown it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I wouldn’t want to be a liberal either, Mr.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President, but you’re stuck with it because that’s your record, that’s your record in Arkansas: The biggest tax increase in history.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The biggest crime increase in history, the biggest drug increase in history in Arkansas.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Well, just for the record, when I was governor we had the lowest — second lowest tax burden of any state in the country, the highest job growth rate of any state when I ran for president and were widely recognized for a lot of other advances.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But the important thing is, what are we going to do now.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think a targeted tax cut is better for our future, targeted to education and child rearing, with the rest of the education plan, hooking up all of our classrooms to the Internet by the year 2000.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Making sure we’ve got an army of reading volunteers, trained people to teach with parents and teachers so that our eight year olds can learn to read.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Investing in our environment.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Cleaning up two-thirds of the worst toxic waste dumps.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Those plans are better than this $550 billion tax scheme.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now, remember, folks, even Senator Dole’s campaign co-chair here, Senator D’Amato, says he’s got to cut Medicare to pay for this.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Everybody who’s looked at it, 500 economists, seven Nobel prize winners, say it’s bad for the economy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s going to blow a hole in the deficit It’s going to raise taxes on nine million people and require bigger cuts than the one I vetoed.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Our plan is better, it will take us into the future with a growing economy and healthier families.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, I’m really encouraged to know of your renewed friendship with Al D’Amato, and I know he appreciates it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You didn’t even have tax cuts in your budget, Mr.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President, the first two years you were president.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It wasn’t until we had a Republican Congress you even thought about, you talked about tax cuts.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Getting back to personal differences, I think, Jim, if you are a little more specific, but I think the President could clarify one thing tonight and that’s the question of pardons.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I know you talked about it on the Jim, with Jim Lehrer on the PBS show.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I’ve never discussed Whitewater, as I’ve told you personally.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’m not discussing Whitewater now.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But I am discussing the power the President has to grant pardons.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And hopefully in the next segment you could lay that to rest.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Well, first of all, you know, he made that remark about Senator D’Amato.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: He’s arranged for me to spend a lot more time with Senator D’Amato in the last couple years so I’m more familiar with his comments than I used to be.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let me say what I’ve said already about this pardon issue.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: This is an issue they’ve brought up.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s under, there’s been no consideration of it, no discussion of it.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I will tell you this: I will not give anyone special treatment and I will strictly adhere to the law.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And that is what every president has done, as far as I know, in the past but what every other president’s has done.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: This is something I take seriously and that’s my position.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But it seems to me the president shouldn’t have any comment at all.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Particularly where it’s someone where you’ve had business dealings.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I mean, you may be sending a signal.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I don’t know, I’m not questioning anybody.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But as a President of the United States, when somebody asks you about pardons, you say no comment, period.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I think he made a mistake.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I think when you make a mistake, you say I made a mistake.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But apparently his position hasn’t changed.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: If there are other specific areas, but beyond that I haven’t gotten into any of these things, as the President knows.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We’ve had that discussion.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And again I know Senator D’Amato I think may have had a hearing or two on Whitewater, I can’t remember, but he’s not my general chairman, he’s a friend of mine.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And so is Senator Kennedy a friend of yours.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: You bet.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I remember one day on the floor I said now, gentlemen, let me tax your memories, and Kennedy jumped up and said, why haven’t we thought of that before.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You know, so one of your liberal friends.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Thank you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, 30 seconds.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: No comment.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: What’s the subject matter?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator Dole, if you could single out one thing that you would like for the voters to have in their mind about President Clinton on a policy matter or a personal matter, what would it be?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Something to know about him, understand it and appreciate it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: See, if I say anything it’s going to be misconstrued.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I don’t think there is even a race between the two, it’s about our vision for America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I happen to like President Clinton personally.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’m addressing him all evening as Mr.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I said in 1992 he didn’t extend that courtesy to President Bush.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But I respect the presidency.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’ve served under a number of presidents.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: They all have their strengths and they all have their weaknesses.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So I’d rather talk about my strengths.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I think I have my strengths and I think the best thing going for Bob Dole is that Bob Dole keeps his word.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s a question between trust and fear, and I would say, I think, Mr.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President, about all you’ve got going in this campaign is fear.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You’re spending millions and millions of dollars in negative ads frightening senior citizens.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I know this to be a fact because I had one tell me last week, Senator don’t cut my Medicare.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’m trying to save your Medicare, just as I rescued Social Security with a bipartisan commission.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I have relatives on Medicare.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I used to sign welfare checks for my grandparents.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I know all about poverty and all about need and all about taking care of people, and that’s been my career in the United States Senate.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I’ll keep my word on the economic package.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: If I couldn’t cut taxes and balance the budget the same time, I wouldn’t look at you in the eye in your living room or wherever you might be and say that this is good for America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: People will tell you who served with Bob Dole, agree or disagree, he kept his word.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: That’s what this race is all about.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’d like the American people to know that I have worked very hard to be on their side.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And to move this country forward and we’re better off than we were four years ago.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But the most important thing is my plan for the 21st Century is a better plan.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: A targeted tax cut, a real commitment to educational reform.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: A deep commitment to making welfare reform work with incentives to the private sector to move people from welfare to work.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now we have to create those jobs, now that we’re requiring people to go do work.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: A commitment to continuing step-by-step healthcare reform with the next step helping people who are between jobs to access healthcare and not lose it just because they are out of work for a while.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: A commitment to grow the economy while protecting the environment.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That’s what I’d like them to know about me; that I’ve gotten up every day and worked for the American people and worked so that their children could have their dreams come true.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I believe we’ve got the results to show we’re on the right track.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The most important thing is, I believe we’ve got the right ideas for the future.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I like, I like Senator Dole, you can probably tell we like each other.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We just see the world in different ways.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And you folks out there are going to have to choose who you think is right.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, I’d say the first homeless bill in the Senate was the Dole-Byrd Byrd-Dole bill, I can’t remember who was in control then.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I remember working with Senator Ribicoff from Connecticut on the Hospice program.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We now have 2500 hospices.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: As I said, I’ve worked all my life when I was in the Congress.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I left on June 11th because I wanted the American people to know that I was willing to give up something.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President Clinton ran for governor in 1990 and said he’s going to fill out his term, but he didn’t.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: He’s president so I guess it’s a little better deal.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But I wanted the American people to know I was willing to give up something.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I wasn’t just getting more power and more power.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So I rolled the dice, I put my career on the line because I really believe the future of America is on the line.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We can give you all these numbers, they don’t mean a thing.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: If you are out of work, you have nothing to eat or you can’t have medical care, or you’re holding a crack baby in your arms right now, what do you do next?

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You know, America’s best days are ahead of us.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’ve seen the tough times, I know they can be better and I’ll lead America to a brighter future.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, what do you say to Senator Dole’s point that this election is about keeping one’s word?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let’s look at that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: When I ran for president, I said we’d cut the deficit in half in four years; we cut it by 60 percent.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I said that our economic plan would produce eight million jobs, we have ten and a half million new jobs.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We’re number one in autos again, record numbers of new small businesses.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I said we’d put, pass a crime bill that would put 100,000 police on the street, ban assault weapons, and deal with the problems that ought to be dealt with with capital punishment, including capital punishment for drug kingpins, and we did that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I said we would change the way welfare works, and even before the bill passed we’d moved nearly two million people from welfare to work, working with states and communities.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I said we’d get tougher with child support and child support enforcement’s up 50 percent.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I said that I would work for tax relief for middle class Americans.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The deficit was bigger than I thought it was going to be.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think they’re better off, all of us are, that we got the interest rates down and the deficit down.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Republicans talk about it, but we’re the first the first administration in anybody’s lifetime looking at this program to bring that deficit down four years in a row.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We still gave tax cuts to 15 million working Americans, and now I’ve got a plan that’s been out there for two years, it could have been passed already, but instead the Republicans shut the government down to try to force their budget and their plan on me, and I couldn’t take that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But we’ll get the rest of that tax relief.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And so I think when you look at those results, you know the plan I’ve laid out for the future has a very good chance of being enacted if you’ll give me a chance to build that bridge to the 21st Century.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, there he goes again, that line has been used before, I mean, exaggerating all the things that he did.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: He didn’t do all these things.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Let’s take all these four years in a row.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: He came in with a high growth rate, the 1990 budget agreement, which some, you know, didn’t like, had some very tough cost controls, put a lot of pressure on Congress.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The S & L crisis was over, they’re starting to sell assets, all that money was coming in.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And he cut defense an extra $60 billion, threw a lot of people out of work.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: He talks about a smaller government.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: There are actually more people in government except for people in defense related jobs.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: They’re gone.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The government’s bigger than it was when President Kennedy was around, even though he says it’s not.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: In addition, Republican Congress cut $53 billion.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So let’s just, let’s give credit where credit is due.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Governor Engler of Michigan cut taxes 21 times, created a lot of new jobs.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So did Governor Thompson, so did Governor Rowland.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: A lot of people ought to deserve credit, Mr.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: When I’m President of the United States we’re going to have a governors’ council and we’re going to work directly with the governors to get power back to the people and back to the states.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I think a lot of people deserve credit and I’ve tried to give it to them.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But I believe that my plan is better than Senator Dole’s ill-advised $550 billion scheme which I’ll say again will blow a hole in the deficit.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Our plan will balance the budget, grow the economy, preserve the environment, and invest in education.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We have the right approach for the future and looks at the results.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It is not midnight in America, Senator.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We are better off than we were four years ago.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: That’s the last question, the last answer.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Let’s go now to the closing statements.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, you’re first.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Two minutes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Well, first, Jim, let me thank you and thank you, Senator Dole, and thank you, ladies and gentlemen, all of you listening tonight for the chance you’ve given us to appear.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want to say in the beginning that I am profoundly grateful for the chance that you have given me to serve as president for the last four years.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I never could have dreamed anything like this would come my way in life, and I’ve done my best to be faithful to the charge you’ve given me.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’m proud of the fact that America is stronger and more prosperous and more secure than we were four years ago.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I’m glad we’re going in the right direction.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And I’ve done my best tonight to lay out my plans for going forward to an even better future in the next century.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’d like to leave you with the thought that the things I do as president are basically driven by the people whose lives I have seen affected by what does or doesn’t happen in this country.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The auto worker in Toledo who was unemployed when I was elected and now has a great job because we’re number one in auto production again.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: All the people I’ve met who used to be on welfare who are now working and raising their children.

speaker: Bill Clinton

sentence_text: But we’d like to have a Social Security fund that has about 70 years of life instead of about 30 years of life.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: What we have to do is simply to make some adjustments to take account of the fact that the baby boomers, people like me, are bigger in number than the people that went just before us and the people that come just after us.

sentence_text: And I think what we’ll plainly do is what we did in 1983 when Senator Dole served, and this is something I think he did a good job on when he served on the Social Security commission and they made some modest changes in Social Security to make sure that it would be alive and well into the 21st century.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And we will do that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s obvious that there are certain things that have to be done and there are 50 or 60 different options, and a bipartisan commission to take it out of politics, will make recommendations and build support for the people.

sentence_text: Medicare is different.

sentence_text: Medicare needs help now.

sentence_text: I have proposed a budget which would put ten years on the life of the Medicare trust fund.

sentence_text: That’s more than it’s had a lot of the time in the last years.

sentence_text: It would save a lot of money through more managed care, by giving more options, more preventative care and lowering the inflation rate and the prices we’re paying providers without having the kind of big premium increases and out-of-pocket costs that the budget I vetoed would provide.

sentence_text: Then that would give us ten years to do with Medicare what we’re going to do with Social Security; have a bipartisan group look at what we have to do to save it when the baby boomers retire.
