sentence_text: But now we can, we ought to pass this budget now and put ten years on it right away so no one has to worry about it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But we got to be more aggressive.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Once you have a policy, then you have to go out and be aggressive and enforce that policy.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: There are American jobs that are being lost.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is what Ross Perot complains about.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I’d say to the Reform party, take a look at the Republican party.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We’re the reform party, and we’re going to make things better, and one of the things we’re going to do is stop exporting jobs.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let me say again, we’ve had over 200 separate trade agreements in the last four years.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: By far, the largest number in American history — not just the big ones you read about, but a lot of smaller ones.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And now what we have to do is to focus on those things we’re real good at and make sure we’re getting a fair deal.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We just had a pretty serious dispute with China because they were copying our CDs, and costing thousands of jobs in places like California.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So we have — as we said, if you want to keep doing business and selling your products over here, you’re going to have to quit pirating our CDs, and they agreed to do things and verify that they had done it, which will make the problem much better.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: There is not a simple answer.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: You have to work on this day in and day out, every month ,every year, every issue, to make sure that we have not only free trade but fair trade.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I’m proud that we’re better off on that than we were four years ago.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: The next question is for Senator Dole — in this section.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Yes, sir?

speaker: Mr. Kite
sentence_text: Rod Kite, minister.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Hi, Rod.

speaker: Mr. Kite
sentence_text: This great nation has been established by the founding fathers who possessed a very strong Christian belief in godly principles.

speaker: Mr. Kite
sentence_text: If elected president of the United States, what could you do to return this nation to these basic principles?

speaker: Mr. Kite
sentence_text: And also, do you feel that the president — the office of president has the responsibility to set the role example to inspire our young people?

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well no doubt about it, our founding fathers had a great deal of wisdom.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: In addition to what you mentioned, they also were concerned about this all-powerful central government in Washington, D.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: , that’d in effect confiscate your property, so — I carry it in my pocket — I can’t pull it out or I’d violate the rules — a copy of the Tenth Amendment which says we ought to return power to the states and the people, the people here.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You ought to make more decisions.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Honor, duty, and country, that’s what America is all about.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Certainly the President of the United States, the highest office in the world, the most important office in the world, has a responsibility to young people, as we talked about earlier.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: To everyone.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: By example.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And when it comes to public ethics, he has a responsibility.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And you have 30-some in your administration, either left or being investigated or in jail or whatever, then you’ve got an ethical problem.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is public ethics; I’m not talking about private ethics.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Talking about public ethics.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: When you have 900 files gathered up by some guy who is a bouncer in a bar and hired a security officer to collect files, in Watergate — I know a person who went to jail for looking at one file, one FBI file.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: There are 900 sequestered in the White House.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: People like you.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Why should they be rifling through your files?

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The president has a great responsibility.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: That’s one that I understand and certainly will carry out.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: This is the most religious, great country in history.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And yet, interestingly enough, we have the most religious freedom of any country in the world, including the freedom not to believe.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And now we have all these people just up the road in Los Angeles County, we have people from 150 different racial and ethnic groups and tons of different religions, but the fundamental tenets of virtually every religion are the same, and what I try to do is to support policies that would respect religion and then help parents inculcate those values to their children.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let me very briefly give you some examples.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: One of my proudest moments was signing the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, that says the government has got to bend over backwards before we interfere with religious practice.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So I changed the Justice Department’s effort to get a church to pay back a man tithe, because he was bankrupt when he gave it.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I have supported character education programs in our schools, drug-free schools programs.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I supported giving parents a V-chip on their television so if they don’t want their young kids to watch things they shouldn’t watch, they wouldn’t have to.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That is the kind of thing we have to do, give people like you and our families the power to give those values to our children.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I think it’s — before I came in, my wife and daughter and I had a prayer.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Because it’s God’s will, whatever happens.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s God’s will, it’ll happen.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: The constitutional amendment for voluntary prayer in school, in my view would be a great idea.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I support it; the president opposes it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It seems to me the president, whoever the president may be, this is one of his highest responsibilities.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: People look to the President of the United States more than any other person in America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And that’s the way it’s always been, and that’s the way it always will be.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: This is our last question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It goes to President Clinton and it’s from this section.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Yes, ma’am.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: My name is Yvette Dube and I too am a minister.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: I’m with the Universal Metropolitan Community Churches.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: President Clinton, perhaps you can help me with something tonight.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: I heard Mr.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: Dole say several times “all of us together,” and when he was asked if he would support equal rights and employment for gay and lesbian people, you said that you favored that, and he said that he did not believe in special rights.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: And I thought the question was equal rights for all people.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: And I don’t understand why people are using the term “special rights” when the question is “equal rights.

speaker: Ms. Dube
sentence_text: ” Could you help me in understanding that?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want to answer your question, but let me say one other thing.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We don’t need a constitutional amendment for kids to pray, and what I did was to have the justice department and the education department for the first time ever issue a set of guidelines that we gave to every school in America, saying that children could not be interfered with in religious advocacy when they were praying, when they were doing whatever they could do under the constitution, just because they were on a public school ground, and I think anyone who’s experienced this will tell you that our administration has done more than any in years to clarify the freedom of religion in the public square, including in the public schools.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Now, I think I have to let Senator Dole speak for himself.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It wouldn’t be fair for me to do that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I would wind up — I mean, it’s the last question and I would mischaracterize it to try to make you happy.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let me tell you what I feel.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We have a lot of differences in our country, and some of us believe that other people’s decisions are wrong, even immoral.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: But under our constitution, if you show up tomorrow and obey the law, and you work hard and you do what you’re supposed to do, you are entitled to equal treatment.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: That’s the way the system works.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: All over the world, people are being torn apart — Bosnia, the Middle East, Northern Ireland, Rwanda, Burundi — you name it — because of all their differences.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We still have some of that hatred inside us.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: You see it in the church burnings.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And one of the things I’ve tried hardest to do is to tell the American people that we have to get beyond that, we have to understand that we’re stronger when we unite around shared values instead of being divided by our differences.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator Dole.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, I hope I made my answer clear.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I said I’m opposed to discrimination.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: You know we’ve suffered discrimination in the disability community.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: There are 43 million of us.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I can recall cases where people would cross the street rather than meet somebody in a wheelchair.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So we want to end discrimination.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I think that answers itself.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: No discrimination in America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We’ve made that clear.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I would just say that it seems to me that that’s the way it ought to be.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We shouldn’t discriminate — race, color, whatever — life-style, disability.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And we’re all proud of it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But we’re not there yet.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: What we need is good, strong leadership going in the next century.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I’m sorry we didn’t have a foreign policy question, because just this week Secretary Christopher said, “Well, we really didn’t know much the first couple of years about foreign policy.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: ” Now that was quite an admission.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It underscores what I had to say in the Hartford debate, that there is really no foreign policy in this administration.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s sort of ad hoc, just whatever comes up, we’ll deal with it.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Unfortunately, we didn’t have more questions on that.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Let me say again, there is no more important responsibility for the president than to say if you believe in the constitution, the Bill of Rights, and the Declaration of Independence, that’s all we need to know.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And you can be part of our America and you can walk across that bridge to the 21st century with us.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And we are not well served when we attack each other in a kind of ad hominem way.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It doesn’t create jobs.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It doesn’t educate children.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It doesn’t solve problems.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: We need to be disagreeing on ideas, honestly, and talking about the future.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The future will be the greatest time in this country’s history if we can beat this division that is bedeviling the whole rest of the world.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Now we go to the closing statement.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator Dole, you’re first.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Two minutes, sir.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Well, let me thank everybody here at the University and, Jim, thank you.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: All the people who may still be watching or viewing.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is what it’s all about.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s not about me.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s not about President Clinton.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s about the process.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s about selecting a president of the United States.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: So we have our differences.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We should have our differences.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Mentioned other parties.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: They have their differences.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We all agreed it would be a pretty dull place.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We should have more debates.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Maybe we will have another debate on the economy.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But I would just say this.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: This is the highest honor that I have ever had in my life, to think that somebody from Russell, Kansas, somebody who grew up living in a basement apartment, someone whose parents didn’t finish high school, somebody who spent about 39 months in hospitals after World War II, someone who uses a buttonhook every day to get dressed.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Somebody who understands that there’re real Americans out there with real problems, whether soccer moms, or the single parents, the families or the seniors, or people with disabilities, whoever it may be.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: There are some very fundamental differences in this campaign.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President Clinton opposes term limits, President Clinton opposes a constitutional amendment to balance the budget.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: President Clinton opposes voluntary prayer amendment.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Opposes an amendment to protect the flag of the United States of America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: People give their lives.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Couple of service men here.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: They sacrifice, they give everything for America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We ought to protect the American flag with a constitutional amendment.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: But beyond that we need to address the economy.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I will just say my time is running out here.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: It’s a very proud moment for me.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: What I want the voters to do is to make a decision.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I want them to be proud of their vote in the years ahead.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Proud that they voted for the right candidate.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Proud that they voted hopefully for me.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: And I’ll just make you one promise, my word is good.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Democrats and Republicans said Bob Dole’s word is good.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I keep my word.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: I promise you the economy is going to get better.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We’re going to have a good economic package.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: We’re going into the next century a better America.

speaker: Bob Dole
sentence_text: Thank you.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Thank you, Jim.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And thank you, ladies and gentlemen, and all the people who are watching.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: One thing I would like to say is I agree with what Senator Dole said.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: It’s a remarkable thing in a country like ours, a man who grew up in Russell, Kansas, and one who was born to a widowed mother in Hope, Arkansas, could wind up running for president.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Could have a chance to serve as president.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: First thing I want to say is thank you for giving me the chance to be president.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: This election is about two different visions about how we should go into the 21st Century.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Would we be better off as I believe, working together to give each other the tools we need to make the most of our God-given potential, or are we better off saying, you’re on your own?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Would we be better off building that bridge to the future together so we can all walk across it or saying you can get across yourself?

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: If you don’t agree — leave this room with anything else tonight and if the people watching us don’t leave with anything else, I hope you will leave with this.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: This is a real important election.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: The world is changing dramatically in how we work and how we live, how we relate to each other, huge changes.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: And the decisions we make will have enormous practical consequences.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: So we’ve talked about our responsibility tonight.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: I want to talk about your responsibility, and your responsibility.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Your responsibility is to show up on November the 5th.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Because you’re going to decide whether we’re going to balance the budget now, but protect Medicare, Medicaid, education and the environment.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: You will decide whether we’re going to keep fighting crime with a Brady Bill, assault weapons and finish putting those 100,000 police.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Whether we’re going to move a million people from welfare to work.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Whether we’re going to give our families more protection for their kids against drugs and tobacco and gangs and guns.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Whether we’re going to give our children a world-class education.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Where every eight-year-old can read.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Every 12-year-old can log in on the Internet.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Every 18-year-old can go to college.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: If we do those things we will build that bridge to the 21st Century and the greatest country in history will be even greater.

speaker: Bill Clinton
sentence_text: Thank you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Thank you, Senator.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: This concludes — this is the last of the three 1996 presidential and vice-presidential debates.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Good evening from the Clark Athletic Center at the University of Massachusetts in Boston.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: I’m Jim Lehrer of the NewsHour on PBS, and I welcome you to the first of three 90-minute debates between the Democratic candidate for president, Vice President Al Gore and the Republican candidate, Governor George W.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Bush of Texas.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: The debates are sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates and they will be conducted within formats and rules agreed to between the commission and the two campaigns.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: We’ll have the candidates at podiums.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: No answer to a question can exceed two minutes.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Rebuttal is limited to one minute.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: But as moderator I have the option to follow up and to extend any particular give and take another three-and-a-half minutes.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Even then, no single answer can exceed two minutes.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: The candidates under their rules may not question each other directly.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: There will be no opening statements, but each candidate may have up to two minutes for a closing statement.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: The questions and the subjects were chosen by me alone.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: I have told no one from the two campaigns, or the Commission, or anyone else involved what they are.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: There is a small audience in the hall tonight.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: They are not here to participate, only to listen.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: I have asked, and they have agreed, to remain silent for the next 90 minutes.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Except for right now, when they will applaud as we welcome the two candidates, Governor Bush and Vice President Gore.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: And now the first question as determined by a flip of a coin, it goes to Vice President Gore.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Vice President Gore, you have questioned whether Governor Bush has the experience to be President of the United States.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What exactly do you mean?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Well, Jim, first of all, I would like to thank the sponsors of this debate and the people of Boston for hosting the debate.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I would like to thank Governor Bush for participating, and I would like to say I’m happy to be here with Tipper and our family.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I have actually not questioned Governor Bush’s experience.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I have questioned his proposals.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And here is why.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think this is a very important moment for our country.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We have achieved extraordinary prosperity.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And in this election, America has to make an important choice.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Will we use our prosperity to enrich not just the few, but all of our families?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I believe we have to make the right and responsible choices.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: If I’m entrusted with the presidency, here are the choices that I will make.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I will balance the budget every year.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I will pay down the national debt.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I will put Medicare and Social Security in a lockbox and protect them.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I will cut taxes for middle-class families.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I believe it’s important to resist the temptation to squander our surplus.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: If we make the right choices, we can have a prosperity that endures and enriches all of our people.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: If I’m entrusted with the presidency, I will help parents and strengthen families because, you know, if we have prosperity that grows and grows, we still won’t be successful unless we strengthen families by, for example, ensuring that children can always go to schools that are safe.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: By giving parents the tools to protect their children against cultural pollution.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I will make sure that we invest in our country and our families.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I mean investing in education, health care, the environment, and middle-class tax cuts and retirement security.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: That is my agenda and that is why I think that it’s not just a question of experience.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Governor Bush, one minute rebuttal.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, we do come from different places.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I come from West Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The governor is the chief executive officer.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We know how to set agendas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think you’ll find the difference reflected in our budgets.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to take one-half of the surplus and dedicate it to Social Security.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: One-quarter of the surplus for important projects, and I want to send one-quarter of the surplus back to the people who pay the bills.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I want everybody who pays taxes to have their tax rates cut.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that stands in contrast to my worthy opponent’s plan, which will increase the size of government dramatically.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: His plan is three times larger than President Clinton’s proposed plan eight years ago.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It is a plan that will have 200 new programs — expanded programs and creates 20,000 new bureaucrats.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It it empowers Washington.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Tonight youâ€™re going to hear that my passion and my vision is to empower Americans to be able to make decisions for themselves in their own lives.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: So I take it by your answer, then, Mr.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Vice President, that in an interview recently with the “New York Times” when you said that you questioned whether or not Governor Bush has experience enough to be president, you were talking about strictly policy differences.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Yes, Jim.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I said that his tax cut plan, for example, raises the question of whether it’s the right choice for the country.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And let me give you an example of what I mean.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Under Governor Bush’s tax cut proposal, he would spend more money on tax cuts for the wealthiest 1% than all of the new spending that he proposes for education, health care, prescription drugs and national defense all combined.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, I think those are the wrong priorities.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, under my proposal, for every dollar that I propose in spending for things like education and health care, I will put another dollar into middle class tax cuts.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And for every dollar that I spend in those two categories, I’ll put $2 toward paying down the national debt.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think it’s very important to keep the debt going down and completely eliminate it.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I also think it’s very important to go to the next stage of welfare reform.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Our country has cut the welfare rolls in half.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I fought hard from my days in the Senate and as vice president to cut the welfare rolls and we’ve moved millions of people in America into good jobs.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But it’s now time for the next stage of welfare reform, and include fathers and not only mothers.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: We’re going to get a lot of those.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me just say that obviously tonight we’re going to hear some phony numbers about what I think and what we ought to do.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: People need to know that over the next ten years it is going to be $25 trillion of revenue that comes into our treasurey and we anticipate spending $21 trillion.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And my plan say why don’t we pass 1.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: 3 trillion of that back to the people who pay the bills?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Surely we can afford 5% of the $25 trillion that are coming into the treasury to the hard working people that pay the bills.

speaker: George W. Bush

sentence_text: I just think, Jim, that this is an absolutely unique period in world history.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: First, a couple of follow-ups from the vice presidential debate last week.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Vice President Gore, would you support or sign, as president, a federal law banning racial profiling by police and other authorities at all levels of government?

sentence_text: Yes, I would.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The only thing an executive order can accomplish is to ban it in federal law enforcement agencies, but I would also support a law in the Congress that would have the effect of doing the same thing.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I just — I think that racial profiling is a serious problem.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I remember when the stories first came out about the stops in New Jersey by the highway patrol there.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I know it’s been going on a long time.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: In some ways this is just a new label for something that has been going on for years.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I have to confess that it was the first time that I really focused on it in a new way.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I was surprised at the extent of it.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I think we’ve now got so many examples around the country that we really have to find ways to end this.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Imagine what it — what it is like for someone to be singled out unfairly, unjustly, and feel the unfair force of law simply because of race or ethnicity.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, that runs counter to what the United States of America is all about at our core.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And it’s not an easy problem to solve.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But if I am entrusted with the presidency, it will be the first Civil Rights Act of the 21st century.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Yeah, I can’t imagine what it would be like to be singled out because of race and stopped and harassed.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s just flat wrong, and that’s not what America is all about.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so we ought to do everything we can to end racial profiling.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: One of my concerns, though, is I don’t want to federalize the local police forces.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to — obviously in the egregious cases we need to enforce civil rights law, but we need to make sure that internal affairs divisions at the local level do their job and be given a chance to do their job.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe in local control of governments, and obviously if they don’t there needs to be a consequence at the federal level.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But it’s very important that we not overstep our bounds and I think most people — most police officers are good, dedicated, honorable citizens who are doing their job, putting their lives at risk who aren’t bigoted or aren’t prejudiced.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think they ought to be held guilty.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I do think we need to find out where racial profiling occurs and do something about it and say to the local folks, get it done.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And if you can’t, there will be a federal consequence.

sentence_text: And that could be a federal law?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Yeah.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: And you would agree?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I would agree.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I also agree that most police officers, of course, are doing a good job and hate this practice also.

sentence_text: I talked to an African-American police officer in Springfield, Massachusetts not long ago who raised this question and said that in his opinion one of the biggest solutions is in the training.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And not only the training in police procedures, but human relations.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I think that racial profiling is part of a larger issue of how we deal with race in America.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And as for singling people out because of race, you know, James Byrd was singled out because of his race in Texas.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And other Americans have been singled out because of their race or ethnicity.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And that’s why I think we can embody our values by passing a hate crimes law.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think these crimes are different.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think they’re different because they’re based on prejudice and hatred, which gives rise to crimes that have not just a single victim, but they’re intended to stigmatize and dehumanize a whole group of people.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: You have a different view of that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: No, I don’t, really.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: On hate crimes laws?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: No.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve got one in Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And guess what?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The three men who murdered James Byrd, guess what’s going to happen to them?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They’re going to be put to death.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: A jury found them guilty.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s going to be hard to punish them any worse after they get put to death.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And it’s the right cause.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s the right decision.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Secondly, there is other forms of racial profiling that goes on in America.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Arab-Americans are racially profiled in what is called secret evidence.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: People are stopped, and we have to do something about that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My friend, Senator Spencer Abraham of Michigan, is pushing a law to make sure that Arab-Americans are treated with respect.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So racial profiling isn’t just an issue at local police forces.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s an issue throughout our society.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And as we become a diverse society, we’re going to have to deal with it more and more.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe, though — I believe, as sure as I’m sitting here, that most Americans really care.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They’re tolerant people.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They’re good, tolerant people.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s the very few that create most of the crises, and we just have to find them and deal with them.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What — if you become president, Governor, are there other areas, racial problem areas, that you would deal with as president involving discrimination?

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Like you said, Arab-Americans, but also Hispanics, Asians, as well as Blacks in this country.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me tell you where the biggest discrimination comes.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: In public education when we just move children through the schools.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My friend, Phyllis Hunter, is here.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: She had one of the greatest lines of all lines.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: She said, reading is the new civil right.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: She’s right.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And to make sure our society is as hopeful as it possibly can be, every single child in America must be educated.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I mean every child.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It starts with making sure every child learns to read.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: K-2 diagnostic testing so we know whether or not there’s a deficiency.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Curriculum that works and phonics needs to be an integral part of our reading curriculum.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Intensive reading laboratories, teacher retraining.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I mean, there needs to be a wholesale effort against racial profiling, which is illiterate children.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We can do better in our public schools.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We can close an achievement gap, and it starts with making sure we have strong accountability, Jim.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: One of the cornerstones of reform, and good reform, is to measure.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Because when you measure you can ask the question, do they know?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Is anybody being profiled?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Is anybody being discriminated against?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It becomes a tool, a corrective tool.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I believe the federal government must say that if you receive any money, any money from the federal government for disadvantaged children, for example, you must show us whether or not the children are learning.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And if they are, fine.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And if they’re not, there has to be a consequence.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so to make sure we end up getting rid of basic structural prejudice is education.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: There is nothing more prejudiced than not educating a child.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Vice President Gore, what would be on your racial discrimination elimination list as president?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Well, I think we need tough enforcement of the civil rights laws.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think we still need affirmative action.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I would pass a hate crimes law, as I said, and I guess I had misunderstood the governor’s previous position.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The Byrd family may have a misunderstanding of it in Texas also.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I would like to shift, if I could, to the big issue of education.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Hold on one second.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What is the misunderstanding?

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Let’s clear this up.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Well, I had thought that there was a controversy at the end of the legislative session where the hate crimes law in Texas was — failed, and that the Byrd family, among others, asked you to support it, Governor, and it died in committee for lack of support.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Am I wrong about that?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, you don’t realize we have a hate crimes statute?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We do.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: GORE: I’m talking about the one that was proposed to deal —

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: No — well, what the Vice President must not understand is we’ve got a hate crimes bill in Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And secondly, the people that murdered Mr.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Byrd got the ultimate punishment.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The death penalty.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: They were prosecuted under the murder laws, were they not, in Texas?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: In this case when you murder somebody it’s hate, Jim.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The crime is hate.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And they got the ultimate punishment.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m not exactly sure how you enhance the penalty any more than the death penalty.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We happen to have a statute on the books that’s a hate crimes statute in Texas.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: May I respond?

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Sure.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I don’t want to jump in.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I may have been misled by all the news reports about this matter, because the law that was proposed in Texas that had the support of the Byrd family and a whole lot of people in Texas did, in fact, die in committee.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: There may be some other statute that was already on the books, but certainly the advocates of the hate crimes law felt that a tough new law was needed.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And it’s important, Jim, not only — not just because of Texas, but because this mirrors the national controversy.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: There is pending now in the Congress a national hate crimes law because of James Byrd, because of Matthew Shepard, who was crucified on a split rail fence by bigots, and because of others.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And that law has died in committee also because of the same kind of opposition.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: And you would support that bill.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Absolutely.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Would you support a national hate crimes law?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I would support the Orrin Hatch version of it, not the Senator Kennedy version.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But let me say to you, Mr.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Vice President, we’re happy with our laws on our books.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That bill did — there was another bill that did die in committee.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I want to repeat, if you have a state that fully supports the law like we do in Texas, we’re going to go after all crime.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’re going to make sure people get punished for the crime.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And in this case we can’t enhance the penalty any more than putting those three thugs to death.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that’s what’s gonna happen in the State of Texas.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: New subject, new question.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Another vice presidential debate follow-up.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Governor, both Senator Lieberman and Secretary Cheney said they were sympathetically rethinking their views on same sex relationships.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What’s your position on that?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m not for gay marriage.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think marriage is a sacred institution between a man and a woman.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I appreciated the way the administration signed the Defense of Marriage Act.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I presume the Vice President supported it when the President signed that bill and supports it now.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I think marriage is a sacred institution.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m going to be respectful for people who may disagree with me.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve had a record of doing so in the State of Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve been a person that had been called a uniter, not a divider, because I accept other people’s points of view.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I feel strongly that marriage should be between a man and a woman.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Vice President Gore?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I agree with that, and I did support that law.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I think that we should find a way to allow some kind of civic unions, and I basically agree with Dick Cheney and Joe Lieberman.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I think the three of us have one view and the Governor has another view.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Is that right?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m not sure what kind of view he’s describing to me.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I can just tell you, I’m a person who respects other people.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I respect their — I respect — on the one hand he says he agrees with me and then he says he doesn’t.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m not sure where he’s coming from.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I will be a tolerant person.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve been a tolerant person all my life.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I just happen to believe strongly that marriage is between a man and a woman.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Do you believe in general terms that gays and lesbians should have the same rights as other Americans?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Yes.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think they ought to have special rights, but I think they ought to have the same rights.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Well, there’s a law pending called the Employment Non-Discrimination Act.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I strongly support it.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: What it says is that gays and lesbians can’t be fired from their job because they’re gay or lesbian.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And it would be a federal law preventing that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, I wonder if the — it’s been blocked by the opponents in the majority in the Congress.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I wonder if the Governor would lend his support to that law.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Governor?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The question —

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Well, but it’s a logical response.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I have no idea.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I mean, he can throw out all kinds — I don’t know the particulars of this law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I will tell you I’m the kind of person, I don’t hire or fire somebody based upon their sexual orientation.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: As a matter of fact, I would like to take the issue a little further.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t really think it’s any of my — you know, any of my concerns what — how you conduct your sex life.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think that’s a private matter.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think that’s the way it ought to be.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I’m going to be respectful for people, I’ll tolerate people, and I support equal rights but not special rights for people.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Special rights, how does that affect gays and lesbians?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, it would be if they’re given special protective status.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t fully enforce laws and fully protect people and fully honor people, which I will do as the President of the United States.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: New subject, new question, Vice President Gore.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: How do you see the connection between controlling gun sales in this country and the incidence of death by accidental or intentional use of guns?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Jim, I hope that we can come back to the subject of education because the governor made an extensive statement on it and I have a very different view than the one he expressed.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But that having been said, I believe that — well, first of all, let me say that the governor and I agree on some things where this subject is concerned.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I will not do anything to affect the rights of hunters or sportsmen.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think that homeowners have to be respected and their right to have a gun if they wish to.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The problem I see is that there are too many guns getting into the hands of children, and criminals, and people who, for whatever reason, some kind of history of stalking or domestic abuse really should not be able to get guns.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think these assault weapons are a problem.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: So I favor closing the gun show loophole.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: In fact, I cast the tie-breaking vote to close it, but then the majority in the House of Representatives went the other way.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: That’s still pending.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: If we could get agreement on that, maybe they could pass that in the final days of this Congress.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think we ought to restore the three-day waiting period under the Brady Law.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think we should toughen the enforcement of gun laws so that the ones that are already on the books can be enforced much more effectively.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Some of the restrictions that have been placed by the Congress in the last couple of years.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think — in the last few years I think have been unfortunate.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think that we ought to make all schools gun free.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Have a gun-free zone around every school in this country.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think that measures like these are important.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Child safety trigger locks on a mandatory basis, and others.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Governor?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, it starts with enforcing law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: When you say loud and clear to somebody if you’re going to carry a gun illegally, we’re going to arrest you.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: If you’re going to sell a gun illegally, you need to be arrested.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: If you commit a crime with a gun, there needs to be absolute certainty in the law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that means that the local law enforcement officials need help at the federal level.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Programs like Project Exile where the federal government intensifies arresting people who illegally use guns.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we haven’t done a very good job of that at the federal level recently.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I’m going to make it a priority.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Secondly, I don’t think we ought to be selling guns to people who shouldn’t have them.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s why I support instant background checks at gun shows.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: One of the reasons we have an instant background check is so that we instantly know whether or not somebody should have a gun or not.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: In Texas I tried to do something innovative.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: There’s a lot of talk about trigger locks being on guns sold in the future.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I support that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I said if you want a trigger lock to make your gun safe, come and get one for free.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So we’re distributing in our State of Texas for free.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we ought to raise the age at which a juvenile can carry a handgun from 18 to 21.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I disagree with the vice president on this issue.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He is for registration of guns.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think the only people that are going to show up to register or get a license — I guess licensing like a driver’s license for a gun, the only people that are going to show up are law-abiding citizens.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The criminal is not going to show up and say hey, give me my I.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: card.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s the law-abiding citizens who will do that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: An I don’t think that is going to be an effective tool to make the — keep our society safe.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: So on guns, somebody wants to cast a vote based on your differences, where are the differences?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Well, I’m not for registration.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I am for licensing by states of new handgun purchases.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What’s that mean?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: A photo license I.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: like a driver’s license for new handguns and, you know, the Los Angeles —

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Excuse me, you would have to get the license — a photo I.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: to go in and before you could buy the gun?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Correct.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Who would issue the —

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The state.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The state.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think states should do that for new handguns, because too many criminals are getting guns.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: There was a recent investigation of the number in Texas who got — who were given concealed weapons permits in spite of the fact that they had records.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And the “Los Angeles Times” spent a lot of ink going into that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I am not for doing anything that would affect hunters or sportsmen, rifles, shotguns, existing handguns.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I do think that sensible gun safety measures are warranted now.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Look, this is the year — this is in the aftermath of Columbine, and Paducah, and all the places in our country where the nation has been shocked by these weapons in the hands of the wrong people.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The woman who bought the guns for the two boys who did that killing at Columbine said that if she had had to give her name and fill out a form there, she would not have bought those guns.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: That conceivably could have prevented that tragedy.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Back to the question about the differences on gun control.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What are they, Governor, from your point of view, between you and the Vice President?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I’m not for photo licensing.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me say something about Columbine.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Listen, we’ve got gun laws.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He says we ought to have gun-free schools.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Everybody believes that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m sure every state in the union has got them.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You can’t carry a gun into a school.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And there ought to be a consequence when you do carry a gun into a school.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But Columbine spoke to a larger issue.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s really a matter of culture.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s a culture that somewhere along the line we’ve begun to disrespect life.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Where a child can walk in and have their heart turned dark as a result of being on the Internet and walk in and decide to take somebody else’s life?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So gun laws are important, no question about it, but so is loving children, and character education classes, and faith-based programs being a part of after-school programs.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Some desperate child needs to have somebody put their arm around them and say, we love you.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So there’s a — this is a society that — of ours that’s got to do a better job of teaching children right from wrong.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we can enforce law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But there seems to be a lot of preoccupation on — not certainly only in this debate, but just in general on law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But there’s a larger law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Love your neighbor like you would like to be loved yourself.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that’s where our society must head if we’re going to be a peaceful and prosperous society.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I also believe in the Golden Rule.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I agree with a lot of the other things that the governor has said.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We do have a serious problem in our culture.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Tipper and I have worked on the problem of violence in entertainment aimed at children.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: She’s worked on it longer than I have.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I feel very strongly about that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And if I’m elected president, I will do something about that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I think that we — I think we have to start with better parenting.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I don’t think that we can ignore the role played by guns.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I mean, the fact is that there — even though no state wants them, there are guns in some schools.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And the reason it’s so difficult for schools to control that is because in recent years there has been a flood of cheap handguns that are so widely available that kids are finding ways to get ahold of them.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I think that if you look at the situation as it exists here in the United States compared to any other country in the world, it seems to me pretty obvious that while we respect the rights of hunters and sportsmen, we do need some common sense gun safety steps to stem this flood of guns that are getting into the wrong hands.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Yeah, no question about that, but there also needs to be strong enforcement of the law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Some kid who feels like — doesn’t matter where the gun comes from, it could be a cheap gun, expensive gun.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: What matters is something in this person’s head says there is not going to be a consequence.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So in my state we toughen up the juvenile justice laws.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We added beds.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’re tough.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We believe in tough love.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We say, if you get caught carrying a gun, you’re automatically detained.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that’s what needs to happen.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve got laws.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: If laws need to be strengthened, like instant background checks, that’s important.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: New question.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: As I was saying.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Both of you — Governor, both of you have talked much about Medicare and health care for seniors.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What about the more than 40 million younger Americans who do not have health insurance right now?

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What would you do about that?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I’ve got a plan to do something about that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s to make health care affordable and available this way.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: First, there’s some who should be buying health care who choose not to.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: There’s some —

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Some of the 40 million.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Some of the healthy folks, healthy young kids say I’ll never get sick, therefore I don’t need health care right now.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: For those what I think we need to do is to develop an investment-type vehicle that would be an incentive for them to invest, like medical savings accounts with rollover capacity.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: In other words, you say to a youngster, it will be in your financial interest to start saving for future illness, but for the working folks that do want to have health care that can’t afford it, a couple of things we need to do.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: One, we need more community health centers.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve developed — put out money in my budget to expand community health centers all around the country.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: These are places where people can get primary care.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Secondly — and they’re good.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They’re very important parts of the safety net of health care.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Secondly, that you get a $2,000 rebate from the government if you’re a family of $30,000 or less — it scales down as you get higher — that you can use to purchase health care in the private markets.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It will be a huge down payment for a pretty darn good system.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: If you allow — also allow — convince states to — allow states to allow the mother to match some of the children’s health insurance money with it, the pool purchasing power.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And to make health care more affordable, allow business associations like the National Federal of Independent Business or the Chamber of Commerce or the National Restaurant Association to write association plans across jurisdictional lines so that small businesses have got the capacity to have national pooling to drive the cost of insurance down.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think that’s the very best way to go.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It empowers people, it trusts people, it makes — and it’s a practical way to encourage people to purchase health care insurance.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Vice President Gore?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: It’s one of my top priorities, Jim, to give every single child in the United States affordable health care within the next four years.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I would like to see eventually in this country some form of universal health care, but I’m not for a government-run system.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: In fact, I’m for shrinking the size of government.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I want a smaller and smarter government.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I have been in charge of this reinventing government streamlining project that’s reduced the size of government by more than 300,000 people in the last several years.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And the budget plan that I’ve put out, according to the “Los Angeles Times” again, the way these things are typically measured as a percentage of the GDP, will bring government spending down to the lowest level in 50 years.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: So I want to proceed carefully to cover more people.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I think we should start by greatly expanding the so-called child health insurance or CHIP program to give health insurance to every single child in this country.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think it’s intolerable that we have so many millions of children without any health insurance.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: So it’s one of my top priorities.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, I know that we have some disagreements on this.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I’m sorry to tell you that, you know, there is a record here.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And Texas ranks 49th out of the 50 states in health care — in children with health care.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: 49th for women with health care, and 50th for families with health care.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: So it is a priority for me.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I guarantee you.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I’m not aware of any program — well, I’ll just leave it at that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think it ought to be a top priority.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Governor, did the — are the vice president’s figures correct about Texas?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: First of all, let me say he’s not for a government-run health care system?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I thought that’s exactly what he and Mrs.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Clinton and them fought for in 1993 was a government-run health care system.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It was fortunately stopped in its tracks.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Secondly, we spend $4.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: 7 billion a year on the uninsured in the State of Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Our rate of uninsured, the percentage of uninsured in Texas has gone down, while the percentage of uninsured in America has gone up.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Our CHIPS program got a late start because our government meets only four months out of every two years, Mr.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Vice President.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It may come as a shock for somebody who has been in Washington for so long.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But actually limited government can work in the second largest state in the union.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And therefore Congress passes the bill after our session in 1997 ended, we passed an enabling legislation in 1999.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve signed up over 110,000 children to the CHIPS program.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: For comparable states our size, we’re signing them up as fast as any other state.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You can quote all the numbers you want, but I’m telling you we care about our people in Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We spent a lot of money to make sure people get health care in the State of Texas, and we’re doing a better job than they are at the national level for reducing uninsured.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Is he right?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Well, I don’t know about all these percentages that he throws out, but I do know that — I speculate that the reason why he didn’t answer your question directly as to whether my numbers were right, the facts were right about Texas ranking dead last in families with health insurance and 49th out of 50 for both children and women, is because those facts are correct.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And as for why it happened, I’m no expert on the Texas procedures, but what my friends there tell me is that the governor opposed a measure put forward by Democrats in the legislature to expand the number of children that would be covered.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And instead directed the money toward a tax cut, a significant part of which went to wealthy interests.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: He declared the need for a new tax cut for the oil companies in Texas an emergency need, and so the money was taken away from the CHIP program.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: There’s — you don’t have to take my word for this.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: There is now a federal judge’s opinion about the current management of this program ordering the State of Texas to do — you should read that judge’s language about this.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I believe there are 1.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: 4 million children in Texas who do not have health insurance.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: 600,000 of whom, and maybe some of those have since gotten it, but as of a year ago 600,000 of them were actually eligible for it but they couldn’t sign up for it because of the barriers that they had set up.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Let’s let the governor respond to that.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Are those numbers correct?

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Are his charges correct?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: If he’s trying to allege that I’m a hard-hearted person and I don’t care about children, he’s absolutely wrong.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve spent $4.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: 7 billion a year in the State of Texas for uninsured people.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And they get health care.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, it’s not the most efficient way to get people health care.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I want to remind you, the number of uninsured in America during their watch has increased.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He can make any excuse he wants, but the facts are that we’re reducing the number of uninsured percentage of our population.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And as the percentage of the population is increasing nationally, somehow the allegation that we don’t care and we’re going to give money for this interest or that interest and not for children in the State of Texas is totally absurd.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me just tell you who the jury is.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The people of Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: There’s only been one governor ever elected to back-to-back four-year terms, and that was me.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I was able to do so with a lot of Democrat votes, nearly 50% of the Hispanic vote, about 27% of the African-American vote, because people know I’m a conservative person and a compassionate person.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So he can throw all the kinds of numbers around.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m just telling you our state comes together to do what is right.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We come together both Republicans and Democrats.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Let me put that directly to you, Vice President Gore.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: The reason you brought this up, is it — are you suggesting that those numbers and that record will reflect the way Governor Bush will operate in this area of health insurance as president?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Yes, yes.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But it’s not a statement about his heart.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I don’t claim to know his heart.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think he’s a good person.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I make no allegations about that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I believe him when he says that he has a good heart.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I know enough about your story to admire a lot of the things that you have done as a person.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I think it’s about his priorities.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And let me tell you exactly why I think that the choice he made to give a tax cut for the oil companies and others before addressing this — I mean, if you were the governor of a state that was dead last in health care for families, and all of a sudden you found yourself with the biggest surplus your state had ever had in its history, wouldn’t you want to maybe use some of it to climb from 50th to, say, 45 or 40 or something or maybe better?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I would.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, but here is why it’s directly relevant, Jim.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Because by his own budget numbers, his proposals for spending on tax cuts for the wealthiest of the wealthy are more than the new spending proposals that he has made for health care and education and national defense all combined.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: According to his own numbers.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: So it’s not a question of his heart, as far as I know.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: It’s a question of priorities and values.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: See, you know —

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Let me ask —

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: First of all, that’s simply not true what he just said, of course.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And secondly, I repeat to you —

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What is not true, Governor?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That we spent — the top 1% receive 223 as opposed to 445 billion in new spending.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The top — let’s talk about my tax plan.

sentence_text: The top 1% will pay one-third of all the federal income taxes.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And in return, get one-fifth of the benefits, because most of the tax reductions go to the people at the bottom end of the economic ladder.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That stands in stark contrast, by the way, to a man who is going to leave 50 million — 50 million Americans out of tax relief.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We just have a different point of view.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s a totally different point of view.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He believes only the right people ought to get tax relief.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe everybody who pays taxes ought to get tax relief.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me go back to Texas, for example, for a minute.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We pay 4.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: 7 billion.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I can’t emphasize to you how much.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I signed a bill that puts CHIPS in place.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The bill finally came out at the end of the 1999 session.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’re working hard to sign up children.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’re doing it faster than any other state our size, comparable state.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’re making really good progress.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And our state cares a lot about our children.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My priority is going to be the health of our citizens.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: These folks have had eight years to get something done in Washington, D.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: on the uninsured.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They have not done it.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They’ve had eight years to get something done on Medicare.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And they have not got it done.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And my case to the American people is, if you’re happy with inactivity, stay with the horse.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The horse is up here now.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But if you want change, you need to get somebody that knows how to bring Republicans and Democrats together to get positive things done for America.

sentence_text: New question, new subject.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Vice President Gore, on the environment.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: In your 1992 book you said, quote, “We must make the rescue of our environment the central organizing principle for civilization and there must be a wrenching transformation to save the planet.

sentence_text: ” Do you still feel that way?
