sentence_text: I do.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think that in this 21st century we will soon see the consequences of what’s called global warming.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: There was a study just a few weeks ago suggesting that in summertime the north polar ice cap will be completely gone in 50 years.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Already many people see the strange weather conditions that the old timers say they’ve never seen before in their lifetimes.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And what’s happening is the level of pollution is increasing significantly.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, here is the good news, Jim.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: If we take the leadership role and build the new technologies, like the new kinds of cars and trucks that Detroit is itching to build, then we can create millions of good new jobs by being first into the market with these new kinds of cars and trucks and other kinds of technologies.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: You know the Japanese are breathing down our necks on this.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: They’re moving very rapidly because they know that it is a fast-growing world market.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Some of these other countries, particularly in the developing world, their pollution is much worse than anywhere else and their people want higher standards of living.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And so they’re looking for ways to satisfy their desire for a better life and still reduce pollution at the same time.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think that holding onto the old ways and the old argument that the environment and the economy are in conflict is really outdated.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We have to be bold.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We have to provide leadership.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now it’s true that we disagree on this.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The governor said that he doesn’t think this problem is necessarily caused by people.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: He’s for letting the oil companies into the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Houston has just become the smoggiest city in the country.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And Texas is number one in industrial pollution.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We have a very different outlook.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I’ll tell you this, I will fight for a clean environment in ways that strengthen our economy.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Governor?

sentence_text: Well, let me start with Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We are a big industrial state.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We reduced our industrial waste by 11%.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We cleaned up more brown fields than any other administration in my state’s history, 450 of them.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Our water is cleaner now.

sentence_text: A brown field is an abandoned industrial site that just sits idle in some of our urban centers.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And people are willing to invest capital in the brown fields don’t want to do so for fear of lawsuit.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we ought to have federal liability protection, depending upon whether or not standards have been met.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The book you mentioned that Vice President Gore wrote, he also called for taxing — big energy taxes in order to clean up the environment.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And now that the energy prices are high, I guess he’s not advocating those big energy taxes right now.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe we ought to fully fund the Land and Water Conservation Fund to — with half the money going to states so states can make the right decisions for environmental quality.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we need to have clean coal technologies.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I propose $2 billion worth.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: By the way, I just found out the other day an interesting fact, that there is a national petroleum reserve right next to — in Prudhoe Bay that your administration opened up for exploration in that pristine area.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And it was a smart move because there’s gas reserves up there.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We need gas pipelines to bring the gas down.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Gas is a clean fuel that we can burn to — we need to make sure that if we decontrol our plants that there’s mandatory — that the plants must conform to clean air standards, the grandfathered plants, that’s what we did in Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: No excuses.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You must conform.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: In other words, there are practical things we can do.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But it starts with working in a collaborative effort with states and local folks.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: If you own the land, every day is Earth Day.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: People care a lot about their land and care about their environment.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Not all wisdom is in Washington, D.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: on this issue.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Where do you see the basic difference in very simple terms in two or three sentences between you and the governor on the environment?

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: If a voter wants to make a choice, what is it?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I’m really strongly committed to clean water and clean air, and cleaning up the new kinds of challenges like global warming.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: He is right that I’m not in favor of energy taxes.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I am in favor of tax cuts to encourage and give incentives for the quicker development of these new kinds of technologies.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And let me say again, Detroit is rearing to go on that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We differ on the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, as I have said.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We differ on whether or not pollution controls ought to be voluntary.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I don’t think you can — I don’t think you can get results that way.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We differ on the kinds of appointments that we would make.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Would you say it’s a fundamental difference?

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think it’s a fundamental difference.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Let me give you an example.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Hold on one second.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Okay, sure.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: We’ve talked about supply.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: I just want to know for somebody — we’re getting close to the end of our time here.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: If somebody wanted to vote on the environment, how would you draw the differences, Governor?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I don’t believe in command and control out of Washington, D.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe Washington ought to set standards, but again I think we ought to be collaborative at the local levels and I think we ought to work with people at the local levels.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And by the way, I just want to make sure — I can’t let him just say something and not correct it.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The electric decontrol bill that I fought for and signed in Texas has mandatory emission standards, Mr.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Vice President.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s what we ought to do at the federal level when it comes to grandfathered plants for utilities.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think there’s a difference.

sentence_text: I think, for example, take — when they took 40 million acres of land out of circulation without consulting local officials, I thought that was —

sentence_text: That was out in the west?

sentence_text: And so — on the logging issue.

sentence_text: That’s not the way I would have done it.

sentence_text: Perhaps some of that land needs to be set aside.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I certainly would have consulted with governors and elected officials before I would have acted unilaterally.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: Would you believe the federal government still has some new rules and new regulations and new laws to pass in the environmental area or do you think —

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Sure, absolutely, so long as they’re based upon science and they’re reasonable.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So long as people have input.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: What about global warming?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think it’s an issue that we need to take very seriously.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I don’t think we know the solution to global warming yet.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I don’t think we’ve got all the facts before we make decisions.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I tell you one thing I’m not going to do is I’m not going to let the United States carry the burden for cleaning up the world’s air.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Like Kyoto Treaty would have done.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: China and India were exempted from that treaty.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we need to be more even-handed, as evidently 99 senators — I think it was 99 senators supported that position.

speaker: Moderator
sentence_text: I think —

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: 99 to nothing.

sentence_text: Well, that vote wasn’t exactly — a lot of the supporters of the Kyoto Treaty actually ended up voting for that because the way it was worded.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But there’s no doubt there’s a lot of opposition to it in the Senate.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I’m not for command and control techniques either.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I’m for working with the groups, not just with industry but also with the citizen groups and local communities to control sprawl in ways that the local communities themselves come up with.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But I disagree that we don’t know the cause of global warming.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I think that we do.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: It’s pollution, carbon dioxide, and other chemicals that are even more potent, but in smaller quantities, that cause this.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Look, the world’s temperature is going up, weather patterns are changing, storms are getting more violent and unpredictable.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: What are we going to tell our children?

sentence_text: I’m a grandfather now.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I want to be able to tell my grandson when I’m in my later years that I didn’t turn away from the evidence that showed that we were doing some serious harm.

sentence_text: In my faith tradition, it is — it’s written in the book of Matthew, “Where your heart is, there is your treasure also.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: ” And I believe that — that we ought to recognize the value to our children and grandchildren of taking steps that preserve the environment in a way that’s good for them.

sentence_text: Yeah, I agree.

sentence_text: I just — I think there has been — some of the scientists, I believe, Mr.

sentence_text: Now you just — twice, sorry.

sentence_text: I’m sorry, go ahead and finish your thought.

sentence_text: People care about these things I’ve found out.

sentence_text: Go ahead.

sentence_text: And before we react, I think it’s best to have the full accounting, full understanding of what’s taking place.

sentence_text: And I think to answer your question, I think both of us care a lot about the environment.

sentence_text: We may have different approaches.

sentence_text: We may have different approaches in terms of how we deal with local folks.

sentence_text: I just cited an example of the administration just unilaterally acting without any input.

sentence_text: And I remember you gave a very good answer to New Hampshire about the White Mountains, about how it was important to keep that collaborative effort in place.

sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: And of course, this debate also takes place at a time when the tragedy of the USS Cole is on our minds and hearts and insofar as the memorial service is tomorrow, I would like to also extend sympathy to the families of those who have died and those who are still missing, and the injured.

sentence_text: Now, Mr.

sentence_text: Hankins, I think that the situation that you describe has gotten completely out of hand.

sentence_text: Doctors are giving prescriptions, they’re recommending treatments, and then their recommendations are being overruled by HMOs and insurance companies.

sentence_text: That is unacceptable.

sentence_text: I support a strong national patient’s bill of rights.

sentence_text: It is actually a disagreement between us, a national law that is pending on this, the Dingle-Norwood bill, a bipartisan bill, is one that I support and that the governor does not.

sentence_text: I, too, want to extend my prayers and blessings, God’s blessings on the families whose lives were overturned yes — tod — last night.

sentence_text: Actually, Mr.

sentence_text: It requires a different kind of leadership style to do it, though.

sentence_text: You see, in order to get something done on behalf of the people, you have to put partisanship aside, and that’s what we did in my state.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s time for our nation to come together and do what’s right for the people, and I think this is right for the people.

sentence_text: You know, I support a national patient’s bill of rights, Mr.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Vice President, and I want all people covered.

sentence_text: I think —

sentence_text: MEMBER OF AUDIENCE: Are either of you concerned with — are either of you concerned with finding some feasible way to lower the price of pharmaceutical drugs such as education on minimizing intake, revamp of the FDA process or streamlining the drug companies’ procedures instead of just finding more money to pay for them?

sentence_text: And therefore, when they have to try to purchase drugs they do so on their own, there’s no kind of collective bargaining, no power of purchasing among seniors.

sentence_text: So I think step one to make sure prescription drugs is more affordable for seniors, and those are the folks who really rely upon prescription drugs a lot these days, is to reform the Medicare system, is to have prescription drugs as an integral part of Medicare once and for all.

sentence_text: The problem we have today is like the patient’s bill of rights, particularly with health care, there’s a lot of bickering in Washington, D.

sentence_text: So what I want to do is I want to call upon Republicans and Democrats to forget all the arguing and finger pointing, and come together and take care of our seniors’ prescription drug program, that says we’ll pay for the poor seniors, we’ll help all seniors with prescription drugs.

sentence_text: The purchasing powers.

sentence_text: I think price controls would hurt our ability to continue important research and development.

sentence_text: The amount of money that has to be raised in taxes for middle-class families to make up for completely eliminating that on the very wealthiest, the billionaires, that would be an extra heavy burden on middle-class families.

sentence_text: Thank you.

sentence_text: We can work with the entertainment industry to provide family hour.

sentence_text: There ought to be filters in public libraries and filters in public schools so if kids get on the Internet, there is not going to be pornography or violence coming in.

sentence_text: I think we ought to have character education in our schools.

sentence_text: I know that doesn’t directly talk about Hollywood, but it does reinforce the values you’re teaching.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Greatly expand character education funding so that public schools will teach children values, values which have stood the test of time.

sentence_text: There’s afterschool money available.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think that afterschool money ought to be available for faith-based programs and charitable programs that exist because somebody has heard the call to love a neighbor like you would like to be loved yourself.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That will help reinforce the values that parents teach at home as well.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Ours is a great land, and one of the reasons why is because we’re free.

sentence_text: But I do believe that we ought to talk plainly to the Hollywood moguls and people who produce this stuff and explain the consequences.

sentence_text: I think we need to have rating systems that are clear.

sentence_text: I happen to like the idea of having technology for the TV, easy for parents to use so you can tune out these programs you don’t want in your house.

sentence_text: But if you can check up on them, that’s real power.

sentence_text: MEMBER OF AUDIENCE: It seems that when we hear about issues of this campaign, it’s usually Medicare, Social Security or prescription drugs.

sentence_text: We’ve got to change it.

sentence_text: I spend a good deal of time talking to young people, and in my standard speech out there on the stump I usually end my speech by saying, I want to ask you for something and I want to direct it especially to the young people in the audience.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I want to tell you what I tell them.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Sometimes people who are very idealistic and have great dreams, as young people do, are apt to stay at arm’s length from the political process because they think their good hearts might be brittle, and if they invest their hopes and allow themselves to believe, then they’re gonna be let down and disappointed.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: But thank goodness we’ve always had enough people who have been willing in every generation to push past the fear of a broken heart and become deeply involved in forming a more perfect union.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We’re America, and we believe in our future and we know we have the ability to shape our future.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Now, we’ve got to address one of the biggest threats to our democracy.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And that is the current campaign financing system.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And I know they say it doesn’t rank anywhere on the polls.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I don’t believe that’s a fair measure.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I’m telling you, I will make it the — I will make the McCain-Feingold Campaign Finance Reform bill the very first measure that I send to the Congress as president.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Governor Bush opposes it.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I wish that he would consider changing his mind on that.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Because I think that the special interests have too much power, and we need to give our democracy back to the American people.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Let me tell you why.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Those issues you mentioned, Social Security, prescription drugs, the big drug companies are against the prescription drug proposal that I’ve made.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The HMOs are against the patient’s rights bill, the Dingle-Norwood bill that I support, and that Gov.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Bush does not support.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: The big oil companies are against the measures to get more energy independence and renewable fuel.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: They ought to have their voices heard, but they shouldn’t have a big megaphone that drowns out the American people.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We need campaign finance reform and we need to shoot straight with young and old alike and tell them what the real choices are.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And we can renew and rekindle the American spirit and make our future what our founders dreamed it could be.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: We can.

sentence_text: Governor Bush, two minutes.

sentence_text: Tell you what I hear.

sentence_text: A lot of people are sick and tired of the bitterness in Washington, D.

sentence_text: There’s a lot of young folks saying, you know, why do I want to be involved with this mess?

sentence_text: And what I think needs to happen in order to encourage the young to become involved is to shoot straight, is to set aside the partisan differences, and set an agenda that will make sense.

sentence_text: Medicare, I know you talked about it, but Medicare is relevant for all of us, young and old alike.

sentence_text: We better get it right now.

sentence_text: I don’t think it’s the issues that turn kids off.

sentence_text: I think it’s the tone.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think it’s the attitude.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think it’s a cynicism in Washington and it doesn’t have to be that way.

sentence_text: Before I decided to run, I had to resolve two issues in my mind.

sentence_text: One, could our family endure all this business.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I came to the conclusion that our love was strong enough to be able to do it.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The other was could an administration change the tone in Washington, D.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I believe the answer is yes, otherwise I wouldn’t be asking for your vote.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s what happened in Texas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We worked together.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: There is a man here in this audience named Hugo Berlanga.

sentence_text: He is the chairman of the health committee.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He came here for a reason, to tout our record on health in Texas.

sentence_text: He’s a Democrat.

sentence_text: I didn’t care whether he was a Republican or Democrat.

sentence_text: What I cared about is could we work together.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s what Washington, D.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: needs.

sentence_text: And finally, sir, to answer your question, you need somebody in office who will tell the truth.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s the best way to get people back in the system.

sentence_text: I’ve had a record of bringing people from all walks of life into my administration, and my administration is better off for it in Texas.

sentence_text: I’m going to find people that want to serve their country.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I want a diverse administration, I think it’s important.

sentence_text: I’ve worked hard in the State of Texas to make sure our institutions reflect the state with good, smart policy.

sentence_text: Quotas tend to pit one group of people against another.

sentence_text: Quotas are bad for America.

sentence_text: It’s not the way America is all about.

sentence_text: But policies that give people a helping hand so they can help themselves.

sentence_text: And as a result, our universities are now more diverse.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It was a smart thing to do.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: What I called it, I labeled it affirmative access.

sentence_text: I think the contracting business in government can help.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Not with quotas, but help meet a goal of ownership of small businesses, for example.

sentence_text: The contracts need to be smaller, the agencies need to be — need to recruit and to work hard to find people to bid on the state contracts.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think we can do that in a way that represents what America is all about, which is equal opportunity and an opportunity for people to realize their potential.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So to answer your question, I support, I guess the way to put it, is affirmative access.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ll have an administration that will make you proud.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Thank you.

sentence_text: Once you have that understanding and mutual respect, then we can transcend the differences and embrace the highest common denominator of the American spirit.

sentence_text: I’m for that proposed law, the governor is against it.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I know what it means to have a commitment to diversity.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: I am part of an administration that has the finest record on diversity.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: And incidentally, an excellent — I mean, I think our success over the last eight years has not been in spite of diversity but because of it.

speaker: Al Gore
sentence_text: Because we’re able to draw on the wisdom and experience from different parts of the society that hadn’t been tapped in the same way before.

sentence_text: And incidentally, Mel Carnahan in Missouri had the finest record on diversity in any governor in the entire history of the State of Missouri.

sentence_text: And I want to honor that among his other achievements here.

sentence_text: Now, I just believe that what we have to do is enforce the civil rights laws.

sentence_text: I’m against quotas.

sentence_text: This is, with all due respect, Governor, that’s a red herring.

sentence_text: Affirmative action means that you take extra steps to acknowledge the history of discrimination and injustice and prejudice and bring all people into the American dream because it helps everybody, not just those who are directly benefitting.

sentence_text: Governor, what is your — are you opposed to affirmative action?

sentence_text: The vice president keeps saying I’m against things.

sentence_text: Prior to Darfur, Ambassador Jack Danforth had been negotiating a north-south agreement that we would have hoped would have brought peace to the Sudan.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I agree with my opponent that we shouldn’t be committing troops.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We ought to be working with the African Union to do so — precisely what we did in Liberia.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We helped stabilize the situation with some troops, and when the African Union came, we moved them out.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My hope is that the African Union moves rapidly to help save lives.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And fortunately the rainy season will be ending shortly, which will make it easier to get aid there and help the long-suffering people there.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: New question, President Bush.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Clearly, as we have heard, major policy differences between the two of you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Are there also underlying character issues that you believe, that you believe are serious enough to deny Senator Kerry the job as commander in chief of the United States?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s a loaded question.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, first of all, I admire Senator Kerry’s service to our country.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I admire the fact that he is a great dad.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I appreciate the fact that his daughters have been so kind to my daughters in what has been a pretty hard experience for, I guess, young girls, seeing their dads out there campaigning.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I admire the fact that he served for 20 years in the Senate.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Although I’m not so sure I admire the record.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I won’t hold it against him that he went to Yale.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: There’s nothing wrong with that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My concerns about the senator is that, in the course of this campaign, I’ve been listening very carefully to what he says, and he changes positions on the war in Iraq.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He changes positions on something as fundamental as what you believe in your core, in your heart of hearts, is right in Iraq.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You cannot lead if you send mixed messages.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to our troops.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to our allies.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to the Iraqi citizens.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that’s my biggest concern about my opponent.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I admire his service.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I just know how this world works, and that in the councils of government, there must be certainty from the U.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: president.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Of course, we change tactics when need to, but we never change our beliefs, the strategic beliefs that are necessary to protect this country in the world.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Ninety second response, Senator.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Well, first of all, I appreciate enormously the personal comments the president just made.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I share them with him.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I think only if you’re doing this — and he’s done it more than I have in terms of the presidency — can you begin to get a sense of what it means to your families.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And it’s tough.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And so I acknowledge that his daughters — I’ve watched them.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’ve chuckled a few times at some of their comments.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And…

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m trying to put a leash on them.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Well, I know.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’ve learned not to do that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I have great respect and admiration for his wife.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I think she’s a terrific person…

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Thank you.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: … and a great first lady.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But we do have differences.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m not going to talk about a difference of character.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I don’t think that’s my job or my business.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But let me talk about something that the president just sort of finished up with.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Maybe someone would call it a character trait, maybe somebody wouldn’t.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But this issue of certainty.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: It’s one thing to be certain, but you can be certain and be wrong.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: It’s another to be certain and be right, or to be certain and be moving in the right direction, or be certain about a principle and then learn new facts and take those new facts and put them to use in order to change and get your policy right.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: What I worry about with the president is that he’s not acknowledging what’s on the ground, he’s not acknowledging the realities of North Korea, he’s not acknowledging the truth of the science of stem-cell research or of global warming and other issues.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And certainty sometimes can get you in trouble.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, I think — listen, I fully agree that one should shift tactics, and we will, in Iraq.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Our commanders have got all the flexibility to do what is necessary to succeed.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But what I won’t do is change my core values because of politics or because of pressure.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And it is one of the things I’ve learned in the White House, is that there’s enormous pressure on the president, and he cannot wilt under that pressure.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Otherwise, the world won’t be better off.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I have no intention of wilting.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’ve never wilted in my life.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I’ve never wavered in my life.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I know exactly what we need to do in Iraq, and my position has been consistent: Saddam Hussein is a threat.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: He needed to be disarmed.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We needed to go to the U.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The president needed the authority to use force in order to be able to get him to do something, because he never did it without the threat of force.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But we didn’t need to rush to war without a plan to win the peace.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: New question, two minutes, Senator Kerry.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: If you are elected president, what will you take to that office thinking is the single most serious threat to the national security to the United States?

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Nuclear proliferation.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Nuclear proliferation.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: There’s some 600-plus tons of unsecured material still in the former Soviet Union and Russia.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: At the rate that the president is currently securing it, it’ll take 13 years to get it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I did a lot of work on this.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I wrote a book about it several years ago — six, seven years ago — called “The New War,” which saw the difficulties of this international criminal network.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And back then, we intercepted a suitcase in a Middle Eastern country with nuclear materials in it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And the black market sale price was about $250 million.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now, there are terrorists trying to get their hands on that stuff today.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And this president, I regret to say, has secured less nuclear material in the last two years since 9/11 than we did in the two years preceding 9/11.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We have to do this job.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And to do the job, you can’t cut the money for it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The president actually cut the money for it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You have to put the money into it and the funding and the leadership.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And part of that leadership is sending the right message to places like North Korea.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Right now the president is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to research bunker-busting nuclear weapons.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The United States is pursuing a new set of nuclear weapons.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: It doesn’t make sense.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You talk about mixed messages.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We’re telling other people, “You can’t have nuclear weapons,” but we’re pursuing a new nuclear weapon that we might even contemplate using.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Not this president.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m going to shut that program down, and we’re going to make it clear to the world we’re serious about containing nuclear proliferation.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And we’re going to get the job of containing all of that nuclear material in Russia done in four years.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And we’re going to build the strongest international network to prevent nuclear proliferation.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: This is the scale of what President Kennedy set out to do with the nuclear test ban treaty.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: It’s our generation’s equivalent.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I intend to get it done.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Ninety seconds, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Actually, we’ve increased funding for dealing with nuclear proliferation about 35 percent since I’ve been the president.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Secondly, we’ve set up what’s called the — well, first of all, I agree with my opponent that the biggest threat facing this country is weapons of mass destruction in the hands of a terrorist network.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that’s why proliferation is one of the centerpieces of a multi-prong strategy to make the country safer.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My administration started what’s called the Proliferation Security Initiative.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Over 60 nations involved with disrupting the trans-shipment of information and/or weapons of mass destruction materials.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’ve been effective.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We busted the A.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Khan network.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: This was a proliferator out of Pakistan that was selling secrets to places like North Korea and Libya.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We convinced Libya to disarm.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s a central part of dealing with weapons of mass destruction and proliferation.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ll tell you another way to help protect America in the long run is to continue with missile defenses.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’ve got a robust research and development program that has been ongoing during my administration.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ll be implementing a missile-defense system relatively quickly.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that is another way to help deal with the threats that we face in the 21st century.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My opponent opposed the missile defenses.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Just for this one-minute discussion here, just for whatever seconds it takes: So it’s correct to say, that if somebody is listening to this, that both of you agree, if you’re reelected, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, and if you are elected, the single most serious threat you believe, both of you believe, is nuclear proliferation?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: In the hands of a terrorist enemy.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Weapons of mass destruction, nuclear proliferation.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But again, the test or the difference between us, the president has had four years to try to do something about it, and North Korea has got more weapons; Iran is moving towards weapons.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And at his pace, it will take 13 years to secure those weapons in Russia.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m going to do it in four years, and I’m going to immediately set out to have bilateral talks with North Korea.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Your response to that?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Again, I can’t tell you how big a mistake I think that is, to have bilateral talks with North Korea.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s precisely what Kim Jong Il wants.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It will cause the six-party talks to evaporate.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It will mean that China no longer is involved in convincing, along with us, for Kim Jong Il to get rid of his weapons.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s a big mistake to do that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We must have China’s leverage on Kim Jong Il, besides ourselves.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And if you enter bilateral talks, they’ll be happy to walk away from the table.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t think that’ll work.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, this is the last question.

sentence_text: And two minutes.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It’s a new subject — new question, and it has to do with President Putin and Russia.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Did you misjudge him or are you — do you feel that what he is doing in the name of antiterrorism by changing some democratic processes is OK?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: No, I don’t think it’s OK, and said so publicly.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think that there needs to be checks and balances in a democracy, and made that very clear that by consolidating power in the central government, he’s sending a signal to the Western world and United States that perhaps he doesn’t believe in checks and balances, and I told him that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I mean, he’s also a strong ally in the war on terror.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He is — listen, they went through a horrible situation in Beslan, where these terrorists gunned down young school kids.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s the nature of the enemy, by the way.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s why we need to be firm and resolved in bringing them to justice.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s precisely what Vladimir Putin understands, as well.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ve got a good relation with Vladimir.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And it’s important that we do have a good relation, because that enables me to better comment to him, and to better to discuss with him, some of the decisions he makes.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I found that, in this world, that it’s important to establish good personal relationships with people so that when you have disagreements, you’re able to disagree in a way that is effective.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so I’ve told him my opinion.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I look forward to discussing it more with him, as time goes on.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Russia is a country in transition.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Vladimir is going to have to make some hard choices.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I think it’s very important for the American president, as well as other Western leaders, to remind him of the great benefits of democracy, that democracy will best help the people realize their hopes and aspirations and dreams.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I will continue working with him over the next four years.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Ninety seconds, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Well, let me just say quickly that I’ve had an extraordinary experience of watching up close and personal that transition in Russia, because I was there right after the transformation.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I was probably one of the first senators, along with Senator Bob Smith of New Hampshire, a former senator, to go down into the KGB underneath Treblinka Square and see reams of files with names in them.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: It sort of brought home the transition to democracy that Russia was trying to make.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I regret what’s happened in these past months.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I think it goes beyond just the response to terror.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Putin now controls all the television stations.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: His political opposition is being put in jail.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I think it’s very important to the United States, obviously, to have a working relationship that is good.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: This is a very important country to us.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We want a partnership.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But we always have to stand up for democracy.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: As George Will said the other day, “Freedom on the march; not in Russia right now.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: ” Now, I’d like to come back for a quick moment, if I can, to that issue about China and the talks.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Because that’s one of the most critical issues here: North Korea.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Just because the president says it can’t be done, that you’d lose China, doesn’t mean it can’t be done.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I mean, this is the president who said “There were weapons of mass destruction,” said “Mission accomplished,” said we could fight the war on the cheap — none of which were true.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We could have bilateral talks with Kim Jong Il.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And we can get those weapons at the same time as we get China.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Because China has an interest in the outcome, too.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Thirty seconds, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You know my opinion on North Korea.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I can’t say it any more plainly.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Well, but when he used the word “truth” again…

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Pardon me?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: … talking about the truth of the matter.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: He used the word “truth” again.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Did that raise any hackles with you?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Oh, I’m a pretty calm guy.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I don’t take it personally.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You know, we looked at the same intelligence and came to the same conclusion: that Saddam Hussein was a grave threat.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I don’t hold it against him that he said grave threat.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m not going to go around the country saying he didn’t tell the truth, when he looked at the same intelligence I did.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: It was a threat.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: That’s not the issue.

sentence_text: The issue is what you do about it.

sentence_text: The president said he was going to build a true coalition, exhaust the remedies of the U.

sentence_text: and go to war as a last resort.

sentence_text: Those words really have to mean something.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And, unfortunately, he didn’t go to war as a last resort.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now we have this incredible mess in Iraq — $200 billion.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: It’s not what the American people thought they were getting when they voted.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, that brings us to closing statements.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And, again, as determined by a coin toss, Senator Kerry, you go first, and you have two minutes.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Thank you, Jim, very much.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Thank you very much to the university, again.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: President.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: My fellow Americans, as I’ve said at the very beginning of this debate, both President Bush and I love this country very much.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: There’s no doubt, I think, about that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But we have a different set of convictions about how we make our country stronger here at home and respected again in the world.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I know that for many of you sitting at home, parents of kids in Iraq, you want to know who’s the person who could be a commander in chief who could get your kids home and get the job done and win the peace.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And for all the rest of the parents in America who are wondering about their kids going to the school or anywhere else in the world, what kind of world they’re going to grow up in, let me look you in the eye and say to you: I defended this country as a young man in war, and I will defend it as president of the United States.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But I have a difference with this president.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I believe when we’re strongest when we reach out and lead the world and build strong alliances.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I have a plan for Iraq.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I believe we can be successful.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m not talking about leaving.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m talking about winning.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And we need a fresh start, a new credibility, a president who can bring allies to our side.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I also have a plan to win the war on terror, funding homeland security, strengthening our military, cutting our finances, reaching out to the world, again building strong alliances.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I believe America’s best days are ahead of us because I believe that the future belongs to freedom, not to fear.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: That’s the country that I’m going to fight for.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I ask you to give me the opportunity to make you proud.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I ask you to give me the opportunity to lead this great nation, so that we can be stronger here at home, respected again in the world, and have responsible leadership that we deserve.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Thank you.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And God bless America.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, two minutes.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Thank you very much tonight, Jim.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Senator.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: If America shows uncertainty or weakness in this decade, the world will drift toward tragedy.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s not going to happen, so long as I’m your president.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The next four years we will continue to strengthen our homeland defenses.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We will strengthen our intelligence-gathering services.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We will reform our military.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The military will be an all-volunteer army.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We will continue to stay on the offense.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We will fight the terrorists around the world so we do not have to face them here at home.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ll continue to build our alliances.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’ll never turn over America’s national security needs to leaders of other countries, as we continue to build those alliances.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’ll continue to spread freedom.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe in the transformational power of liberty.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe that the free Iraq is in this nation’s interests.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I believe a free Afghanistan is in this nation’s interest.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I believe both a free Afghanistan and a free Iraq will serve as a powerful example for millions who plead in silence for liberty in the broader Middle East.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve done a lot of hard work together over the last three and a half years.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve been challenged, and we’ve risen to those challenges.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve climbed the mighty mountain.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I see the valley below, and it’s a valley of peace.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: By being steadfast and resolute and strong, by keeping our word, by supporting our troops, we can achieve the peace we all want.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I appreciate your listening tonight.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I ask for your vote.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And may God continue to bless our great land.

sentence_text: ” I welcome you to the second of the 2004 presidential debates between President George W.
