speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I proposed to the United States Congress a Clear Skies Initiative to reduce sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and mercury by 70 percent.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I have — was fought for a very strong title in the farm bill for the conservation reserve program to set aside millions of acres of land to help improve wildlife and the habitat.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We proposed and passed a healthy forest bill which was essential to working with — particularly in Western states — to make sure that our forests were protected.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: What happens in those forests, because of lousy federal policy, is they grow to be — they are not — they’re not harvested.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They’re not taken care of.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And as a result, they’re like tinderboxes.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And over the last summers I’ve flown over there.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so, this is a reasonable policy to protect old stands of trees and at the same time make sure our forests aren’t vulnerable to the forest fires that have destroyed acres after acres in the West.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve got a good, common-sense policy.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, I’m going to tell you what I really think is going to happen over time is technology is going to change the way we live for the good for the environment.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s why I proposed a hydrogen automobile — hydrogen-generated automobile.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’re spending $1 billion to come up with the technologies to do that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s why I’m a big proponent of clean coal technology, to make sure we can use coal but in a clean way.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I guess you’d say I’m a good steward of the land.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The quality of the air’s cleaner since I’ve been the president.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Fewer water complaints since I’ve been the president.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: More land being restored since I’ve been the president.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Thank you for your question.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Boy, to listen to that — the president, I don’t think, is living in a world of reality with respect to the environment.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now, if you’re a Red Sox fan, that’s OK.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But if you’re a president, it’s not.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Let me just say to you, number one, don’t throw the labels around.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Labels don’t mean anything.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I supported welfare reform.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I led the fight to put 100,000 cops on the streets of America.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’ve been for faith-based initiatives helping to intervene in the lives of young children for years.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I was — broke with my party in 1985, one of the first three Democrats to fight for a balanced budget when it was heresy.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Labels don’t fit, ladies and gentlemen.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now, when it comes to the issue of the environment, this is one of the worst administrations in modern history.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The Clear Skies bill that he just talked about, it’s one of those Orwellian names you pull out of the sky, slap it onto something, like “No Child Left Behind” but you leave millions of children behind.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Here they’re leaving the skies and the environment behind.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: If they just left the Clean Air Act all alone the way it is today, no change, the air would be cleaner than it is if you pass the Clear Skies act.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We’re going backwards.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: In fact, his environmental enforcement chief air-quality person at the EPA resigned in protest over what they’re doing to what they are calling the new source performance standards for air quality.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: They’re going backwards on the definition for wetlands.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: They’re going backwards on the water quality.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: They pulled out of the global warming, declared it dead, didn’t even accept the science.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m going to be a president who believes in science.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: President?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Well, had we joined the Kyoto treaty, which I guess he’s referring to, it would have cost America a lot of jobs.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s one of these deals where, in order to be popular in the halls of Europe, you sign a treaty.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I thought it would cost a lot — I think there’s a better way to do it.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I just told you the facts, sir.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The quality of the air is cleaner since I’ve been the president of the United States.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’ll continue to spend money on research and development, because I truly believe that’s the way to get from how we live today to being able to live a standard of living that we’re accustomed to and being able to protect our environment better, the use of technologies.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, 30 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The fact is that the Kyoto treaty was flawed.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I was in Kyoto, and I was part of that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I know what happened.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But this president didn’t try to fix it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: He just declared it dead, ladies and gentlemen, and we walked away from the work of 160 nations over 10 years.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You wonder, Nikki, why it is that people don’t like us in some parts of the world.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You just say: Hey, we don’t agree with you.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Goodbye.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The president’s done nothing to try to fix it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I will.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, the next question is for you.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: It involves jobs, which is a topic of the news today.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: And for the question, we’re going to turn to Jane Barrow.

speaker: Barrow
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, how can the U.

speaker: Barrow
sentence_text: be competitive in manufacturing given — in manufacturing, excuse me — given the wage necessary and comfortably accepted for American workers to maintain the standard of living that they expect?

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Jane, there are a lot of ways to be competitive.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And unfortunately again I regret this administration has not seized them and embraced them.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Let me give you an example.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: There is a tax loophole right now.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: If you’re a company in St.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Louis working, trying to make jobs here, there is actually an incentive for you to go away.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You get more money, you keep more of your taxes by going abroad.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m going to shut that loophole, and I’m going to give the tax benefit to the companies that stay here in America to help make them more competitive.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Secondly, we’re going to create a manufacturing jobs credit and a new jobs credit for people to be able to help hire and be more competitive here in America.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Third, what’s really hurting American business more than anything else is the cost of health care.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now, you didn’t hear any plan from the president, because he doesn’t have a plan to lower the cost of health care.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Five million Americans have lost their health care; 620,000 Missourians have no health care at all; 96,000 Missourians have lost their health care under President Bush.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I have a plan to cover those folks.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And it’s a plan that lowers cost for everybody, covers all children.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And the way I pay for it — I’m not fiscally irresponsible — is I roll back the tax cut this president so fiercely wants to defend, the one for him and me and Charlie.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I think you ought to get the break.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I want to lower your cost to health care.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I want to fully fund education, No Child Left Behind, special-needs education.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And that’s how we’re going to be more competitive, by making sure our kids are graduating from school and college.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: China and India are graduating more graduates in technology and science than we are.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We’ve got to create the products of the future.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: That’s why I have a plan for energy independence within 10 years.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And we’re going to put our laboratories and our colleges and our universities to work.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And we’re going to get the great entrepreneurial spirit of this country, and we’re going to free ourselves from this dependency on Mideast oil.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: That’s how you create jobs and become competitive.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: President, minute and a half.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me start with how to control the cost of health care: medical liability reform, for starters, which he’s opposed.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Secondly, allow small businesses to pool together so they can share risk and buy insurance at the same discounts big businesses get to do.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Thirdly, spread what’s called health savings accounts.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s good for small businesses, good for owners.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You own your own account.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You can save tax-free.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You get a catastrophic plan to help you on it.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: This is different from saying, “OK, let me incent you to go on the government.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: ” He’s talking about his plan to keep jobs here.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: You know he calls it an outsourcing to keep — stop outsourcing.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Robert Rubin looked at his plan and said it won’t work.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The best way to keep jobs here in America is, one, have an energy plan.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I proposed one to the Congress two years ago, encourages conservation, encourages technology to explore for environmentally friendly ways for coal — to use coal and gas.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It encourages the use of renewables like ethanol and biodiesel.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s stuck in the Senate.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He and his running-mate didn’t show up to vote when they could have got it going in the Senate.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Less regulations if we want jobs here; legal reform if we want jobs here; and we’ve got to keep taxes low.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Now, he says he’s only going to tax the rich.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Do you realize, 900,000 small businesses will be taxed under his plan because most small businesses are Subchapter S corps or limited partnerships, and they pay tax at the individual income tax level.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so when you’re running up the taxes like that, you’re taxing job creators, and that’s not how you keep jobs here.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator, I want to extend for a minute, you talk about tax credits to stop outsourcing.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: But when you have IBM documents that I saw recently where you can hire a programmer for $12 in China, $56 an hour here, tax credits won’t cut it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You can’t stop all outsourcing, Charlie.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’ve never promised that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’m not going to, because that would be pandering.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You can’t.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But what you can do is create a fair playing field, and that’s what I’m talking about.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But let me just address what the president just said.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Ladies and gentlemen, that’s just not true what he said.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The Wall Street Journal said 96 percent of small businesses are not affected at all by my plan.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And you know why he gets that count?

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: The president got $84 from a timber company that owns, and he’s counted as a small business.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Dick Cheney’s counted as a small business.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: That’s how they do things.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: That’s just not right.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I own a timber company?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s news to me.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Need some wood?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Most small businesses are Subchapter S corps.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: They just are.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I met Grant Milliron, Mansfield, Ohio.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: He’s creating jobs.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Most small businesses — 70 percent of the new jobs in America are created by small businesses.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Taxes are going up when you run up the top two brackets.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It’s a fact.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: President Bush, the next question is for you, and it comes from Rob Fowler, who I believe is over in this area.

speaker: Fowler
sentence_text: President Bush, 45 days after 9/11, Congress passed the Patriot Act, which takes away checks on law enforcement and weakens American citizens’ rights and freedoms, especially Fourth Amendment rights.

speaker: Fowler
sentence_text: With expansions to the Patriot Act and Patriot Act II, my question to you is, why are my rights being watered down and my citizens’ around me?

speaker: Fowler
sentence_text: And what are the specific justifications for these reforms?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I appreciate that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I really don’t think your rights are being watered down.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: As a matter of fact, I wouldn’t support it if I thought that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Every action being taken against terrorists requires court order, requires scrutiny.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: As a matter of fact, the tools now given to the terrorist fighters are the same tools that we’ve been using against drug dealers and white-collar criminals.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: So I really don’t think so.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I hope you don’t think that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I mean, I — because I think whoever is the president must guard your liberties, must not erode your rights in America.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The Patriot Act is necessary, for example, because parts of the FBI couldn’t talk to each other.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The intelligence-gathering and the law-enforcement arms of the FBI just couldn’t share intelligence under the old law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that didn’t make any sense.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Our law enforcement must have every tool necessary to find and disrupt terrorists at home and abroad before they hurt us again.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s the task of the 21st century.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so, I don’t think the Patriot Act abridges your rights at all.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I know it’s necessary.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I can remember being in upstate New York talking to FBI agents that helped bust a Lackawanna cell up there.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And they told me they could not have performed their duty, the duty we all expect of them, if they did not have the ability to communicate with each other under the Patriot Act.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Former Governor Racicot, as chairman of the Republican Party, said he thought that the Patriot Act has to be changed and fixed.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Congressman Jim Sensenbrenner, he is the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, said over his dead body before it gets renewed without being thoroughly rechecked.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: A whole bunch of folks in America are concerned about the way the Patriot Act has been applied.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: In fact, the inspector general of the Justice Department found that John Ashcroft had twice applied it in ways that were inappropriate.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: People’s rights have been abused.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I met a man who spent eight months in prison, wasn’t even allowed to call his lawyer, wasn’t allowed to get — finally, Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois intervened and was able to get him out.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: This is in our country, folks, the United States of America.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: They’ve got sneak-and-peek searches that are allowed.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: They’ve got people allowed to go into churches now and political meetings without any showing of potential criminal activity or otherwise.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now, I voted for the Patriot Act.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Ninety-nine United States senators voted for it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And the president’s been very busy running around the country using what I just described to you as a reason to say I’m wishy-washy, that I’m a flip-flopper.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now that’s not a flip-flop.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I believe in the Patriot Act.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We need the things in it that coordinate the FBI and the CIA.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We need to be stronger on terrorism.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But you know what we also need to do as Americans is never let the terrorists change the Constitution of the United States in a way that disadvantages our rights.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, the next question is for you, and it comes from Elizabeth Long.

speaker: Long
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, thousands of people have already been cured or treated by the use of adult stem cells or umbilical cord stem cells.

speaker: Long
sentence_text: However, no one has been cured by using embryonic stem cells.

speaker: Long
sentence_text: Wouldn’t it be wise to use stem cells obtained without the destruction of an embryo?

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: You know, Elizabeth, I really respect your — the feeling that’s in your question.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I understand it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I know the morality that’s prompting that question, and I respect it enormously.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But like Nancy Reagan, and so many other people — you know, I was at a forum with Michael J.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Fox the other day in New Hampshire, who’s suffering from Parkinson’s, and he wants us to do stem cell, embryonic stem cell.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And this fellow stood up, and he was quivering.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: His whole body was shaking from the nerve disease, the muscular disease that he had.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And he said to me and to the whole hall, he said, “You know, don’t take away my hope, because my hope is what keeps me going.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: ” Chris Reeve is a friend of mine.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Chris Reeve exercises every single day to keep those muscles alive for the day when he believes he can walk again, and I want him to walk again.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I think we can save lives.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now, I think we can do ethically guided embryonic stem-cell research.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We have 100,000 to 200,000 embryos that are frozen in nitrogen today from fertility clinics.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: These weren’t taken from abortion or something like that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: They’re from a fertility clinic.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And they’re either going to be destroyed or left frozen.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I believe if we have the option, which scientists tell us we do, of curing Parkinson’s, curing diabetes, curing, you know, some kind of a, you know, paraplegic or quadriplegic or, you know, a spinal cord injury, anything, that’s the nature of the human spirit.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I think it is respecting life to reach for that cure.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I think it is respecting life to do it in an ethical way.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And the president has chosen a policy that makes it impossible for our scientists to do that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I want the future, and I think we have to grab it.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: President, a minute and a half.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Embryonic stem-cell research requires the destruction of life to create a stem cell.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m the first president ever to allow funding — federal funding — for embryonic stem-cell research.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I did to because I too hope that we’ll discover cures from the stem cells and from the research derived.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But I think we’ve got to be very careful in balancing the ethics and the science.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so I made the decision we wouldn’t spend any more money beyond the 70 lines, 22 of which are now in action, because science is important, but so is ethics, so is balancing life.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: To destroy life to save life is — it’s one of the real ethical dilemmas that we face.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: There is going to be hundreds of experiments off the 22 lines that now exist that are active, and hopefully we find a cure.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: But as well, we need to continue to pursue adult stem-cell research.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I helped double the NIH budget to $28 billion a year to find cures.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And the approach I took is one that I think is a balanced and necessary approach, to balance science and the concerns for life.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator, 30 seconds, less extent.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Well, you talk about walking a waffle line — he says he’s allowed it, which means he’s going to allow the destruction of life up to a certain amount and then he isn’t going to allow it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I don’t know how you draw that line.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: But let me tell you, point blank, the lines of stem cells that he’s made available, every scientist in the country will tell you, “Not adequate,” because they’re contaminated by mouse cells, and because there aren’t 60 or 70 — they’re are only about 11 to 20 now — and there aren’t enough to be able to do the research because they’re contaminated.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: We’ve got to open up the possibilities of this research.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And when I am president, I’m going to do it because we have to.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: President?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me make sure you understand my decision.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Those stem- cells lines already existed.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The embryo had already been destroyed prior to my decision.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I had to make the decision to destroy more life, so do we continue to destroy life — I made the decision to balance science and ethics.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: President, the next question is for you, and it comes from Jonathan Michaelson, over here.

speaker: Michaelson
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Michaelson
sentence_text: President, if there were a vacancy in the Supreme Court and you had the opportunity to fill that position today, who would you choose and why?

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m not telling.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I really don’t have — haven’t picked anybody yet.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Plus, I want them all voting for me.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I would pick somebody who would not allow their personal opinion to get in the way of the law.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I would pick somebody who would strictly interpret the Constitution of the United States.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Let me give you a couple of examples, I guess, of the kind of person I wouldn’t pick.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I wouldn’t pick a judge who said that the Pledge of Allegiance couldn’t be said in a school because it had the words “under God” in it.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I think that’s an example of a judge allowing personal opinion to enter into the decision-making process as opposed to a strict interpretation of the Constitution.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Another example would be the Dred Scott case, which is where judges, years ago, said that the Constitution allowed slavery because of personal property rights.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s a personal opinion.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: That’s not what the Constitution says.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: The Constitution of the United States says we’re all — you know, it doesn’t say that.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: It doesn’t speak to the equality of America.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And so, I would pick people that would be strict constructionists.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve got plenty of lawmakers in Washington, D.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Legislators make law; judges interpret the Constitution.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And I suspect one of us will have a pick at the end of next year — the next four years.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And that’s the kind of judge I’m going to put on there.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: No litmus test except for how they interpret the Constitution.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Thank you.

speaker: Gibson
sentence_text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Thank you, Charlie.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: A few years ago when he came to office, the president said — these are his words — “What we need are some good conservative judges on the courts.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: ” And he said also that his two favorite justices are Justice Scalia and Justice Thomas.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: So you get a pretty good sense of where he’s heading if he were to appoint somebody.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Now, here’s what I believe.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I don’t believe we need a good conservative judge, and I don’t believe we need a good liberal judge.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I don’t believe we need a good judge of that kind of definition on either side.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I subscribe to the Justice Potter Stewart standard.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: He was a justice on the Supreme Court of the United States.

sentence_text: Neighborhoods are safer when we crack down on people who commit crimes with guns.

sentence_text: I believe it was a failure of presidential leadership not to reauthorize the assault weapons ban.

sentence_text: I know something about prosecuting.

sentence_text: We just did a drug bust a week earlier, and the guy we arrested had an AK-47 lying on the bed right beside him.

sentence_text: “ Because of the president’s decision today, law enforcement officers will walk into a place that will be more dangerous.

sentence_text: This is a president who has not met with the civil rights leadership of our country.

sentence_text: If a president doesn’t reach out and bring people in and be inclusive, then how are we going to get over those barriers?

sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: I believe the best way to help our small businesses is not only through small-business loans, which we have increased since I’ve been the president of the United States, but to unbundle government contracts so people have a chance to be able to bid and receive a contract to help get their business going.

sentence_text: And that’s been part of my foreign policy.

sentence_text: Senator Kerry, after 9/11 — and this is a new question for you — it seemed to me that the country came together as I’ve never seen it come together since World War II.

sentence_text: Or what would be your attitude on that?

sentence_text: Let me pay a compliment to the president, if I may.

sentence_text: I think in those days after 9/11, I thought the president did a terrific job.

sentence_text: And I really was moved, as well as impressed, by the speech that he gave to the Congress.

sentence_text: And I think the hug Tom Daschle gave him at that moment was about as genuine a sense of there being no Democrats, no Republicans, we were all just Americans.

sentence_text: I regret to say that the president who called himself a uniter, not a divider, is now presiding over the most divided America in the recent memory of our country.

sentence_text: I’ve never seen members of a party locked out of meetings the way they’re locked out today.

sentence_text: We have to change that.

sentence_text: And as president, I am committed to changing that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I don’t care if the idea comes from the other side or this side.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I think we have to come together and work to change it.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And I’ve done that.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: Over 20 years in the United States Senate, I’ve worked with John McCain, who’s sitting here, I’ve worked with other colleagues.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’ve reached across the aisle.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: I’ve tried to find the common ground, because that’s what makes us strong as Americans.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And if Americans trust me with the presidency, I can pledge to you, we will have the most significant effort, openly — not secret meetings in the White House with special interests, not ideologically driven efforts to push people aside — but a genuine effort to try to restore America’s hope and possibilities by bringing people together.

speaker: John Kerry
sentence_text: And one of the ways we’re going to do it is, I’m going to work with my friend, John McCain, to further campaign finance reform so we get these incredible amounts of money out of the system and open it up to average people, so America is really represented by the people who make up America.

sentence_text: “ I love the optimism in that painting, because that’s how I feel about America.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And we’ve been through a lot together during the last 3 3/4 years.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We’ve come through a recession, a stock market decline, an attack on our country.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And yet, because of the hard work of the American people and good policies, this economy is growing.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Over the next four years, we’ll make sure the economy continues to grow.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We reformed our school system, and now there’s an achievement gap in America that’s beginning to close.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Over the next four years, we’ll continue to insist on excellence in every classroom in America so that our children have a chance to realize the great promise of America.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Over the next four years, we’ll continue to work to make sure health care is available and affordable.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: Over the next four years, we’ll continue to rally the armies of compassion, to help heal the hurt that exists in some of our country’s neighborhoods.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m optimistic that we’ll win the war on terror, but I understand it requires firm resolve and clear purpose.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We must never waver in the face of this enemy that — these ideologues of hate.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: And as we pursue the enemy wherever it exists, we’ll also spread freedom and liberty.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: We got great faith in the ability of liberty to transform societies, to convert a hostile world to a peaceful world.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: My hope for America is a prosperous America, a hopeful America and a safer world.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I want to thank you for listening tonight.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: I’m asking for your vote.

speaker: George W. Bush
sentence_text: God bless you.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Thank you, Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Thank you, Senator Kerry.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Well, that brings these debates to a close, but the campaign goes on.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I want to wish both of you the very best of luck between now and Election Day.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’m Bob Schieffer at CBS News.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Goodnight, everyone.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, thank you very much, Jim, and thanks to the commission and the University of Mississippi, Ole Miss, for hosting us tonight.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I can’t think of a more important time for us to talk about the future of the country.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, we are at a defining moment in our history.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Our nation is involved in two wars, and we are going through the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And although we’ve heard a lot about Wall Street, those of you on Main Street I think have been struggling for a while, and you recognize that this could have an impact on all sectors of the economy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And you’re wondering, how’s it going to affect me?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: How’s it going to affect my job?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: How’s it going to affect my house?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: How’s it going to affect my retirement savings or my ability to send my children to college?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So we have to move swiftly, and we have to move wisely.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I’ve put forward a series of proposals that make sure that we protect taxpayers as we engage in this important rescue effort.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number one, we’ve got to make sure that we’ve got oversight over this whole process; $700 billion, potentially, is a lot of money.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number two, we’ve got to make sure that taxpayers, when they are putting their money at risk, have the possibility of getting that money back and gains, if the market — and when the market returns.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number three, we’ve got to make sure that none of that money is going to pad CEO bank accounts or to promote golden parachutes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, number four, we’ve got to make sure that we’re helping homeowners, because the root problem here has to do with the foreclosures that are taking place all across the country.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, we also have to recognize that this is a final verdict on eight years of failed economic policies promoted by George Bush, supported by Senator McCain, a theory that basically says that we can shred regulations and consumer protections and give more and more to the most, and somehow prosperity will trickle down.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It hasn’t worked.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think that the fundamentals of the economy have to be measured by whether or not the middle class is getting a fair shake.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s why I’m running for president, and that’s what I hope we’re going to be talking about tonight.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator McCain, two minutes.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, thank you, Jim.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And thanks to everybody.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I do have a sad note tonight.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Kennedy is in the hospital.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He’s a dear and beloved friend to all of us.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Our thoughts and prayers go out to the lion of the Senate.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I also want to thank the University of Mississippi for hosting us tonight.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, Jim, I — I’ve been not feeling too great about a lot of things lately.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So have a lot of Americans who are facing challenges.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I’m feeling a little better tonight, and I’ll tell you why.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Because as we’re here tonight in this debate, we are seeing, for the first time in a long time, Republicans and Democrats together, sitting down, trying to work out a solution to this fiscal crisis that we’re in.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And have no doubt about the magnitude of this crisis.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’re not talking about failure of institutions on Wall Street.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’re talking about failures on Main Street, and people who will lose their jobs, and their credits, and their homes, if we don’t fix the greatest fiscal crisis, probably in — certainly in our time, and I’ve been around a little while.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the point is — the point is, we have finally seen Republicans and Democrats sitting down and negotiating together and coming up with a package.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This package has transparency in it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It has to have accountability and oversight.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It has to have options for loans to failing businesses, rather than the government taking over those loans.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We have to — it has to have a package with a number of other essential elements to it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, yes, I went back to Washington, and I met with my Republicans in the House of Representatives.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And they weren’t part of the negotiations, and I understand that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it was the House Republicans that decided that they would be part of the solution to this problem.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I want to emphasize one point to all Americans tonight.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This isn’t the beginning of the end of this crisis.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This is the end of the beginning, if we come out with a package that will keep these institutions stable.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’ve got a lot of work to do.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’ve got to create jobs.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And one of the areas, of course, is to eliminate our dependence on foreign oil.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, let’s go back to my question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: How do you all stand on the recovery plan?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And talk to each other about it.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’ve got five minutes.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We can negotiate a deal right here.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But, I mean, are you — do you favor this plan, Senator Obama, and you, Senator McCain?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you — are you in favor of this plan?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We haven’t seen the language yet.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I do think that there’s constructive work being done out there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So, for the viewers who are watching, I am optimistic about the capacity of us to come together with a plan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The question, I think, that we have to ask ourselves is, how did we get into this situation in the first place?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Two years ago, I warned that, because of the subprime lending mess, because of the lax regulation, that we were potentially going to have a problem and tried to stop some of the abuses in mortgages that were taking place at the time.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Last year, I wrote to the secretary of the Treasury to make sure that he understood the magnitude of this problem and to call on him to bring all the stakeholders together to try to deal with it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So — so the question, I think, that we’ve got to ask ourselves is, yes, we’ve got to solve this problem short term.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we are going to have to intervene; there’s no doubt about that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we’re also going to have to look at, how is it that we shredded so many regulations?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We did not set up a 21st-century regulatory framework to deal with these problems.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that in part has to do with an economic philosophy that says that regulation is always bad.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Are you going to vote for the plan, Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I — I hope so.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: As a United States senator…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Sure.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: … you’re going to vote for the plan?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Sure.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But — but let me — let me point out, I also warned about Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and warned about corporate greed and excess, and CEO pay, and all that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: A lot of us saw this train wreck coming.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But there’s also the issue of responsibility.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You’ve mentioned President Dwight David Eisenhower.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: President Eisenhower, on the night before the Normandy invasion, went into his room, and he wrote out two letters.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: One of them was a letter congratulating the great members of the military and allies that had conducted and succeeded in the greatest invasion in history, still to this day, and forever.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And he wrote out another letter, and that was a letter of resignation from the United States Army for the failure of the landings at Normandy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Somehow we’ve lost that accountability.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve been heavily criticized because I called for the resignation of the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to start also holding people accountable, and we’ve got to reward people who succeed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But somehow in Washington today — and I’m afraid on Wall Street — greed is rewarded, excess is rewarded, and corruption — or certainly failure to carry out our responsibility is rewarded.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: As president of the United States, people are going to be held accountable in my administration.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I promise you that that will happen.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you have something directly to say, Senator Obama, to Senator McCain about what he just said?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, I think Senator McCain’s absolutely right that we need more responsibility, but we need it not just when there’s a crisis.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I mean, we’ve had years in which the reigning economic ideology has been what’s good for Wall Street, but not what’s good for Main Street.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And there are folks out there who’ve been struggling before this crisis took place.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s why it’s so important, as we solve this short-term problem, that we look at some of the underlying issues that have led to wages and incomes for ordinary Americans to go down, the — a health care system that is broken, energy policies that are not working, because, you know, 10 days ago, John said that the fundamentals of the economy are sound.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Say it directly to him.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I do not think that they are.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Say it directly to him.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, the — John, 10 days ago, you said that the fundamentals of the economy are sound.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Are you afraid I couldn’t hear him?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I’m just determined to get you all to talk to each other.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I’m going to try.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The — and I just fundamentally disagree.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And unless we are holding ourselves accountable day in, day out, not just when there’s a crisis for folks who have power and influence and can hire lobbyists, but for the nurse, the teacher, the police officer, who, frankly, at the end of each month, they’ve got a little financial crisis going on.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They’re having to take out extra debt just to make their mortgage payments.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We haven’t been paying attention to them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if you look at our tax policies, it’s a classic example.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: So, Senator McCain, do you agree with what Senator Obama just said?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And, if you don’t, tell him what you disagree with.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: No, I — look, we’ve got to fix the system.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got fundamental problems in the system.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And Main Street is paying a penalty for the excesses and greed in Washington, D.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: , and in the Wall Street.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So there’s no doubt that we have a long way to go.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, obviously, stricter interpretation and consolidation of the various regulatory agencies that weren’t doing their job, that has brought on this crisis.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I have a fundamental belief in the goodness and strength of the American worker.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the American worker is the most productive, the most innovative.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: America is still the greatest producer, exporter and importer.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But we’ve got to get through these times, but I have a fundamental belief in the United States of America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I still believe, under the right leadership, our best days are ahead of us.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, let’s go to the next lead question, which is essentially following up on this same subject.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And you get two minutes to begin with, Senator McCain.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And using your word “fundamental,” are there fundamental differences between your approach and Senator Obama’s approach to what you would do as president to lead this country out of the financial crisis?

sentence_text: Well, the first thing we have to do is get spending under control in Washington.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s completely out of control.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s gone — we have now presided over the largest increase in the size of government since the Great Society.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We Republicans came to power to change government, and government changed us.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the — the worst symptom on this disease is what my friend, Tom Coburn, calls earmarking as a gateway drug, because it’s a gateway.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s a gateway to out-of-control spending and corruption.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we have former members of Congress now residing in federal prison because of the evils of this earmarking and pork-barrel spending.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You know, we spent $3 million to study the DNA of bears in Montana.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I don’t know if that was a criminal issue or a paternal issue, but the fact is that it was $3 million of our taxpayers’ money.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it has got to be brought under control.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: As president of the United States, I want to assure you, I’ve got a pen.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This one’s kind of old.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve got a pen, and I’m going to veto every single spending bill that comes across my desk.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I will make them famous.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You will know their names.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, Senator Obama, you wanted to know one of the differences.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He has asked for $932 million of earmark pork-barrel spending, nearly a million dollars for every day that he’s been in the United States Senate.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I suggest that people go up on the Web site of Citizens Against Government Waste, and they’ll look at those projects.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That kind of thing is not the way to rein in runaway spending in Washington, D.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s one of the fundamental differences that Senator Obama and I have.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator Obama, two minutes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, Senator McCain is absolutely right that the earmarks process has been abused, which is why I suspended any requests for my home state, whether it was for senior centers or what have you, until we cleaned it up.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And he’s also right that oftentimes lobbyists and special interests are the ones that are introducing these kinds of requests, although that wasn’t the case with me.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But let’s be clear: Earmarks account for $18 billion in last year’s budget.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain is proposing — and this is a fundamental difference between us — $300 billion in tax cuts to some of the wealthiest corporations and individuals in the country, $300 billion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, $18 billion is important; $300 billion is really important.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And in his tax plan, you would have CEOs of Fortune 500 companies getting an average of $700,000 in reduced taxes, while leaving 100 million Americans out.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So my attitude is, we’ve got to grow the economy from the bottom up.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What I’ve called for is a tax cut for 95 percent of working families, 95 percent.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that means that the ordinary American out there who’s collecting a paycheck every day, they’ve got a little extra money to be able to buy a computer for their kid, to fill up on this gas that is killing them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And over time, that, I think, is going to be a better recipe for economic growth than the — the policies of President Bush that John McCain wants to — wants to follow.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, again, I don’t mean to go back and forth, but he…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: No, that’s fine.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama suspended those requests for pork-barrel projects after he was running for president of the United States.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He didn’t happen to see that light during the first three years as a member of the United States Senate, $932 million in requests.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Maybe to Senator Obama it’s not a lot of money.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the point is that — you see, I hear this all the time.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: “It’s only $18 billion.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” Do you know that it’s tripled in the last five years?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Do you know that it’s gone completely out of control to the point where it corrupts people?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It corrupts people.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s why we have, as I said, people under federal indictment and charges.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s a system that’s got to be cleaned up.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have fought against it my career.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have fought against it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I was called the sheriff, by the — one of the senior members of the Appropriations Committee.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I didn’t win Miss Congeniality in the United States Senate.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, Senator Obama didn’t mention that, along with his tax cuts, he is also proposing some $800 billion in new spending on new programs.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, that’s a fundamental difference between myself and Senator Obama.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want to cut spending.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want to keep taxes low.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The worst thing we could do in this economic climate is to raise people’s taxes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I — I don’t know where John is getting his figures.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let’s just be clear.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What I do is I close corporate loopholes, stop providing tax cuts to corporations that are shipping jobs overseas so that we’re giving tax breaks to companies that are investing here in the United States.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I make sure that we have a health care system that allows for everyone to have basic coverage.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think those are pretty important priorities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I pay for every dime of it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But let’s go back to the original point.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: John, nobody is denying that $18 billion is important.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, absolutely, we need earmark reform.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when I’m president, I will go line by line to make sure that we are not spending money unwisely.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But the fact is that eliminating earmarks alone is not a recipe for how we’re going to get the middle class back on track.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when you look at your tax policies that are directed primarily at those who are doing well, and you are neglecting people who are really struggling right now, I think that is a continuation of the last eight years, and we can’t afford another four.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Respond directly to him about that, to Senator Obama about that, about the — he’s made it twice now, about your tax — your policies about tax cuts.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well — well, let me give you an example of what Senator Obama finds objectionable, the business tax.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Right now, in the United States of America, business pays the second-highest business taxes in the world, 35 percent.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Ireland pays 11 percent.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, if you’re a business person, and you can locate any place in the world, then, obviously, if you go to the country where it’s 11 percent tax versus 35 percent, you’re going to be able to create jobs, increase your business, make more investment, et cetera.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want to cut that business tax.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want to cut it so that businesses will remain in — in the United States of America and create jobs.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But, again, I want to return.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s a lot more than $18 billion in pork-barrel spending.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I can tell you, it’s rife.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s throughout.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The United States Senate will take up a continuing resolution tomorrow or the next day, sometime next week, with 2,000 — 2,000 — look at them, my friends.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Look at them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You’ll be appalled.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And Senator Obama is a recent convert, after requesting $932 million worth of pork-barrel spending projects.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So the point is, I want people to have tax cuts.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want every family to have a $5,000 refundable tax credit so they can go out and purchase their own health care.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want to double the dividend from $3,500 to $7,000 for every dependent child in America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I know that the worst thing we could possibly do is to raise taxes on anybody, and a lot of people might be interested in Senator Obama’s definition of “rich.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator Obama, you have a question for Senator McCain on that?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, let me just make a couple of points.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: My definition — here’s what I can tell the American people: 95 percent of you will get a tax cut.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if you make less than $250,000, less than a quarter-million dollars a year, then you will not see one dime’s worth of tax increase.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, John mentioned the fact that business taxes on paper are high in this country, and he’s absolutely right.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Here’s the problem: There are so many loopholes that have been written into the tax code, oftentimes with support of Senator McCain, that we actually see our businesses pay effectively one of the lowest tax rates in the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what that means, then, is that there are people out there who are working every day, who are not getting a tax cut, and you want to give them more.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s not like you want to close the loopholes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You just want to add an additional tax cut over the loopholes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s a problem.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Just one last point I want to make, since Senator McCain talked about providing a $5,000 health credit.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, what he doesn’t tell you is that he intends to, for the first time in history, tax health benefits.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So you may end up getting a $5,000 tax credit.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Here’s the only problem: Your employer now has to pay taxes on the health care that you’re getting from your employer.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if you end up losing your health care from your employer, you’ve got to go out on the open market and try to buy it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is not a good deal for the American people.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But it’s an example of this notion that the market can always solve everything and that the less regulation we have, the better off we’re going to be.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, you know, let me just…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’ve got to go to another lead question.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I know we have to, but this is a classic example of walking the walk and talking the talk.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We had an energy bill before the United States Senate.

speaker: John McCain

sentence_text: Senator McCain cut — Senator McCain opposed funding for troops in legislation that had a timetable, because he didn’t believe in a timetable.
