sentence_text: I opposed funding a mission that had no timetable, and was open- ended, giving a blank check to George Bush.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We had a difference on the timetable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We didn’t have a difference on whether or not we were going to be funding troops.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We had a legitimate difference, and I absolutely understand the difference between tactics and strategy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the strategic question that the president has to ask is not whether or not we are employing a particular approach in the country once we have made the decision to be there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The question is, was this wise?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have seen Afghanistan worsen, deteriorate.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We need more troops there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We need more resources there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain, in the rush to go into Iraq, said, you know what?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve been successful in Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There is nobody who can pose a threat to us there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is a time when bin Laden was still out, and now they’ve reconstituted themselves.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Secretary of Defense Robert Gates himself acknowledges the war on terrorism started in Afghanistan and it needs to end there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we can’t do it if we are not willing to give Iraq back its country.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, what I’ve said is we should end this war responsibly.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We should do it in phases.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But in 16 months we should be able to reduce our combat troops, put — provide some relief to military families and our troops and bolster our efforts in Afghanistan so that we can capture and kill bin Laden and crush al Qaeda.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And right now, the commanders in Afghanistan, as well as Admiral Mullen, have acknowledged that we don’t have enough troops to deal with Afghanistan because we still have more troops in Iraq than we did before the surge.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Admiral Mullen suggests that Senator Obama’s plan is dangerous for America.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s not the case.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s what …

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What he said was a precipitous…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s what Admiral Mullen said.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: … withdrawal would be dangerous.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He did not say that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And also General Petraeus said the same thing.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Osama bin Laden and General Petraeus have one thing in common that I know of, they both said that Iraq is the central battleground.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now General Petraeus has praised the successes, but he said those successes are fragile and if we set a specific date for withdrawal — and by the way, Senator Obama’s original plan, they would have been out last spring before the surge ever had a chance to succeed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’m — I’m — understand why Senator Obama was surprised and said that the surge succeeded beyond his wildest expectations.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It didn’t exceed beyond mine, because I know that that’s a strategy that has worked and can succeed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But if we snatch defeat from the jaws of victory and adopt Senator Obama’s plan, then we will have a wider war and it will make things more complicated throughout the region, including in Afghanistan.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Afghanistan, lead — a new — a new lead question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Now, having resolved Iraq, we’ll move to Afghanistan.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And it goes to you, Senator Obama, and it’s a — it picks up on a point that’s already been made.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you think more troops — more U.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: troops should be sent to Afghanistan, how many, and when?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Yes, I think we need more troops.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’ve been saying that for over a year now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think that we have to do it as quickly as possible, because it’s been acknowledged by the commanders on the ground the situation is getting worse, not better.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We had the highest fatalities among U.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: troops this past year than at any time since 2002.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we are seeing a major offensive taking place — Al Qaida and Taliban crossing the border and attacking our troops in a brazen fashion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They are feeling emboldened.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we cannot separate Afghanistan from Iraq, because what our commanders have said is we don’t have the troops right now to deal with Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So I would send two to three additional brigades to Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, keep in mind that we have four times the number of troops in Iraq, where nobody had anything to do with 9/11 before we went in, where, in fact, there was no Al Qaida before we went in, but we have four times more troops there than we do in Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that is a strategic mistake, because every intelligence agency will acknowledge that Al Qaida is the greatest threat against the United States and that Secretary of Defense Gates acknowledged the central front — that the place where we have to deal with these folks is going to be in Afghanistan and in Pakistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So here’s what we have to do comprehensively, though.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s not just more troops.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have to press the Afghan government to make certain that they are actually working for their people.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I’ve said this to President Karzai.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number two, we’ve got to deal with a growing poppy trade that has exploded over the last several years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number three, we’ve got to deal with Pakistan, because Al Qaida and the Taliban have safe havens in Pakistan, across the border in the northwest regions, and although, you know, under George Bush, with the support of Senator McCain, we’ve been giving them $10 billion over the last seven years, they have not done what needs to be done to get rid of those safe havens.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And until we do, Americans here at home are not going to be safe.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Afghanistan, Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: First of all, I won’t repeat the mistake that I regret enormously, and that is, after we were able to help the Afghan freedom fighters and drive the Russians out of Afghanistan, we basically washed our hands of the region.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the result over time was the Taliban, Al Qaida, and a lot of the difficulties we are facing today.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So we can’t ignore those lessons of history.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, on this issue of aiding Pakistan, if you’re going to aim a gun at somebody, George Shultz, our great secretary of state, told me once, you’d better be prepared to pull the trigger.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m not prepared at this time to cut off aid to Pakistan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So I’m not prepared to threaten it, as Senator Obama apparently wants to do, as he has said that he would announce military strikes into Pakistan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to get the support of the people of — of Pakistan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He said that he would launch military strikes into Pakistan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, you don’t do that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You don’t say that out loud.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: If you have to do things, you have to do things, and you work with the Pakistani government.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, the new president of Pakistan, Kardari , has got his hands full.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And this area on the border has not been governed since the days of Alexander the Great.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve been to Waziristan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I can see how tough that terrain is.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s ruled by a handful of tribes.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, yes, Senator Obama calls for more troops, but what he doesn’t understand, it’s got to be a new strategy, the same strategy that he condemned in Iraq.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s going to have to be employed in Afghanistan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’re going to have to help the Pakistanis go into these areas and obtain the allegiance of the people.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it’s going to be tough.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They’ve intermarried with Al Qaida and the Taliban.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it’s going to be tough.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But we have to get the cooperation of the people in those areas.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the Pakistanis are going to have to understand that that bombing in the Marriott Hotel in Islamabad was a signal from the terrorists that they don’t want that government to cooperate with us in combating the Taliban and jihadist elements.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So we’ve got a lot of work to do in Afghanistan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I’m confident, now that General Petraeus is in the new position of command, that we will employ a strategy which not only means additional troops — and, by the way, there have been 20,000 additional troops, from 32,000 to 53,000, and there needs to be more.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So it’s not just the addition of troops that matters.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s a strategy that will succeed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And Pakistan is a very important element in this.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I know how to work with them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I guarantee you I would not publicly state that I’m going to attack them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Nobody talked about attacking Pakistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Here’s what I said.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if John wants to disagree with this, he can let me know, that, if the United States has Al Qaida, bin Laden, top-level lieutenants in our sights, and Pakistan is unable or unwilling to act, then we should take them out.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, I think that’s the right strategy; I think that’s the right policy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, John, I — you’re absolutely right that presidents have to be prudent in what they say.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But, you know, coming from you, who, you know, in the past has threatened extinction for North Korea and, you know, sung songs about bombing Iran, I don’t know, you know, how credible that is.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think this is the right strategy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, Senator McCain is also right that it’s difficult.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is not an easy situation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You’ve got cross-border attacks against U.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: troops.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we’ve got a choice.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We could allow our troops to just be on the defensive and absorb those blows again and again and again, if Pakistan is unwilling to cooperate, or we have to start making some decisions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the problem, John, with the strategy that’s been pursued was that, for 10 years, we coddled Musharraf, we alienated the Pakistani population, because we were anti-democratic.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We had a 20th-century mindset that basically said, “Well, you know, he may be a dictator, but he’s our dictator.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” And as a consequence, we lost legitimacy in Pakistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We spent $10 billion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And in the meantime, they weren’t going after Al Qaida, and they are more powerful now than at any time since we began the war in Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s going to change when I’m president of the United States.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I — I don’t think that Senator Obama understands that there was a failed state in Pakistan when Musharraf came to power.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Everybody who was around then, and had been there, and knew about it knew that it was a failed state.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But let me tell you, you know, this business about bombing Iran and all that, let me tell you my record.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Back in 1983, when I was a brand-new United States congressman, the one — the person I admired the most and still admire the most, Ronald Reagan, wanted to send Marines into Lebanon.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I saw that, and I saw the situation, and I stood up, and I voted against that, because I was afraid that they couldn’t make peace in a place where 300 or 400 or several hundred Marines would make a difference.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Tragically, I was right: Nearly 300 Marines lost their lives in the bombing of the barracks.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And then we had Somalia — then we had the first Gulf War.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I supported — I supported that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I supported us going into Bosnia, when a number of my own party and colleagues was against that operation in Bosnia.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That was the right thing to do, to stop genocide and to preserve what was necessary inside of Europe.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I supported what we did in Kosovo.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I supported it because ethnic cleansing and genocide was taking place there.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I have a record — and Somalia, I opposed that we should turn — turn the force in Somalia from a peacekeeping force into a peacemaking force, which they were not capable of.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So I have a record.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have a record of being involved in these national security issues, which involve the highest responsibility and the toughest decisions that any president can make, and that is to send our young men and women into harm’s way.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’ll tell you, I had a town hall meeting in Wolfeboro, New Hampshire, and a woman stood up and she said, “Senator McCain, I want you to do me the honor of wearing a bracelet with my son’s name on it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” He was 22 years old and he was killed in combat outside of Baghdad, Matthew Stanley, before Christmas last year.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This was last August, a year ago.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I said, “I will — I will wear his bracelet with honor.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” And this was August, a year ago.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And then she said, “But, Senator McCain, I want you to do everything — promise me one thing, that you’ll do everything in your power to make sure that my son’s death was not in vain.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” That means that that mission succeeds, just like those young people who re-enlisted in Baghdad, just like the mother I met at the airport the other day whose son was killed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And they all say to me that we don’t want defeat.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I know what thatâ€™s like when an army is defeated.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: A war that I was in, where we had an Army, that it wasn’t through any fault of their own, but they were defeated.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I know how hard it is for that — for an Army and a military to recover from that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it did and we will win this one and we won’t come home in defeat and dishonor and probably have to go back if we fail.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Jim, let me just make a point.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’ve got a bracelet, too, from Sergeant – from the mother of Sergeant Ryan David Jopeck , given to me in green bay.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: She asked me, can you please make sure another mother is not going through what I’m going through.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: No U.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: soldier ever dies in vain because they’re carrying out the missions of their commander in chief.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we honor all the service that they’ve provided.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Our troops have performed brilliantly.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The question is for the next president, are we making good judgments about how to keep America safe precisely because sending our military into battle is such an enormous step.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the point that I originally made is that we took our eye off Afghanistan, we took our eye off the folks who perpetrated 9/11, they are still sending out videotapes and Senator McCain, nobody is talking about defeat in Iraq, but I have to say we are having enormous problems in Afghanistan because of that decision.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it is not true you have consistently been concerned about what happened in Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: At one point, while you were focused on Iraq, you said well, we can “muddle through” Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You don’t muddle through the central front on terror and you don’t muddle through going after bin Laden.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You don’t muddle through stamping out the Taliban.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that is something we have to take seriously.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when I’m president, I will.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: New …

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You might think that with that kind of concern that Senator Obama would have gone to Afghanistan, particularly given his responsibilities as a subcommittee chairman.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: By the way, when I’m subcommittee chairman, we take up the issues under my subcommittee.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the important thing is — the important thing is I visited Afghanistan and I traveled to Waziristan and I traveled to these places and I know what our security requirements are.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I know what our needs are.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So the point is that we will prevail in Afghanistan, but we need the new strategy and we need it to succeed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the important thing is, if we suffer defeat in Iraq, which General Petraeus predicts we will, if we adopted Senator Obama’s set date for withdrawal, then that will have a calamitous effect in Afghanistan and American national security interests in the region.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama doesn’t seem to understand there is a connected between the two.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I have some good news and bad news for the two of you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You all are even on time, which is remarkable, considering we’ve been going at it …

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: A testimony to you, Jim.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I don’t know about that.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But the bad news is all my little five minute things have run over, so, anyhow, we’ll adjust as we get there.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But the amount of time is even.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: New lead question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And it goes two minutes to you, Senator McCain, what is your reading on the threat from Iran right now to the security of the United States?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: My reading of the threat from Iran is that if Iran acquires nuclear weapons, it is an existential threat to the State of Israel and it is a threat to other countries in the region because the other countries in the region will feel compelling requirement to acquire nuclear weapons as well.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now we cannot allow a second Holocaust.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let’s just make that very clear.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: What I have proposed for a long time, and I’ve had conversation with foreign leaders about forming a league of democracies, let’s be clear and let’s have some straight talk.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The Russians are preventing significant action in the United Nations Security Council.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have proposed a league of democracies, a group of people – a group of countries that share common interests, common values, common ideals, they also control a lot of the world’s economic power.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We could impose significant meaningful, painful sanctions on the Iranians that I think could have a beneficial effect.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The Iranians have a lousy government, so therefore their economy is lousy, even though they have significant oil revenues.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So I am convinced that together, we can, with the French, with the British, with the Germans and other countries, democracies around the world, we can affect Iranian behavior.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But have no doubt, but have no doubt that the Iranians continue on the path to the acquisition of a nuclear weapon as we speak tonight.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it is a threat not only in this region but around the world.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: What I’d also like to point out the Iranians are putting the most lethal IEDs into Iraq which are killing young Americans, there are special groups in Iran coming into Iraq and are being trained in Iran.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: There is the Republican Guard in Iran, which Senator Kyl had an amendment in order to declare them a sponsor of terror.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama said that would be provocative.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So this is a serious threat.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This is a serious threat to security in the world, and I believe we can act and we can act with our friends and allies and reduce that threat as quickly as possible, but have no doubt about the ultimate result of them acquiring nuclear weapons.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Two minutes on Iran, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, let me just correct something very quickly.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I believe the Republican Guard of Iran is a terrorist organization.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’ve consistently said so.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What Senator McCain refers to is a measure in the Senate that would try to broaden the mandate inside of Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: To deal with Iran.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And ironically, the single thing that has strengthened Iran over the last several years has been the war in Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Iraq was Iran’s mortal enemy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That was cleared away.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what we’ve seen over the last several years is Iran’s influence grow.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They have funded Hezbollah, they have funded Hamas, they have gone from zero centrifuges to 4,000 centrifuges to develop a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So obviously, our policy over the last eight years has not worked.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain is absolutely right, we cannot tolerate a nuclear Iran.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It would be a game changer.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Not only would it threaten Israel, a country that is our stalwart ally, but it would also create an environment in which you could set off an arms race in this Middle East.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now here’s what we need to do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We do need tougher sanctions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I do not agree with Senator McCain that we’re going to be able to execute the kind of sanctions we need without some cooperation with countries like Russia and China that are, I think Senator McCain would agree, not democracies, but have extensive trade with Iran but potentially have an interest in making sure Iran doesn’t have a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we are also going to have to, I believe, engage in tough direct diplomacy with Iran and this is a major difference I have with Senator McCain, this notion that by not talking to people we are punishing them has not worked.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It has not worked in Iran, it has not worked in North Korea.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In each instance, our efforts at isolation have actually accelerated their efforts to get nuclear weapons.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That will change when I’m president of the United States.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Senator, what about talking?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama twice said in debates he would sit down with Ahmadinejad, Chavez and Raul Castro without precondition.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Without precondition.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Here is Ahmadinenene , Ahmadinejad, who is, Ahmadinejad, who is now in New York, talking about the extermination of the State of Israel, of wiping Israel off the map, and we’re going to sit down, without precondition, across the table, to legitimize and give a propaganda platform to a person that is espousing the extermination of the state of Israel, and therefore then giving them more credence in the world arena and therefore saying, they’ve probably been doing the right thing, because you will sit down across the table from them and that will legitimize their illegal behavior.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The point is that throughout history, whether it be Ronald Reagan, who wouldn’t sit down with Brezhnev, Andropov or Chernenko until Gorbachev was ready with glasnost and perestroika.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Or whether it be Nixon’s trip to China, which was preceded by Henry Kissinger, many times before he went.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Look, I’ll sit down with anybody, but there’s got to be pre-conditions.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Those pre-conditions would apply that we wouldn’t legitimize with a face to face meeting, a person like Ahmadinejad.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, Senator Obama said, without preconditions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So let’s talk about this.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: First of all, Ahmadinejad is not the most powerful person in Iran.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So he may not be the right person to talk to.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I reserve the right, as president of the United States to meet with anybody at a time and place of my choosing if I think it’s going to keep America safe.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I’m glad that Senator McCain brought up the history, the bipartisan history of us engaging in direct diplomacy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain mentioned Henry Kissinger, who’s one of his advisers, who, along with five recent secretaries of state, just said that we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is one of your own advisers.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, understand what this means “without preconditions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” It doesn’t mean that you invite them over for tea one day.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What it means is that we don’t do what we’ve been doing, which is to say, “Until you agree to do exactly what we say, we won’t have direct contacts with you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” There’s a difference between preconditions and preparation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Of course we’ve got to do preparations, starting with low-level diplomatic talks, and it may not work, because Iran is a rogue regime.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I will point out that I was called naive when I suggested that we need to look at exploring contacts with Iran.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And you know what?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: President Bush recently sent a senior ambassador, Bill Burns, to participate in talks with the Europeans around the issue of nuclear weapons.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Again, it may not work, but if it doesn’t work, then we have strengthened our ability to form alliances to impose the tough sanctions that Senator McCain just mentioned.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when we haven’t done it, as in North Korea — let me just take one more example — in North Korea, we cut off talks.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They’re a member of the axis of evil.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We can’t deal with them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And you know what happened?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They went — they quadrupled their nuclear capacity.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They tested a nuke.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They tested missiles.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They pulled out of the nonproliferation agreement.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they sent nuclear secrets, potentially, to countries like Syria.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When we re-engaged — because, again, the Bush administration reversed course on this — then we have at least made some progress, although right now, because of the problems in North Korea, we are seeing it on shaky ground.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And — and I just — so I just have to make this general point that the Bush administration, some of Senator McCain’s own advisers all think this is important, and Senator McCain appears resistant.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He even said the other day that he would not meet potentially with the prime minister of Spain, because he — you know, he wasn’t sure whether they were aligned with us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I mean, Spain?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Spain is a NATO ally.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Of course.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If we can’t meet with our friends, I don’t know how we’re going to lead the world in terms of dealing with critical issues like terrorism.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m not going to set the White House visitors schedule before I’m president of the United States.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I don’t even have a seal yet.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Look, Dr.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Kissinger did not say that he would approve of face-to- face meetings between the president of the United States and the president — and Ahmadinejad.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He did not say that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Of course not.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He said that there could be secretary-level and lower level meetings.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve always encouraged them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The Iranians have met with Ambassador Crocker in Baghdad.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: What Senator Obama doesn’t seem to understand that if without precondition you sit down across the table from someone who has called Israel a “stinking corpse,” and wants to destroy that country and wipe it off the map, you legitimize those comments.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This is dangerous.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It isn’t just naive; it’s dangerous.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And so we just have a fundamental difference of opinion.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: As far as North Korea is concerned, our secretary of state, Madeleine Albright, went to North Korea.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: By the way, North Korea, most repressive and brutal regime probably on Earth.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The average South Korean is three inches taller than the average North Korean, a huge gulag.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We don’t know what the status of the dear leader’s health is today, but we know this, that the North Koreans have broken every agreement that they’ve entered into.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we ought to go back to a little bit of Ronald Reagan’s “trust, but verify,” and certainly not sit down across the table from — without precondition, as Senator Obama said he did twice, I mean, it’s just dangerous.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Look, I mean, Senator McCain keeps on using this example that suddenly the president would just meet with somebody without doing any preparation, without having low-level talks.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Nobody’s been talking about that, and Senator McCain knows it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is a mischaracterization of my position.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When we talk about preconditions — and Henry Kissinger did say we should have contacts without preconditions — the idea is that we do not expect to solve every problem before we initiate talks.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, you know, the Bush administration has come to recognize that it hasn’t worked, this notion that we are simply silent when it comes to our enemies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the notion that we would sit with Ahmadinejad and not say anything while he’s spewing his nonsense and his vile comments is ridiculous.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Nobody is even talking about that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So let me get this right.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We sit down with Ahmadinejad, and he says, “We’re going to wipe Israel off the face of the Earth,” and we say, “No, you’re not”?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Oh, please.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: No, let me tell…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: By the way, my friend, Dr.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Kissinger, who’s been my friend for 35 years, would be interested to hear this conversation and Senator Obama’s depiction of his — of his positions on the issue.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve known him for 35 years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We will take a look.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I guarantee you he would not — he would not say that presidential top level.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Nobody’s talking about that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Of course he encourages and other people encourage contacts, and negotiations, and all other things.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We do that all the time.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’re going to go to a new…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And Senator Obama is parsing words when he says precondition means preparation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I am not parsing words.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He’s parsing words, my friends.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’m using the same words that your advisers use.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Please, go ahead.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: New lead question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Russia, goes to you, two minutes, Senator Obama.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: How do you see the relationship with Russia?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you see them as a competitor?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you see them as an enemy?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you see them as a potential partner?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, I think that, given what’s happened over the last several weeks and months, our entire Russian approach has to be evaluated, because a resurgent and very aggressive Russia is a threat to the peace and stability of the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Their actions in Georgia were unacceptable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They were unwarranted.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And at this point, it is absolutely critical for the next president to make clear that we have to follow through on our six-party — or the six-point cease-fire.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They have to remove themselves from South Ossetia and Abkhazia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is absolutely important that we have a unified alliance and that we explain to the Russians that you cannot be a 21st-century superpower, or power, and act like a 20th-century dictatorship.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we also have to affirm all the fledgling democracies in that region, you know, the Estonians, the Lithuanians, the Latvians, the Poles, the Czechs, that we are, in fact, going to be supportive and in solidarity with them in their efforts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They are members of NATO.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And to countries like Georgia and the Ukraine, I think we have to insist that they are free to join NATO if they meet the requirements, and they should have a membership action plan immediately to start bringing them in.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, we also can’t return to a Cold War posture with respect to Russia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s important that we recognize there are going to be some areas of common interest.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: One is nuclear proliferation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They have not only 15,000 nuclear warheads, but they’ve got enough to make another 40,000, and some of those loose nukes could fall into the hands of Al Qaida.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is an area where I’ve led on in the Senate, working with a Republican ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Dick Lugar, to deal with the proliferation of loose nuclear weapons.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s an area where we’re going to have to work with Russia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we have to have a president who is clear that you don’t deal with Russia based on staring into his eyes and seeing his soul.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You deal with Russia based on, what are your — what are the national security interests of the United States of America?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we have to recognize that the way they’ve been behaving lately demands a sharp response from the international community and our allies.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Two minutes on Russia, Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, I was interested in Senator Obama’s reaction to the Russian aggression against Georgia.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: His first statement was, “Both sides ought to show restraint.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” Again, a little bit of naivete there.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He doesn’t understand that Russia committed serious aggression against Georgia.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And Russia has now become a nation fueled by petro-dollars that is basically a KGB apparatchik-run government.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I looked into Mr.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Putin’s eyes, and I saw three letters, a “K,” a “G,” and a “B.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” And their aggression in Georgia is not acceptable behavior.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I don’t believe we’re going to go back to the Cold War.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I am sure that that will not happen.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I do believe that we need to bolster our friends and allies.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And that wasn’t just about a problem between Georgia and Russia.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It had everything to do with energy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: There’s a pipeline that runs from the Caspian through Georgia through Turkey.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, of course, we know that the Russians control other sources of energy into Europe, which they have used from time to time.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s not accidental that the presidents of Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania, Poland, and Ukraine flew to Georgia, flew to Tbilisi, where I have spent significant amount of time with a great young president, Misha Saakashvili.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And they showed solidarity with them, but, also, they are very concerned about the Russian threats to regain their status of the old Russian to regain their status of the old Russian empire.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, I think the Russians ought to understand that we will support — we, the United States — will support the inclusion of Georgia and Ukraine in the natural process, inclusion into NATO.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We also ought to make it very clear that the Russians are in violation of their cease-fire agreement.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They have stationed additional troops in Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: By the way, I went there once, and we went inside and drove in, and there was a huge poster.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And this is — this is Georgian territory.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And there was a huge poster of Vladimir Putin, and it said, “Vladimir Putin, our president.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” It was very clear, the Russian intentions towards Georgia.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They were just waiting to seize the opportunity.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So, this is a very difficult situation.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We want to work with the Russians.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But we also have every right to expect the Russians to behave in a fashion and keeping with a — with a — with a country who respects international boundaries and the norms of international behavior.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And watch Ukraine.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This whole thing has got a lot to do with Ukraine, Crimea, the base of the Russian fleet in Sevastopol.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the breakdown of the political process in Ukraine between Tymoshenko and Yushchenko is a very serious problem.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So watch Ukraine, and let’s make sure that we — that the Ukrainians understand that we are their friend and ally.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You see any — do you have a major difference with what he just said?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: No, actually, I think Senator McCain and I agree for the most part on these issues.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Obviously, I disagree with this notion that somehow we did not forcefully object to Russians going into Georgia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I immediately said that this was illegal and objectionable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, absolutely, I wanted a cessation of the violence, because it put an enormous strain on Georgia, and that’s why I was the first to say that we have to rebuild the Georgian economy and called for a billion dollars that has now gone in to help them rebuild.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because part of Russia’s intentions here was to weaken the economy to the point where President Saakashvili was so weakened that he might be replaced by somebody that Putin favored more.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Two points I think are important to think about when it comes to Russia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number one is we have to have foresight and anticipate some of these problems.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So back in April, I warned the administration that you had Russian peacekeepers in Georgian territory.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That made no sense whatsoever.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what we needed to do was replace them with international peacekeepers and a special envoy to resolve the crisis before it boiled over.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That wasn’t done.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But had it been done, it’s possible we could have avoided the issue.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The second point I want to make is — is the issue of energy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Russia is in part resurgent and Putin is feeling powerful because of petro-dollars, as Senator McCain mentioned.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That means that we, as one of the biggest consumers of oil — 25 percent of the world’s oil — have to have an energy strategy not just to deal with Russia, but to deal with many of the rogue states we’ve talked about, Iran, Venezuela.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that means, yes, increasing domestic production and off-shore drilling, but we only have 3 percent of the world’s oil supplies and we use 25 percent of the world’s oil.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So we can’t simply drill our way out of the problem.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What we’re going to have to do is to approach it through alternative energy, like solar, and wind, and biodiesel, and, yes, nuclear energy, clean-coal technology.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, you know, I’ve got a plan for us to make a significant investment over the next 10 years to do that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I have to say, Senator McCain and I, I think agree on the importance of energy, but Senator McCain mentioned earlier the importance of looking at a record.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Over 26 years, Senator McCain voted 23 times against alternative energy, like solar, and wind, and biodiesel.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so we — we — we’ve got to walk the walk and not just talk the talk when it comes to energy independence, because this is probably going to be just as vital for our economy and the pain that people are feeling at the pump — and, you know, winter’s coming and home heating oil — as it is our national security and the issue of climate change that’s so important.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’ve got time for one more lead question segment.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’re way out of…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Quick response and then…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: No one from Arizona is against solar.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And Senator Obama says he’s for nuclear, but he’s against reprocessing and he’s against storing.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s just not true, John.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: John, I’m sorry, but that’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: … it’s hard to get there from here.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And off-shore drilling is also something that is very important and it is a bridge.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we know that, if we drill off-shore and exploit a lot of these reserves, it will help, at temporarily, relieve our energy requirements.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it will have, I think, an important effect on the price of a barrel of oil.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I just have to respond very quickly, just to correct — just to correct the record.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So I want to say that, with the Nunn-Lugar thing…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Excuse me, Senator.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: John?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: … I supported Nunn-Lugar back in the early 1990s when a lot of my colleagues didn’t.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That was the key legislation at the time and put us on the road to eliminating this issue of nuclear waste and the nuclear fuel that has to be taken care of.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I — I just have to correct the record here.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I have never said that I object to nuclear waste.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What I’ve said is that we have to store it safely.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, Senator McCain, he says — he talks about Arizona.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’ve got to make this point, Jim.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He objects…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have voted for alternate fuel all of my time…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He — he — he objects…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: One at a time, please.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He objected…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: One at a time.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: No one can be opposed to alternate energy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: All right, fair enough.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let’s move on.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You’ve got one more energy — you’ve got one more question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: This is the last — last lead question.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You have two minutes each.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And the question is this, beginning with you, Senator McCain.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: What do you think the likelihood is that there would be another 9/11-type attack on the continental United States?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think it’s much less than it was the day after 9/11.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think it — that we have a safer nation, but we are a long way from safe.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I want to tell you that one of the things I’m most proud of, among others, because I have worked across the aisle.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have a long record on that, on a long series of reforms.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But after 9/11, Senator Joe Lieberman and I decided that we needed a commission, and that was a commission to investigate 9/11, and find out what happened, and fix it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we were — we were opposed by the administration, another area where I differed with this administration.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we were stymied until the families of 9/11 came, and they descended on Washington, and we got that legislation passed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And there were a series of recommendations, as I recall, more than 40.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’m happy to say that we’ve gotten written into law most of those reforms recommended by that commission.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m proud of that work, again, bipartisan, reaching across the aisle, working together, Democrat and Republican alike.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So we have a long way to go in our intelligence services.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We have to do a better job in human intelligence.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’ve got to — to make sure that we have people who are trained interrogators so that we don’t ever torture a prisoner ever again.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We have to make sure that our technological and intelligence capabilities are better.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We have to work more closely with our allies.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I know our allies, and I can work much more closely with them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I can tell you that I think America is safer today than it was on 9/11.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But that doesn’t mean that we don’t have a long way to go.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’d like to remind you, also, as a result of those recommendations, we’ve probably had the largest reorganization of government since we established the Defense Department.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I think that those men and women in those agencies are doing a great job.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But we still have a long way to go before we can declare America safe, and that means doing a better job along our borders, as well.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Two minutes, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, first of all, I think that we are safer in some ways.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Obviously, we’ve poured billions of dollars into airport security.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have done some work in terms of securing potential targets, but we still have a long way to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to make sure that we’re hardening our chemical sites.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We haven’t done enough in terms of transit; we haven’t done enough in terms of ports.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the biggest threat that we face right now is not a nuclear missile coming over the skies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s in a suitcase.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is why the issue of nuclear proliferation is so important.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is the — the biggest threat to the United States is a terrorist getting their hands on nuclear weapons.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we — we are spending billions of dollars on missile defense.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I actually believe that we need missile defense, because of Iran and North Korea and the potential for them to obtain or to launch nuclear weapons, but I also believe that, when we are only spending a few hundred million dollars on nuclear proliferation, then we’re making a mistake.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The other thing that we have to focus on, though, is Al Qaida.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They are now operating in 60 countries.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We can’t simply be focused on Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have to go to the root cause, and that is in Afghanistan and Pakistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s going to be critical.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are going to need more cooperation with our allies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And one last point I want to make.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is important for us to understand that the way we are perceived in the world is going to make a difference, in terms of our capacity to get cooperation and root out terrorism.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And one of the things that I intend to do as president is to restore America’s standing in the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are less respected now than we were eight years ago or even four years ago.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And this is the greatest country on Earth.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But because of some of the mistakes that have been made — and I give Senator McCain great credit on the torture issue, for having identified that as something that undermines our long-term security — because of those things, we, I think, are going to have a lot of work to do in the next administration to restore that sense that America is that shining beacon on a hill.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you agree there’s much to be done in a new administration to restore…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But in the case of missile defense, Senator Obama said it had to be, quote, “proven.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” That wasn’t proven when Ronald Reagan said we would do SDI, which is missile defense.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it was major — a major factor in bringing about the end of the Cold War.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We seem to come full circle again.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama still doesn’t quite understand — or doesn’t get it — that if we fail in Iraq, it encourages Al Qaida.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They would establish a base in Iraq.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The consequences of defeat, which would result from his plan of withdrawal and according to date certain, regardless of conditions, according to our military leaders, according to every expert, would lead to defeat — possible defeat, loss of all the fragile sacrifice that we’ve made of American blood and treasure, which grieves us all.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: All of that would be lost if we followed Senator Obama’s plan to have specific dates with withdrawal, regardless of conditions on the ground.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And General Petraeus says we have had great success, but it’s very fragile.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we can’t do what Senator Obama wants to do.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That is the central issue of our time.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I think Americans will judge very seriously as to whether that’s the right path or the wrong path and who should be the next president of the United States.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You see the same connections that Senator McCain does?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Oh, there’s no doubt.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Look, over the last eight years, this administration, along with Senator McCain, have been solely focused on Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That has been their priority.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That has been where all our resources have gone.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the meantime, bin Laden is still out there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He is not captured.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He is not killed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Al Qaida is resurgent.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the meantime, we’ve got challenges, for example, with China, where we are borrowing billions of dollars.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They now hold a trillion dollars’ worth of our debt.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they are active in countries like — in regions like Latin America, and Asia, and Africa.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They are — the conspicuousness of their presence is only matched by our absence, because we’ve been focused on Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have weakened our capacity to project power around the world because we have viewed everything through this single lens, not to mention, look at our economy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are now spending $10 billion or more every month.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that means we can’t provide health care to people who need it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We can’t invest in science and technology, which will determine whether or not we are going to be competitive in the long term.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There has never been a country on Earth that saw its economy decline and yet maintained its military superiority.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So this is a national security issue.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We haven’t adequately funded veterans’ care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I sit on the Veterans Affairs Committee, and we’ve got — I meet veterans all across the country who are trying to figure out, “How can I get disability payments?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’ve got post-traumatic stress disorder, and yet I can’t get treatment.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” So we have put all chips in, right there, and nobody is talking about losing this war.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What we are talking about is recognizing that the next president has to have a broader strategic vision about all the challenges that we face.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s been missing over the last eight years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That sense is something that I want to restore.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve been involved, as I mentioned to you before, in virtually every major national security challenge we’ve faced in the last 20-some years.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: There are some advantages to experience, and knowledge, and judgment.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I — and I honestly don’t believe that Senator Obama has the knowledge or experience and has made the wrong judgments in a number of areas, including his initial reaction to Russian invasion — aggression in Georgia, to his — you know, we’ve seen this stubbornness before in this administration to cling to a belief that somehow the surge has not succeeded and failing to acknowledge that he was wrong about the surge is — shows to me that we — that — that we need more flexibility in a president of the United States than that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: As far as our other issues that he brought up are concerned, I know the veterans.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I know them well.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I know that they know that I’ll take care of them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’ve been proud of their support and their recognition of my service to the veterans.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I love them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’ll take care of them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And they know that I’ll take care of them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And that’s going to be my job.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But, also, I have the ability, and the knowledge, and the background to make the right judgments, to keep this country safe and secure.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Reform, prosperity, and peace, these are major challenges to the United States of America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I don’t think I need any on-the-job training.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m ready to go at it right now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, let me just make a closing point.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, my father came from Kenya.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s where I get my name.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And in the ’60s, he wrote letter after letter to come to college here in the United States because the notion was that there was no other country on Earth where you could make it if you tried.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The ideals and the values of the United States inspired the entire world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I don’t think any of us can say that our standing in the world now, the way children around the world look at the United States, is the same.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And part of what we need to do, what the next president has to do — and this is part of our judgment, this is part of how we’re going to keep America safe — is to — to send a message to the world that we are going to invest in issues like education, we are going to invest in issues that — that relate to how ordinary people are able to live out their dreams.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that is something that I’m going to be committed to as president of the United States.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Few seconds.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’re almost finished.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Jim, when I came home from prison, I saw our veterans being very badly treated, and it made me sad.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I embarked on an effort to resolve the POW-MIA issue, which we did in a bipartisan fashion, and then I worked on normalization of relations between our two countries so that our veterans could come all the way home.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I guarantee you, as president of the United States, I know how to heal the wounds of war, I know how to deal with our adversaries, and I know how to deal with our friends.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And that ends this debate tonight.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: On October 2nd, next Thursday, also at 9:00 p.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Eastern time, the two vice presidential candidates will debate at Washington University in St.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Louis.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: My PBS colleague, Gwen Ifill, will be the moderator.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: For now, from Oxford, Mississippi, thank you, senators, both.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I’m Jim Lehrer.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Thank you, and good night.

speaker: Lehrer
