speaker: Question
sentence_text: With the economy on the downturn and retired and older citizens and workers losing their incomes, what’s the fastest, most positive solution to bail these people out of the economic ruin?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, Alan , thank you very much for the question.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I want to first, obviously, thank Belmont University, Tom, thank you, and to all of you who are participating tonight and those of you who sent e-mail questions in.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think everybody knows now we are in the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And a lot of you I think are worried about your jobs, your pensions, your retirement accounts, your ability to send your child or your grandchild to college.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I believe this is a final verdict on the failed economic policies of the last eight years, strongly promoted by President Bush and supported by Senator McCain, that essentially said that we should strip away regulations, consumer protections, let the market run wild, and prosperity would rain down on all of us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It hasn’t worked out that way.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so now we’ve got to take some decisive action.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, step one was a rescue package that was passed last week.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to make sure that works properly.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that means strong oversight, making sure that investors, taxpayers are getting their money back and treated as investors.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It means that we are cracking down on CEOs and making sure that they’re not getting bonuses or golden parachutes as a consequence of this package.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, in fact, we just found out that AIG, a company that got a bailout, just a week after they got help went on a $400,000 junket.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I’ll tell you what, the Treasury should demand that money back and those executives should be fired.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But that’s only step one.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The middle-class need a rescue package.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that means tax cuts for the middle-class.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It means help for homeowners so that they can stay in their homes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It means that we are helping state and local governments set up road projects and bridge projects that keep people in their jobs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And then long-term we’ve got to fix our health care system, we’ve got to fix our energy system that is putting such an enormous burden on families.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You need somebody working for you and you’ve got to have somebody in Washington who is thinking about the middle class and not just those who can afford to hire lobbyists.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, thank you, Tom.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Thank you, Belmont University.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And Senator Obama, it’s good to be with you at a town hall meeting.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, Alan , thank you for your question.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You go to the heart of America’s worries tonight.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Americans are angry, they’re upset, and they’re a little fearful.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s our job to fix the problem.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, I have a plan to fix this problem and it has got to do with energy independence.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to stop sending $700 billion a year to countries that don’t want us very — like us very much.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We have to keep Americans’ taxes low.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: All Americans’ taxes low.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let’s not raise taxes on anybody today.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We obviously have to stop this spending spree that’s going on in Washington.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Do you know that we’ve laid a $10 trillion debt on these young Americans who are here with us tonight, $500 billion of it we owe to China?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to have a package of reforms and it has got to lead to reform prosperity and peace in the world.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I think that this problem has become so severe, as you know, that we’re going to have to do something about home values.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You know that home values of retirees continues to decline and people are no longer able to afford their mortgage payments.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: As president of the United States, Alan, I would order the secretary of the treasury to immediately buy up the bad home loan mortgages in America and renegotiate at the new value of those homes — at the diminished value of those homes and let people be able to make those — be able to make those payments and stay in their homes.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Is it expensive?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Yes.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But we all know, my friends, until we stabilize home values in America, we’re never going to start turning around and creating jobs and fixing our economy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’ve got to give some trust and confidence back to America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I know how the do that, my friends.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it’s my proposal, it’s not Senator Obama’s proposal, it’s not President Bush’s proposal.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I know how to get America working again, restore our economy and take care of working Americans.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Thank you.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator, we have one minute for a discussion here.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Obviously the powers of the treasury secretary have been greatly expanded.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: The most powerful officer in the cabinet now.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Hank Paulson says he won’t stay on.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Who do you have in mind to appoint to that very important post?

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Not you, Tom.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: No, with good reason.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You know, that’s a tough question and there’s a lot of qualified Americans.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I think the first criteria, Tom, would have to be somebody who immediately Americans identify with, immediately say, we can trust that individual.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: A supporter of Senator Obama’s is Warren Buffett.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He has already weighed in and helped stabilize some of the difficulties in the markets and with companies and corporations, institutions today.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I like Meg Whitman, she knows what it’s like to be out there in the marketplace.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She knows how to create jobs.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Meg Whitman was CEO of a company that started with 12 people and is now 1.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: 3 million people in America make their living off eBay.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Maybe somebody here has done a little business with them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the point is it’s going to have to be somebody who inspires trust and confidence.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Because the problem in America today to a large extent, Tom, is that we don’t have trust and confidence in our institutions because of the corruption on Wall Street and the greed and excess and the cronyism in Washington, D.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain — Senator Obama, who do you have in mind for treasury secretary?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, Warren would be a pretty good choice — Warren Buffett, and I’m pleased to have his support.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But there are other folks out there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The key is making sure that the next treasury secretary understands that it’s not enough just to help those at the top.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Prosperity is not just going to trickle down.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to help the middle class.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we’ve — you know, Senator McCain and I have some fundamental disagreements on the economy, starting with Senator McCain’s statement earlier that he thought the fundamentals of the economy were sound.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Part of the problem here is that for many of you, wages and incomes have flat-lined.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: For many of you, it is getting harder and harder to save, harder and harder to retire.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s why, for example, on tax policy, what I want to do is provide a middle class tax cut to 95 percent of working Americans, those who are working two jobs, people who are not spending enough time with their kids, because they are struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain is right that we’ve got to stabilize housing prices.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But underlying that is loss of jobs and loss of income.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s something that the next treasury secretary is going to have to work on.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator Obama, thank you very much.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: May I remind both of you, if I can, that we’re operating under rules that you signed off on and when we have a discussion, it really is to be confined within about a minute or so.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: We’re going to go now, Senator McCain, to the next question from you from the hall here, and it comes from Oliver Clark , who is over here in section F.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Oliver?

speaker: Question
sentence_text: Well, Senators, through this economic crisis, most of the people that I know have had a difficult time.

speaker: Question
sentence_text: And through this bailout package, I was wondering what it is that’s going to actually help those people out.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, thank you, Oliver, and that’s an excellent question, because as you just described it, bailout, when I believe that it’s rescue, because — because of the greed and excess in Washington and Wall Street, Main Street was paying a very heavy price, and we know that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I left my campaign and suspended it to go back to Washington to make sure that there were additional protections for the taxpayer in the form of good oversight, in the form of taxpayers being the first to be paid back when our economy recovers — and it will recover — and a number of other measures.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But you know, one of the real catalysts, really the match that lit this fire was Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ll bet you, you may never even have heard of them before this crisis.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But you know, they’re the ones that, with the encouragement of Senator Obama and his cronies and his friends in Washington, that went out and made all these risky loans, gave them to people that could never afford to pay back.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And you know, there were some of us that stood up two years ago and said we’ve got to enact legislation to fix this.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to stop this greed and excess.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Meanwhile, the Democrats in the Senate and some — and some members of Congress defended what Fannie and Freddie were doing.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They resisted any change.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Meanwhile, they were getting all kinds of money in campaign contributions.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama was the second highest recipient of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac money in history — in history.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So this rescue package means that we will stabilize markets, we will shore up these institutions.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But it’s not enough.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s why we’re going to have to go out into the housing market and we’re going to have to buy up these bad loans and we’re going to have to stabilize home values, and that way, Americans, like Alan, can realize the American dream and stay in their home.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But Fannie and Freddie were the catalysts, the match that started this forest fire.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: There were some of us — there were some of us that stood up against it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: There were others who took a hike.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator Obama?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, Oliver, first, let me tell you what’s in the rescue package for you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Right now, the credit markets are frozen up and what that means, as a practical matter, is that small businesses and some large businesses just can’t get loans.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If they can’t get a loan, that means that they can’t make payroll.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If they can’t make payroll, then they may end up having to shut their doors and lay people off.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if you imagine just one company trying to deal with that, now imagine a million companies all across the country.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So it could end up having an adverse effect on everybody, and that’s why we had to take action.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we shouldn’t have been there in the first place.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, I’ve got to correct a little bit of Senator McCain’s history, not surprisingly.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let’s, first of all, understand that the biggest problem in this whole process was the deregulation of the financial system.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain, as recently as March, bragged about the fact that he is a deregulator.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: On the other hand, two years ago, I said that we’ve got a sub-prime lending crisis that has to be dealt with.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I wrote to Secretary Paulson, I wrote to Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke, and told them this is something we have to deal with, and nobody did anything about it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: A year ago, I went to Wall Street and said we’ve got to reregulate, and nothing happened.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And Senator McCain during that period said that we should keep on deregulating because that’s how the free enterprise system works.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, with respect to Fannie Mae, what Senator McCain didn’t mention is the fact that this bill that he talked about wasn’t his own bill.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He jumped on it a year after it had been introduced and it never got passed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I never promoted Fannie Mae.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact, Senator McCain’s campaign chairman’s firm was a lobbyist on behalf of Fannie Mae, not me.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So — but, look, you’re not interested in hearing politicians pointing fingers.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What you’re interested in is trying to figure out, how is this going to impact you?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is not the end of the process; this is the beginning of the process.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s why it’s going to be so important for us to work with homeowners to make sure that they can stay in their homes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The secretary already has the power to do that in the rescue package, but it hasn’t been exercised yet.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the next president has to make sure that the next Treasury secretary is thinking about how to strengthen you as a home buyer, you as a homeowner, and not simply think about bailing out banks on Wall Street.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator Obama, time for a discussion.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: I’m going to begin with you.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Are you saying to Mr.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Clark and to the other members of the American television audience that the American economy is going to get much worse before it gets better and they ought to be prepared for that?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: No, I am confident about the American economy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we are going to have to have some leadership from Washington that not only sets out much better regulations for the financial system.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The problem is we still have a archaic, 20th-century regulatory system for 21st-century financial markets.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re going to have to coordinate with other countries to make sure that whatever actions we take work.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But most importantly, we’re going to have to help ordinary families be able to stay in their homes, make sure that they can pay their bills, deal with critical issues like health care and energy, and we’re going to have to change the culture in Washington so that lobbyists and special interests aren’t driving the process and your voices aren’t being drowned out.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain, in all candor, do you think the economy is going to get worse before it gets better?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think it depends on what we do.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think if we act effectively, if we stabilize the housing market — which I believe we can, if we go out and buy up these bad loans, so that people can have a new mortgage at the new value of their home — I think if we get rid of the cronyism and special interest influence in Washington so we can act more effectively.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: My friend, I’d like you to see the letter that a group of senators and I wrote warning exactly of this crisis.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama’s name was not on that letter.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The point is — the point is that we can fix our economy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Americans’ workers are the best in the world.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They’re the fundamental aspect of America’s economy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They’re the most innovative.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They’re the best — they’re most — have best — we’re the best exporters.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’re the best importers.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They’re most effective.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They are the best workers in the world.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’ve got to give them a chance.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They’ve got — we’ve got to give them a chance to do their best again.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And they are the innocent bystanders here in what is the biggest financial crisis and challenge of our time.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We can do it.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Thank you, Senator McCain.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: We’re going to continue over in Section F, as it turns out.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator Obama, this is a question from you from Theresa Finch .

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Theresa ?

speaker: Question
sentence_text: How can we trust either of you with our money when both parties got — got us into this global economic crisis?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, look, I understand your frustration and your cynicism, because while you’ve been carrying out your responsibilities — most of the people here, you’ve got a family budget.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If less money is coming in, you end up making cuts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Maybe you don’t go out to dinner as much.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Maybe you put off buying a new car.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s not what happens in Washington.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And you’re right.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There is a lot of blame to go around.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I think it’s important just to remember a little bit of history.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When George Bush came into office, we had surpluses.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And now we have half-a-trillion-dollar deficit annually.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When George Bush came into office, our debt — national debt was around $5 trillion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s now over $10 trillion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve almost doubled it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so while it’s true that nobody’s completely innocent here, we have had over the last eight years the biggest increases in deficit spending and national debt in our history.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And Senator McCain voted for four out of five of those George Bush budgets.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So here’s what I would do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’m going to spend some money on the key issues that we’ve got to work on.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, you may have seen your health care premiums go up.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to reform health care to help you and your budget.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are going to have to deal with energy because we can’t keep on borrowing from the Chinese and sending money to Saudi Arabia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are mortgaging our children’s future.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to have a different energy plan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to invest in college affordability.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So we’re going to have to make some investments, but we’ve also got to make spending cuts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what I’ve proposed, you’ll hear Senator McCain say, well, he’s proposing a whole bunch of new spending, but actually I’m cutting more than I’m spending so that it will be a net spending cut.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The key is whether or not we’ve got priorities that are working for you as opposed to those who have been dictating the policy in Washington lately, and that’s mostly lobbyists and special interests.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to put an end to that.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, Theresa , thank you.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I can see why you feel that cynicism and mistrust, because the system in Washington is broken.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I have been a consistent reformer.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have advocated and taken on the special interests, whether they be the big money people by reaching across the aisle and working with Senator Feingold on campaign finance reform, whether it being a variety of other issues, working with Senator Lieberman on trying to address climate change.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have a clear record of bipartisanship.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The situation today cries out for bipartisanship.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama has never taken on his leaders of his party on a single issue.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we need to reform.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And so let’s look at our records as well as our rhetoric.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s really part of your mistrust here.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And now I suggest that maybe you go to some of these organizations that are the watchdogs of what we do, like the Citizens Against Government Waste or the National Taxpayers Union or these other organizations that watch us all the time.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I don’t expect you to watch every vote.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And you know what you’ll find?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This is the most liberal big-spending record in the United States Senate.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have fought against excessive spending and outrages.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have fought to reduce the earmarks and eliminate them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Do you know that Senator Obama has voted for — is proposing $860 billion of new spending now?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: New spending.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Do you know that he voted for every increase in spending that I saw come across the floor of the United States Senate while we were working to eliminate these pork barrel earmarks?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He voted for nearly a billion dollars in pork barrel earmark projects, including, by the way, $3 million for an overhead projector at a planetarium in Chicago, Illinois.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: My friends, do we need to spend that kind of money?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think you have to look at my record and you have to look at his.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Then you have to look at our proposals for our economy, not $860 billion in new spending, but for the kinds of reforms that keep people in their jobs, get middle-income Americans working again, and getting our economy moving again.

sentence_text: Senator McCain and I actually agree on something.

sentence_text: He said a while back that the big problem with energy is that for 30 years, politicians in Washington haven’t done anything.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What Senator McCain doesn’t mention is he’s been there 26 of them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And during that time, he voted 23 times against alternative fuels, 23 times.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So it’s easy to talk about this stuff during a campaign, but it’s important for us to understand that it requires a sustained effort from the next president.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: One last point I want to make on energy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain talks a lot about drilling, and that’s important, but we have three percent of the world’s oil reserves and we use 25 percent of the world’s oil.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So what that means is that we can’t simply drill our way out of the problem.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we’re not going to be able to deal with the climate crisis if our only solution is to use more fossil fuels that create global warming.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re going to have to come up with alternatives, and that means that the United States government is working with the private sector to fund the kind of innovation that we can then export to countries like China that also need energy and are setting up one coal power plant a week.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to make sure that we’re giving them the energy that they need or helping them to create the energy that they need.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Gentlemen, you may not have noticed, but we have lights around here.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: They have red and green and yellow and they are to signal…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’m just trying to keep up with John.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Tom, wave like that and I’ll look at you.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: All right, Senator.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Here’s a follow-up to that, one-minute discussion.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: It’s a simple question.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Sure.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Should we fund a Manhattan-like project that develops a nuclear bomb to deal with global energy and alternative energy or should we fund 100,000 garages across America, the kind of industry and innovation that developed Silicon Valley?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think pure research and development investment on the part of the United States government is certainly appropriate.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think once it gets into productive stages, that we ought to, obviously, turn it over to the private sector.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: By the way, my friends, I know you grow a little weary with this back-and-forth.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It was an energy bill on the floor of the Senate loaded down with goodies, billions for the oil companies, and it was sponsored by Bush and Cheney.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You know who voted for it?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You might never know.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That one.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You know who voted against it?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Me.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have fought time after time against these pork barrel — these bills that come to the floor and they have all kinds of goodies and all kinds of things in them for everybody and they buy off the votes.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I vote against them, my friends.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I vote against them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the point is, also, on oil drilling, oil drilling offshore now is vital so that we can bridge the gap.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We can bridge the gap between imported oil, which is a national security issue, as well as any other, and it will reduce the price of a barrel of oil, because when people know there’s a greater supply, then the cost of that will go down.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s fundamental economics.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to drill offshore, my friends, and we’ve got to do it now, and we can do it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And as far as nuclear power is concerned, again, look at the record.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama has approved storage and reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’ll stop, Tom, and you didn’t even wave.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Thanks.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Thank you very much, Senator.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Next question for you, Senator Obama, and it comes from the E section over here and it’s from Lindsey Trellow .

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Lindsey?

speaker: Question
sentence_text: Senator, selling health care coverage in America as the marketable commodity has become a very profitable industry.

speaker: Question
sentence_text: Do you believe health care should be treated as a commodity?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, you know, as I travel around the country, this is one of the single most frequently asked issues that I get, is the issue of health care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is breaking family budgets.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I can’t tell you how many people I meet who don’t have health insurance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you’ve got health insurance, most of you have seen your premiums double over the last eight years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And your co-payments and deductibles have gone up 30 percent just in the last year alone.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you’re a small business, it’s a crushing burden.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So one of the things that I have said from the start of this campaign is that we have a moral commitment as well as an economic imperative to do something about the health care crisis that so many families are facing.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So here’s what I would do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you’ve got health care already, and probably the majority of you do, then you can keep your plan if you are satisfied with it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You can keep your choice of doctor.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re going to work with your employer to lower the cost of your premiums by up to $2,500 a year.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we’re going to do it by investing in prevention.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re going to do it by making sure that we use information technology so that medical records are actually on computers instead of you filling forms out in triplicate when you go to the hospital.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That will reduce medical errors and reduce costs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you don’t have health insurance, you’re going to be able to buy the same kind of insurance that Senator McCain and I enjoy as federal employees.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because there’s a huge pool, we can drop the costs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And nobody will be excluded for pre-existing conditions, which is a huge problem.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, Senator McCain has a different kind of approach.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He says that he’s going to give you a $5,000 tax credit.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What he doesn’t tell you is that he is going to tax your employer-based health care benefits for the first time ever.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So what one hand giveth, the other hand taketh away.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He would also strip away the ability of states to provide some of the regulations on insurance companies to make sure you’re not excluded for pre-existing conditions or your mammograms are covered or your maternity is covered.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that is fundamentally the wrong way to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact, just today business organizations like the United States Chamber of Commerce, which generally are pretty supportive of Republicans, said that this would lead to the unraveling of the employer-based health care system.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That, I don’t think, is the kind of change that we need.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to have somebody who is fighting for patients and making sure that you get decent, affordable health care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s something that I’m committed to doing as president.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, thank you for the question.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You really identified one of the really major challenges that America faces.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Co-payments go up, costs go up, skyrocketing costs, which make people less and less able to afford health insurance in America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we need to do all of the things that are necessary to make it more efficient.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let’s put health records online, that will reduce medical errors, as they call them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let’s have community health centers.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let’s have walk-in clinics.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let’s do a lot of things to impose efficiencies.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But what is at stake here in this health care issue is the fundamental difference between myself and Senator Obama.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: As you notice, he starts talking about government.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He starts saying, government will do this and government will do that, and then government will, and he’ll impose mandates.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: If you’re a small business person and you don’t insure your employees, Senator Obama will fine you.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Will fine you.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s remarkable.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: If you’re a parent and you’re struggling to get health insurance for your children, Senator Obama will fine you.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want to give every American a $5,000 refundable tax credit.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They can take it anywhere, across state lines.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Why not?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Don’t we go across state lines when we purchase other things in America?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Of course it’s OK to go across state lines because in Arizona they may offer a better plan that suits you best than it does here in Tennessee.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And if you do the math, those people who have employer-based health benefits, if you put the tax on it and you have what’s left over and you add $5,000 that you’re going to get as a refundable tax credit, do the math, 95 percent of the American people will have increased funds to go out and buy the insurance of their choice and to shop around and to get — all of those people will be covered except for those who have these gold-plated Cadillac kinds of policies.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You know, like hair transplants, I might need one of those myself.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the point is that we have got to give people choice in America and not mandate things on them and give them the ability.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Every parent I know would acquire health insurance for their children if they could.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Obviously small business people want to give their employees health insurance.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Of course they all want to do that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to give them the wherewithal to do it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We can do it by giving them, as a start, a $5,000 refundable tax credit to go around and get the health insurance policy of their choice.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Quick discussion.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Is health care in America a privilege, a right, or a responsibility?

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think it’s a responsibility, in this respect, in that we should have available and affordable health care to every American citizen, to every family member.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And with the plan that — that I have, that will do that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But government mandates I — I’m always a little nervous about.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But it is certainly my responsibility.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It is certainly small-business people and others, and they understand that responsibility.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: American citizens understand that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Employers understand that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But they certainly are a little nervous when Senator Obama says, if you don’t get the health care policy that I think you should have, then you’re going to get fined.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, by the way, Senator Obama has never mentioned how much that fine might be.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Perhaps we might find that out tonight.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, why don’t — why don’t — let’s talk about this, Tom, because there was just a lot of stuff out there.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Privilege, right or responsibility.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Let’s start with that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, I think it should be a right for every American.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In a country as wealthy as ours, for us to have people who are going bankrupt because they can’t pay their medical bills — for my mother to die of cancer at the age of 53 and have to spend the last months of her life in the hospital room arguing with insurance companies because they’re saying that this may be a pre-existing condition and they don’t have to pay her treatment, there’s something fundamentally wrong about that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So let me — let me just talk about this fundamental difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, Tom, I know that we’re under time constraints, but Senator McCain through a lot of stuff out there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number one, let me just repeat, if you’ve got a health care plan that you like, you can keep it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: All I’m going to do is help you to lower the premiums on it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You’ll still have choice of doctor.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There’s no mandate involved.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Small businesses are not going to have a mandate.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What we’re going to give you is a 50 percent tax credit to help provide health care for those that you need.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, it’s true that I say that you are going to have to make sure that your child has health care, because children are relatively cheap to insure and we don’t want them going to the emergency room for treatable illnesses like asthma.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when Senator McCain says that he wants to provide children health care, what he doesn’t mention is he voted against the expansion of the Children’s Health Insurance Program that is responsible for making sure that so many children who didn’t have previously health insurance have it now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, the final point I’ll make on this whole issue of government intrusion and mandates — it is absolutely true that I think it is important for government to crack down on insurance companies that are cheating their customers, that don’t give you the fine print, so you end up thinking that you’re paying for something and, when you finally get sick and you need it, you’re not getting it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the reason that it’s a problem to go shopping state by state, you know what insurance companies will do?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They will find a state — maybe Arizona, maybe another state — where there are no requirements for you to get cancer screenings, where there are no requirements for you to have to get pre-existing conditions, and they will all set up shop there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how in banking it works.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Everybody goes to Delaware, because they’ve got very — pretty loose laws when it comes to things like credit cards.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And in that situation, what happens is, is that the protections you have, the consumer protections that you need, you’re not going to have available to you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That is a fundamental difference that I have with Senator McCain.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He believes in deregulation in every circumstance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s what we’ve been going through for the last eight years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It hasn’t worked, and we need fundamental change.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator, we want to move on now.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: If we’d come back to the hall here, we’re going to shift gears here a little bit and we’re going to go to foreign policy and international matters, if we can…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I don’t believe that — did we hear the size of the fine?

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Phil Elliott is over here in this section, and Phil Elliott has a question for Senator McCain.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Phil?

speaker: Question
sentence_text: Yes.

speaker: Question
sentence_text: Senator McCain, how will all the recent economic stress affect our nation’s ability to act as a peacemaker in the world?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, I thank you for that question, because there’s no doubt that history shows us that nations that are strong militarily over time have to have a strong economy, as well.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And that is one of the challenges that America faces.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But having said that, America — and we’ll hear a lot of criticism.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve heard a lot of criticism about America, and our national security policy, and all that, and much of that criticism is justified.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the fact is, America is the greatest force for good in the history of the world.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: My friends, we have gone to all four corners of the Earth and shed American blood in defense, usually, of somebody else’s freedom and our own.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So we are peacemakers and we’re peacekeepers.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the challenge is to know when the United States of American can beneficially effect the outcome of a crisis, when to go in and when not, when American military power is worth the expenditure of our most precious treasure.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And that question can only be answered by someone with the knowledge and experience and the judgment, the judgment to know when our national security is not only at risk, but where the United States of America can make a difference in preventing genocide, in preventing the spread of terrorism, in doing the things that the United States has done, not always well, but we’ve done because we’re a nation of good.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I am convinced that my record, going back to my opposition from sending the Marines to Lebanon, to supporting our efforts in Kosovo and Bosnia and the first Gulf War, and my judgment, I think, is something that I’m — a record that I’m willing to stand on.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama was wrong about Iraq and the surge.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He was wrong about Russia when they committed aggression against Georgia.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And in his short career, he does not understand our national security challenges.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We don’t have time for on-the-job training, my friends.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator Obama, the economic constraints on the U.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: military action around the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, you know, Senator McCain, in the last debate and today, again, suggested that I don’t understand.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s true.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There are some things I don’t understand.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I don’t understand how we ended up invading a country that had nothing to do with 9/11, while Osama Bin Laden and Al Qaeda are setting up base camps and safe havens to train terrorists to attack us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That was Senator McCain’s judgment and it was the wrong judgment.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When Senator McCain was cheerleading the president to go into Iraq, he suggested it was going to be quick and easy, we’d be greeted as liberators.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That was the wrong judgment, and it’s been costly to us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So one of the difficulties with Iraq is that it has put an enormous strain, first of all, on our troops, obviously, and they have performed heroically and honorably and we owe them an extraordinary debt of gratitude.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But it’s also put an enormous strain on our budget.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve spent, so far, close to $700 billion and if we continue on the path that we’re on, as Senator McCain is suggesting, it’s going to go well over $1 trillion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re spending $10 billion a month in Iraq at a time when the Iraqis have a $79 billion surplus, $79 billion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we need that $10 billion a month here in the United States to put people back to work, to do all these wonderful things that Senator McCain suggested we should be doing, but has not yet explained how he would pay for.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, Senator McCain and I do agree, this is the greatest nation on earth.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are a force of good in the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But there has never been a nation in the history of the world that saw its economy decline and maintained its military superiority.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the strains that have been placed on our alliances around the world and the respect that’s been diminished over the last eight years has constrained us being able to act on something like the genocide in Darfur, because we don’t have the resources or the allies to do everything that we should be doing.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s going to change when I’m president, but we can’t change it unless we fundamentally change Senator McCain’s and George Bush’s foreign policy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It has not worked for America.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator Obama, let me ask you if — let’s see if we can establish tonight the Obama doctrine and the McCain doctrine for the use of United States combat forces in situations where there’s a humanitarian crisis, but it does not affect our national security.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Take the Congo, where 4.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: 5 million people have died since 1998, or take Rwanda in the earlier dreadful days, or Somalia.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: What is the Obama doctrine for use of force that the United States would send when we don’t have national security issues at stake?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, we may not always have national security issues at stake, but we have moral issues at stake.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If we could have intervened effectively in the Holocaust, who among us would say that we had a moral obligation not to go in?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If we could’ve stopped Rwanda, surely, if we had the ability, that would be something that we would have to strongly consider and act.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So when genocide is happening, when ethnic cleansing is happening somewhere around the world and we stand idly by, that diminishes us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so I do believe that we have to consider it as part of our interests, our national interests, in intervening where possible.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But understand that there’s a lot of cruelty around the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re not going to be able to be everywhere all the time.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s why it’s so important for us to be able to work in concert with our allies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let’s take the example of Darfur just for a moment.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Right now there’s a peacekeeping force that has been set up and we have African Union troops in Darfur to stop a genocide that has killed hundreds of thousands of people.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We could be providing logistical support, setting up a no-fly zone at relatively little cost to us, but we can only do it if we can help mobilize the international community and lead.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s what I intend to do when I’m president.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain, the McCain Doctrine, if you will.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, let me just follow up, my friends.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: If we had done what Senator Obama wanted done in Iraq, and that was set a date for withdrawal, which General Petraeus, our chief — chairman of our Joint Chiefs of Staff said would be a very dangerous course to take for America, then we would have had a wider war, we would have been back, Iranian influence would have increased, al Qaeda would have re- established a base.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: There was a lot at stake there, my friends.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I can tell you right now that Senator Obama would have brought our troops home in defeat.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ll bring them home with victory and with honor and that is a fundamental difference.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The United States of America, Tom, is the greatest force for good, as I said.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we must do whatever we can to prevent genocide, whatever we can to prevent these terrible calamities that we have said never again.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But it also has to be tempered with our ability to beneficially affect the situation.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That requires a cool hand at the tiller.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This requires a person who understands what our — the limits of our capability are.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We went in to Somalia as a peacemaking organization, we ended up trying to be — excuse me, as a peacekeeping organization, we ended up trying to be peacemakers and we ended up having to withdraw in humiliation.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: In Lebanon, I stood up to President Reagan, my hero, and said, if we send Marines in there, how can we possibly beneficially affect this situation?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And said we shouldn’t.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Unfortunately, almost 300 brave young Marines were killed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So you have to temper your decisions with the ability to beneficially affect the situation and realize you’re sending America’s most precious asset, American blood, into harm’s way.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, again, I know those situations.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve been in them all my life.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I can tell you right now the security of your young men and women who are serving in the military are my first priority right after our nation’s security.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I may have to make those tough decisions.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I won’t take them lightly.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I understand that we have to say never again to a Holocaust and never again to Rwanda.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But we had also better be darn sure we don’t leave and make the situation worse, thereby exacerbating our reputation and our ability to address crises in other parts of the world.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Senator McCain, thank you very much.

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Next question for Senator Obama, it comes from the F section and is from Katie Hamm .

speaker: Brokaw
sentence_text: Katie?

speaker: Question
sentence_text: Should the United States respect Pakistani sovereignty and not pursue al Qaeda terrorists who maintain bases there, or should we ignore their borders and pursue our enemies like we did in Cambodia during the Vietnam War?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Katie, it’s a terrific question and we have a difficult situation in Pakistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I believe that part of the reason we have a difficult situation is because we made a bad judgment going into Iraq in the first place when we hadn’t finished the job of hunting down bin Laden and crushing al Qaeda.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So what happened was we got distracted, we diverted resources, and ultimately bin Laden escaped, set up base camps in the mountains of Pakistan in the northwest provinces there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They are now raiding our troops in Afghanistan, destabilizing the situation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They’re stronger now than at any time since 2001.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s why I think it’s so important for us to reverse course, because that’s the central front on terrorism.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They are plotting to kill Americans right now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: As Secretary Gates, the defense secretary, said, the war against terrorism began in that region and that’s where it will end.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So part of the reason I think it’s so important for us to end the war in Iraq is to be able to get more troops into Afghanistan, put more pressure on the Afghan government to do what it needs to do, eliminate some of the drug trafficking that’s funding terrorism.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I do believe that we have to change our policies with Pakistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We can’t coddle, as we did, a dictator, give him billions of dollars and then he’s making peace treaties with the Taliban and militants.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What I’ve said is we’re going to encourage democracy in Pakistan, expand our nonmilitary aid to Pakistan so that they have more of a stake in working with us, but insisting that they go after these militants.

speaker: Barack Obama

sentence_text: But the Russians must understand that these kinds of actions and activities are not acceptable and hopefully we will use the leverage, economic, diplomatic and others united with our allies, with our allies and friends in Europe who are equally disturbed as we are about their recent behaviors.

sentence_text: It will not be a re-ignition of the Cold War, but Russia is a challenge.

sentence_text: And one last point I want to make about Russia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Energy is going to be key in dealing with Russia.

sentence_text: This requires only a yes or a no.
