sentence_text: But when it comes to economic policies, essentially what you’re proposing is eight more years of the same thing.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it hasn’t worked.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think the American people understand it hasn’t worked.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We need to move in a new direction.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let me just say, Bob.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: About 30 seconds.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But it’s very clear that I have disagreed with the Bush administration.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have disagreed with leaders of my own party.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’ve got the scars to prove it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Whether it be bringing climate change to the floor of the Senate for the first time.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Whether it be opposition to spending and earmarks, whether it be the issue of torture, whether it be the conduct of the war in Iraq, which I vigorously opposed.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Whether it be on fighting the pharmaceutical companies on Medicare prescription drugs, importation.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Whether it be fighting for an HMO patient’s bill of rights.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Whether it be the establishment of the 9/11 Commission.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I have a long record of reform and fighting through on the floor of the United States Senate.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama, your argument for standing up to the leadership of your party isn’t very convincing.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We’re going to move to another question and the topic is leadership in this campaign.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Both of you pledged to take the high road in this campaign yet it has turned very nasty.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator Obama, your campaign has used words like “erratic,” “out of touch,” “lie,” “angry,” “losing his bearings” to describe Senator McCain.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator McCain, your commercials have included words like “disrespectful,” “dangerous,” “dishonorable,” “he lied.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: ” Your running mate said he “palled around with terrorists.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: ” Are each of you tonight willing to sit at this table and say to each other’s face what your campaigns and the people in your campaigns have said about each other?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And, Senator McCain, you’re first.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, this has been a tough campaign.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s been a very tough campaign.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I know from my experience in many campaigns that, if Senator Obama had asked — responded to my urgent request to sit down, and do town hall meetings, and come before the American people, we could have done at least 10 of them by now.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: When Senator Obama was first asked, he said, “Any place, any time,” the way Barry Goldwater and Jack Kennedy agreed to do, before the intervention of the tragedy at Dallas.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So I think the tone of this campaign could have been very different.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the fact is, it’s gotten pretty tough.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I regret some of the negative aspects of both campaigns.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the fact is that it has taken many turns which I think are unacceptable.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: One of them happened just the other day, when a man I admire and respect — I’ve written about him — Congressman John Lewis, an American hero, made allegations that Sarah Palin and I were somehow associated with the worst chapter in American history, segregation, deaths of children in church bombings, George Wallace.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That, to me, was so hurtful.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, Senator Obama, you didn’t repudiate those remarks.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Every time there’s been an out-of-bounds remark made by a Republican, no matter where they are, I have repudiated them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I hope that Senator Obama will repudiate those remarks that were made by Congressman John Lewis, very unfair and totally inappropriate.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So I want to tell you, we will run a truthful campaign.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This is a tough campaign.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it’s a matter of fact that Senator Obama has spent more money on negative ads than any political campaign in history.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I can prove it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, Senator Obama, when he said — and he signed a piece of paper that said he would take public financing for his campaign if I did — that was back when he was a long-shot candidate — you didn’t keep your word.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And when you looked into the camera in a debate with Senator Clinton and said, “I will sit down and negotiate with John McCain about public financing before I make a decision,” you didn’t tell the American people the truth because you didn’t.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And that’s — that’s — that’s an unfortunate part.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now we have the highest spending by Senator Obama’s campaign than any time since Watergate.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Time’s up.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, look, you know, I think that we expect presidential campaigns to be tough.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that, if you look at the record and the impressions of the American people — Bob, your network just did a poll, showing that two-thirds of the American people think that Senator McCain is running a negative campaign versus one-third of mine.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And 100 percent, John, of your ads — 100 percent of them have been negative.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s not true.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It absolutely is true.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, now, I think the American people are less interested in our hurt feelings during the course of the campaign than addressing the issues that matter to them so deeply.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And there is nothing wrong with us having a vigorous debate like we’re having tonight about health care, about energy policy, about tax policy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s the stuff that campaigns should be made of.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The notion, though, that because we’re not doing town hall meetings that justifies some of the ads that have been going up, not just from your own campaign directly, John, but 527s and other organizations that make some pretty tough accusations, well, I don’t mind being attacked for the next three weeks.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What the American people can’t afford, though, is four more years of failed economic policies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what they deserve over the next four weeks is that we talk about what’s most pressing to them: the economic crisis.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain’s own campaign said publicly last week that, if we keep on talking about the economic crisis, we lose, so we need to change the subject.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I would love to see the next three weeks devoted to talking about the economy, devoted to talking about health care, devoted to talking about energy, and figuring out how the American people can send their kids to college.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that is something that I would welcome.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But it requires, I think, a recognition that politics as usual, as been practiced over the last several years, is not solving the big problems here in America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, if you’ll turn on the television, as I — I watched the Arizona Cardinals defeat the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Congratulations.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Every other ad — ever other ad was an attack ad on my health care plan.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And any objective observer has said it’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You’re running ads right now that say that I oppose federal funding for stem cell research.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I don’t.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You’re running ads that misportray completely my position on immigration.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So the fact is that Senator Obama is spending unprecedented — unprecedented in the history of American politics, going back to the beginning, amounts of money in negative attack ads on me.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And of course, I’ve been talking about the economy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Of course, I’ve talked to people like Joe the plumber and tell him that I’m not going to spread his wealth around.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m going to let him keep his wealth.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And of course, we’re talking about positive plan of action to restore this economy and restore jobs in America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s what my campaign is all about and that’s what it’ll continue to be all about.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But again, I did not hear a repudiation of Congressman…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I mean, look, if we want to talk about Congressman Lewis, who is an American hero, he, unprompted by my campaign, without my campaign’s awareness, made a statement that he was troubled with what he was hearing at some of the rallies that your running mate was holding, in which all the Republican reports indicated were shouting, when my name came up, things like “terrorist” and “kill him,” and that you’re running mate didn’t mention, didn’t stop, didn’t say “Hold on a second, that’s kind of out of line.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” And I think Congressman Lewis’ point was that we have to be careful about how we deal with our supporters.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You’ve got to read what he said…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let — let — let… MCCAIN: You’ve got to read what he said.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let me — let me complete…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Go ahead.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: … my response.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I do think that he inappropriately drew a comparison between what was happening there and what had happened during the civil rights movement, and we immediately put out a statement saying that we don’t think that comparison is appropriate.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, in fact, afterwards, Congressman Lewis put out a similar statement, saying that he had probably gone over the line.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The important point here is, though, the American people have become so cynical about our politics, because all they see is a tit- for-tat and back-and-forth.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what they want is the ability to just focus on some really big challenges that we face right now, and that’s what I have been trying to focus on this entire campaign.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I cannot…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We can have serious differences about our health care policy, for example, John, because we do have a difference on health care policy, but we…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We do and I hope…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: … talking about it this evening.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Sure.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But when people suggest that I pal around with terrorists, then we’re not talking about issues.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What we’re talking about…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, let me just say I would…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Let me just say categorically I’m proud of the people that come to our rallies.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Whenever you get a large rally of 10,000, 15,000, 20,000 people, you’re going to have some fringe peoples.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You know that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’ve — and we’ve always said that that’s not appropriate.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But to somehow say that group of young women who said “Military wives for McCain” are somehow saying anything derogatory about you, but anything — and those veterans that wear those hats that say “World War II, Vietnam, Korea, Iraq,” I’m not going to stand for people saying that the people that come to my rallies are anything but the most dedicated, patriotic men and women that are in this nation and they’re great citizens.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I’m not going to stand for somebody saying that because someone yelled something at a rally — there’s a lot of things that have been yelled at your rallies, Senator Obama, that I’m not happy about either.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: In fact, some T-shirts that are very…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: John, I…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: … unacceptable.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So the point is — the point is that I have repudiated every time someone’s been out of line, whether they’ve been part of my campaign or not, and I will continue to do that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But the fact is that we need to absolutely not stand for the kind of things that have been going on.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I haven’t.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, look, Bob, as I said…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I mean, do you take issue with that?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, here’s what I would say.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I mean, we can have a debate back and forth about the merits of each other’s campaigns.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I suspect we won’t agree here tonight.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What I think is most important is that we recognize that to solve the key problems that we’re facing, if we’re going to solve two wars, the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, if we can — if we’re going to focus on lifting wages that have declined over the last eight years and create jobs here in America, then Democrats, independents and Republicans, we’re going to have to be able to work together.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what is important is making sure that we disagree without being disagreeable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it means that we can have tough, vigorous debates around issues.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What we can’t do, I think, is try to characterize each other as bad people.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that has been a culture in Washington that has been taking place for too long.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, Bob, you asked me a direct question.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Short answer, yes, short answer.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Yes, real quick.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Ayers, I don’t care about an old washed-up terrorist.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But as Senator Clinton said in her debates with you, we need to know the full extent of that relationship.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We need to know the full extent of Senator Obama’s relationship with ACORN, who is now on the verge of maybe perpetrating one of the greatest frauds in voter history in this country, maybe destroying the fabric of democracy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The same front outfit organization that your campaign gave $832,000 for “lighting and site selection.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” So all of these things need to be examined, of course.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’m going to let you respond and we’ll extend this for a moment.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Bob, I think it’s going to be important to just — I’ll respond to these two particular allegations that Senator McCain has made and that have gotten a lot of attention.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact, Mr.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Ayers has become the centerpiece of Senator McCain’s campaign over the last two or three weeks.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This has been their primary focus.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So let’s get the record straight.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Bill Ayers is a professor of education in Chicago.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Forty years ago, when I was 8 years old, he engaged in despicable acts with a radical domestic group.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I have roundly condemned those acts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Ten years ago he served and I served on a school reform board that was funded by one of Ronald Reagan’s former ambassadors and close friends, Mr.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Annenberg.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Other members on that board were the presidents of the University of Illinois, the president of Northwestern University, who happens to be a Republican, the president of The Chicago Tribune, a Republican- leaning newspaper.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Ayers is not involved in my campaign.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He has never been involved in this campaign.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And he will not advise me in the White House.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So that’s Mr.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Ayers.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, with respect to ACORN, ACORN is a community organization.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Apparently what they’ve done is they were paying people to go out and register folks, and apparently some of the people who were out there didn’t really register people, they just filled out a bunch of names.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It had nothing to do with us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We were not involved.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The only involvement I’ve had with ACORN was I represented them alongside the U.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Justice Department in making Illinois implement a motor voter law that helped people get registered at DMVs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, the reason I think that it’s important to just get these facts out is because the allegation that Senator McCain has continually made is that somehow my associations are troubling.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let me tell you who I associate with.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: On economic policy, I associate with Warren Buffett and former Fed Chairman Paul Volcker.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If I’m interested in figuring out my foreign policy, I associate myself with my running mate, Joe Biden or with Dick Lugar, the Republican ranking member on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, or General Jim Jones, the former supreme allied commander of NATO.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Those are the people, Democrats and Republicans, who have shaped my ideas and who will be surrounding me in the White House.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think the fact that this has become such an important part of your campaign, Senator McCain, says more about your campaign than it says about me.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, again, while you were on the board of the Woods Foundation, you and Mr.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Ayers, together, you sent $230,000 to ACORN.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So — and you launched your political campaign in Mr.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Ayers’ living room.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s absolutely not true.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the facts are facts and records are records.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s not the facts.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it’s not the fact — it’s not the fact that Senator Obama chooses to associate with a guy who in 2001 said that he wished he had have bombed more, and he had a long association with him.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s the fact that all the — all of the details need to be known about Senator Obama’s relationship with them and with ACORN and the American people will make a judgment.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And my campaign is about getting this economy back on track, about creating jobs, about a brighter future for America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And that’s what my campaign is about and I’m not going to raise taxes the way Senator Obama wants to raise taxes in a tough economy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And that’s really what this campaign is going to be about.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let’s go to the next topic and you — we may want to get back into some of this during this next discussion.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I want to ask both of you about the people that you’re going to bring into the government.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And our best insight yet is who you have picked as your running mates.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: So I’ll begin by asking both of you this question, and I’ll ask you to answer first, Senator Obama.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Why would the country be better off if your running mate became president rather than his running mate?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, Joe Biden, I think, is one of the finest public servants that has served in this country.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s not just that he has some of the best foreign policy credentials of anybody.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And Democrats and Republicans alike, I think, acknowledge his expertise there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But it’s also that his entire life he has never forgotten where he came from, coming from Scranton, fighting on behalf of working families, remembering what it’s like to see his father lose his job and go through a downward spiral economically.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, as a consequence, his consistent pattern throughout his career is to fight for the little guy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s what he’s done when it comes to economic policies that will help working families get a leg up.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s what he’s done when it comes to, for example, passing the landmark 1994 crime bill, the Violence Against Women’s Act.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Joe has always made sure that he is fighting on behalf of working families, and I think he shares my core values and my sense of where the country needs to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because after eight years of failed policies, he and I both agree that what we’re going to have to do is to reprioritize, make sure that we’re investing in the American people, give tax cuts not to the wealthiest corporations, but give them to small businesses and give them to individuals who are struggling right now, make sure that we finally get serious about energy independence, something that has been languishing in Washington for 30 years, and make sure that our kids get a great education and can afford to go to college.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So, on the key issues that are of importance to American families, Joe Biden’s always been on the right side, and I think he will make an outstanding president if, heaven forbid, something happened to me.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, Americans have gotten to know Sarah Palin.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They know that she’s a role model to women and other — and reformers all over America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She’s a reformer.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She is — she took on a governor who was a member of her own party when she ran for governor.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: When she was the head of their energy and natural resources board, she saw corruption, she resigned and said, “This can’t go on.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” She’s given money back to the taxpayers.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She’s cut the size of government.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She negotiated with the oil companies and faced them down, a $40 billion pipeline of natural gas that’s going to relieve the energy needs of the United — of what they call the lower 48.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She’s a reformer through and through.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it’s time we had that bresh of freth air — breath of fresh air coming into our nation’s capital and sweep out the old-boy network and the cronyism that’s been so much a part of it that I’ve fought against for all these years.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She’ll be my partner.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She understands reform.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And, by the way, she also understands special-needs families.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She understands that autism is on the rise, that we’ve got to find out what’s causing it, and we’ve got to reach out to these families, and help them, and give them the help they need as they raise these very special needs children.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: She understands that better than almost any American that I know.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m proud of her.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And she has ignited our party and people all over America that have never been involved in the political process.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I can’t tell how proud I am of her and her family.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Her husband’s a pretty tough guy, by the way, too.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Do you think she’s qualified to be president?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, I think it’s — that’s going to be up to the American people.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that, obviously, she’s a capable politician who has, I think, excited the — a base in the Republican Party.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think it’s very commendable the work she’s done on behalf of special needs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I agree with that, John.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I do want to just point out that autism, for example, or other special needs will require some additional funding, if we’re going to get serious in terms of research.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That is something that every family that advocates on behalf of disabled children talk about.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if we have an across-the-board spending freeze, we’re not going to be able to do it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s an example of, I think, the kind of use of the scalpel that we want to make sure that we’re funding some of those programs.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Do you think Senator Biden is qualified?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think that Joe Biden is qualified in many respects.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I do point out that he’s been wrong on many foreign policy and national security issues, which is supposed to be his strength.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He voted against the first Gulf War.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He voted against it and, obviously, we had to take Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait or it would’ve threatened the Middle Eastern world supply.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: In Iraq, he had this cockamamie idea about dividing Iraq into three countries.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’re seeing Iraq united as Iraqis, tough, hard, but we’re seeing them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’re now about to have an agreement for status of forces in Iraq coming up.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: There are several issues in which, frankly, Joe Biden and I openly and honestly disagreed on national security policy, and he’s been wrong on a number of the major ones.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But again, I want to come back to, notice every time Senator Obama says, “We need to spend more, we need to spend more, that’s the answer” — why do we always have to spend more?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Why can’t we have transparency, accountability, reform of these agencies of government?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Maybe that’s why he’s asked for 860 — sought and proposed $860 billion worth of new spending and wants to raise people’s taxes in a time of incredible challenge and difficulty and heartache for the American families.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let’s go to — let’s go to a new topic.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We’re running a little behind.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let’s talk about energy and climate control.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Every president since Nixon has said what both of you…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Climate change.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Climate change, yes — has said what both of you have said, and, that is, we must reduce our dependence on foreign oil.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: When Nixon said it, we imported from 17 to 34 percent of our foreign oil.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Now, we’re importing more than 60 percent.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Would each of you give us a number, a specific number of how much you believe we can reduce our foreign oil imports during your first term?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And I believe the first question goes to you, Senator McCain.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: MCCAIN: I believe we can, for all intents and purposes, eliminate our dependence on Middle Eastern oil and Venezuelan oil.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Canadian oil is fine.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: By the way, when Senator Obama said he would unilaterally renegotiate the North American Free Trade Agreement, the Canadians said, “Yes, and we’ll sell our oil to China.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: ” You don’t tell countries you’re going to unilaterally renegotiate agreements with them.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We can eliminate our dependence on foreign oil by building 45 new nuclear plants, power plants, right away.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We can store and we can reprocess.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator Obama will tell you, in the — as the extreme environmentalists do, it has to be safe.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Look, we’ve sailed Navy ships around the world for 60 years with nuclear power plants on them.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We can store and reprocess spent nuclear fuel, Senator Obama, no problem.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: So the point is with nuclear power, with wind, tide, solar, natural gas, with development of flex fuel, hybrid, clean coal technology, clean coal technology is key in the heartland of America that’s hurting rather badly.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: So I think we can easily, within seven, eight, ten years, if we put our minds to it, we can eliminate our dependence on the places in the world that harm our national security if we don’t achieve our independence.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Can we reduce our dependence on foreign oil and by how much in the first term, in four years?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that in ten years, we can reduce our dependence so that we no longer have to import oil from the Middle East or Venezuela.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that’s about a realistic timeframe.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And this is the most important issue that our future economy is going to face.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Obviously, we’ve got an immediate crisis right now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But nothing is more important than us no longer borrowing $700 billion or more from China and sending it to Saudi Arabia.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s mortgaging our children’s future.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, from the start of this campaign, I’ve identified this as one of my top priorities and here is what I think we have to do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number one, we do need to expand domestic production and that means, for example, telling the oil companies the 68 million acres that they currently have leased that they’re not drilling, use them or lose them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think that we should look at offshore drilling and implement it in a way that allows us to get some additional oil.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But understand, we only have three to four percent of the world’s oil reserves and we use 25 percent of the world’s oil, which means that we can’t drill our way out of the problem.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s why I’ve focused on putting resources into solar, wind, biodiesel, geothermal.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: These have been priorities of mine since I got to the Senate, and it is absolutely critical that we develop a high fuel efficient car that’s built not in Japan and not in South Korea, but built here in the United States of America.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We invented the auto industry and the fact that we have fallen so far behind is something that we have to work on.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now I just want to make one last point because Senator McCain mentioned NAFTA and the issue of trade and that actually bears on this issue.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I believe in free trade.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I also believe that for far too long, certainly during the course of the Bush administration with the support of Senator McCain, the attitude has been that any trade agreement is a good trade agreement.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And NAFTA doesn’t have — did not have enforceable labor agreements and environmental agreements.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what I said was we should include those and make them enforceable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the same way that we should enforce rules against China manipulating its currency to make our exports more expensive and their exports to us cheaper.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when it comes to South Korea, we’ve got a trade agreement up right now, they are sending hundreds of thousands of South Korean cars into the United States.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s all good.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We can only get 4,000 to 5,000 into South Korea.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That is not free trade.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to have a president who is going to be advocating on behalf of American businesses and American workers and I make no apology for that.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, you know, I admire so much Senator Obama’s eloquence.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And you really have to pay attention to words.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: He said, we will look at offshore drilling.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Did you get that?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Look at.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We can offshore drill now.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’ve got to do it now.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We will reduce the cost of a barrel of oil because we show the world that we have a supply of our own.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: It’s doable.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The technology is there and we have to drill now.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, on the subject of free trade agreements.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I am a free trader.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I need — we need to have education and training programs for displaced workers that work, going to our community colleges.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But let me give you another example of a free trade agreement that Senator Obama opposes.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Right now, because of previous agreements, some made by President Clinton, the goods and products that we send to Colombia, which is our largest agricultural importer of our products, is — there’s a billion dollars that we — our businesses have paid so far in order to get our goods in there.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Because of previous agreements, their goods and products come into our country for free.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So Senator Obama, who has never traveled south of our border, opposes the Colombia Free Trade Agreement.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The same country that’s helping us try to stop the flow of drugs into our country that’s killing young Americans.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And also the country that just freed three Americans that will help us create jobs in America because they will be a market for our goods and products without having to pay — without us having to pay the billions of dollars — the billion dollars and more that we’ve already paid.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Free trade with Colombia is something that’s a no-brainer.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But maybe you ought to travel down there and visit them and maybe you could understand it a lot better.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let me respond.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Actually, I understand it pretty well.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The history in Colombia right now is that labor leaders have been targeted for assassination on a fairly consistent basis and there have not been prosecutions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what I have said, because the free trade — the trade agreement itself does have labor and environmental protections, but we have to stand for human rights and we have to make sure that violence isn’t being perpetrated against workers who are just trying to organize for their rights, which is why, for example, I supported the Peruvian Free Trade Agreement which was a well-structured agreement.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I think that the important point is we’ve got to have a president who understands the benefits of free trade but also is going to enforce unfair trade agreements and is going to stand up to other countries.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the last point I’ll make, because we started on energy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When I talked about the automakers, they are obviously getting hammered right now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They were already having a tough time because of high gas prices.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And now with the financial crisis, car dealerships are closing and people can’t get car loans.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s why I think it’s important for us to get loan guarantees to the automakers, but we do have to hold them responsible as well to start producing the highly fuel-efficient cars of the future.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And Detroit had dragged its feet too long in terms of getting that done.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s going to be one of my highest priorities because transportation accounts for about 30 percent of our total energy consumption.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If we can get that right, then we can move in a direction not only of energy independence, but we can create 5 million new jobs all across America, including in the heartland where we can retool some of these plants to make these highly fuel-efficient cars and also to make wind turbines and solar panels, the kinds of clean energy approaches that should be the driver of our economy for the next century.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, let me just said that that this is — he — Senator Obama doesn’t want a free trade agreement with our best ally in the region but wants to sit down across the table without precondition to — with Hugo Chavez, the guy who has been helping FARC, the terrorist organization.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Free trade between ourselves and Colombia, I just recited to you the benefits of concluding that agreement, a billion dollars of American dollars that could have gone to creating jobs and businesses in the United States, opening up those markets.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So I don’t — I don’t think there’s any doubt that Senator Obama wants to restrict trade and he wants to raise taxes.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the last president of the United States that tried that was Herbert Hoover, and we went from a deep recession into a depression.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We’re not going to follow that path while I’m — when I’m president of the United States.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right, let’s go to a new topic, health care.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Given the current economic situation, would either of you now favor controlling health care costs over expanding health care coverage?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The question is first to Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to do both, and that’s exactly what my plan does.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Look, as I travel around the country, this is the issue that will break your heart over and over again.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Just yesterday, I was in Toledo shaking some hands in a line.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Two women, both of them probably in their mid- to late-50s, had just been laid off of their plant.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Neither of them have health insurance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they were desperate for some way of getting coverage, because, understandably, they’re worried that, if they get sick, they could go bankrupt.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So here’s what my plan does.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you have health insurance, then you don’t have to do anything.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you’ve got health insurance through your employer, you can keep your health insurance, keep your choice of doctor, keep your plan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The only thing we’re going to try to do is lower costs so that those cost savings are passed onto you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we estimate we can cut the average family’s premium by about $2,500 per year.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you don’t have health insurance, then what we’re going to do is to provide you the option of buying into the same kind of federal pool that both Senator McCain and I enjoy as federal employees, which will give you high-quality care, choice of doctors, at lower costs, because so many people are part of this insured group.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re going to make sure that insurance companies can’t discriminate on the basis of pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ll negotiate with the drug companies for the cheapest available price on drugs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are going to invest in information technology to eliminate bureaucracy and make the system more efficient.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we are going to make sure that we manage chronic illnesses, like diabetes and heart disease, that cost a huge amount, but could be prevented.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to put more money into preventive care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This will cost some money on the front end, but over the long term this is the only way that not only are we going to make families healthy, but it’s also how we’re going to save the federal budget, because we can’t afford these escalating costs.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Well, it is a terribly painful situation for Americans.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They’re seeing their premiums, their co-pays go up.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Forty-seven million Americans are without health insurance in America today.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And it really is the cost, the escalating costs of health care that are inflicting such pain on working families and people across this country.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I am convinced we need to do a lot of things.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We need to put health care records online.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The V.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: does that.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That will — that will reduce costs.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We need to have more community health centers.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We need to have walk-in clinics.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The rise of obesity amongst young Americans is one of the most alarming statistics that there is.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We should have physical fitness programs and nutrition programs in schools.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Every parent should know what’s going on there.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We — we need to have — we need to have employers reward employees who join health clubs and practice wellness and fitness.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I want to give every American family a $5,000 refundable tax credit.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Take it and get anywhere in America the health care that you wish.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, my old buddy, Joe, Joe the plumber, is out there.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, Joe, Senator Obama’s plan, if you’re a small business and you are able — and your — the guy that sells to you will not have his capital gains tax increase, which Senator Obama wants, if you’re out there, my friend, and you’ve got employees, and you’ve got kids, if you don’t get — adopt the health care plan that Senator Obama mandates, he’s going to fine you.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, Senator Obama, I’d like — still like to know what that fine is going to be, and I don’t think that Joe right now wants to pay a fine when he is seeing such difficult times in America’s economy.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama wants to set up health care bureaucracies, take over the health care of America through — as he said, his object is a single payer system.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: If you like that, you’ll love Canada and England.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: So the point is…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: So that’s your objective?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is not and I just described it…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: No, you stated it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I just…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Excuse me.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I just described what my plan is.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I’m happy to talk to you, Joe, too, if you’re out there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Here’s your fine — zero.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You won’t pay a fine, because…

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Zero?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Zero, because as I said in our last debate and I’ll repeat, John, I exempt small businesses from the requirement for large businesses that can afford to provide health care to their employees, but are not doing it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I exempt small businesses from having to pay into a kitty.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But large businesses that can afford it, we’ve got a choice.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Either they provide health insurance to their employees or somebody has to.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Right now, what happens is those employees get dumped into either the Medicaid system, which taxpayers pick up, or they’re going to the emergency room for uncompensated care, which everybody picks up in their premiums.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The average family is paying an additional $900 a year in higher premiums because of the uninsured.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So here’s what we do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We exempt small businesses.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact, what, Joe, if you want to do the right thing with your employees and you want to provide them health insurance, we’ll give you a 50 percent credit so that you will actually be able to afford it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you don’t have health insurance or you want to buy into a group plan, you will be able to buy into the plan that I just described.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, what we haven’t talked about is Senator McCain’s plan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He says he’s going to give you all a $5,000 tax credit.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That sounds pretty good.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And you can go out and buy your own insurance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Here’s the problem — that for about 20 million people, you may find yourselves no longer having employer-based health insurance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This is because younger people might be able to get health insurance for $5,000, young and healthy folks.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Older folks, less healthy folks, what’s going to end up happening is that you’re going to be the only ones left in your employer-based system, your employers won’t be able to afford it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And once you’re out on your own with this $5,000 credit, Senator McCain, for the first time, is going to be taxing the health care benefits that you have from your employer.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And this is your plan, John.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: For the first time in history, you will be taxing people’s health care benefits.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: By the way, the average policy costs about $12,000.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So if you’ve got $5,000 and it’s going to cost you $12,000, that’s a loss for you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Last point about Senator McCain’s plan is that insurers right now, the main restrictions on what they do is primarily state law and, under Senator McCain’s plan, those rules would be stripped away and you would start seeing a lot more insurance companies cherry-picking and excluding people from coverage.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That, I think, is a mistake and I think that this is a fundamental difference in our campaign and how we would approach health care.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What about that?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Hey, Joe, you’re rich, congratulations, because what Joe wanted to do was buy the business that he’s been working for 10-12 hours a day, seven days a week, and you said that you wanted to spread the wealth, but — in other words, take Joe’s money and then you decide what to do with it.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, Joe, you’re rich, congratulations, and you will then fall into the category where you’ll have to pay a fine if you don’t provide health insurance that Senator Obama mandates, not the kind that you think is best for your family, your children, your employees, but the kind that he mandates for you.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s big government at its best.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, 95 percent of the people in America will receive more money under my plan because they will receive not only their present benefits, which may be taxed, which will be taxed, but then you add $5,000 onto it, except for those people who have the gold-plated Cadillac insurance policies that have to do with cosmetic surgery and transplants and all of those kinds of things.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And the good thing about this is they’ll be able to go across America.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: The average cost of a health care insurance plan in America today is $5,800.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m going to give them $5,000 to take with them wherever they want to go, and this will give them affordability.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This will give them availability.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This will give them a chance to choose their own futures, not have Senator Obama and government decide that for them.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This really gets down to the fundamental difference in our philosophies.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: If you notice that in all of this proposal, Senator — government wants — Senator Obama wants government to do the job.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama wants government to do the job.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want, Joe, you to do the job.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want to leave money in your pocket.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I want you to be able to choose the health care for you and your family.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s what I’m all about.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And we’ve got too much government and too much spending and the government is — the size of government has grown by 40 percent in the last eight years.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We can’t afford that in the next eight years and Senator Obama, with the Democrats in charge of Congress, things have gotten worse.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Have you noticed, they’ve been in charge the last two years.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: A short response.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Very briefly.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You all just heard my plan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If you’ve got an employer-based health care plan, you keep it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, under Senator McCain’s plan there is a strong risk that people would lose their employer-based health care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s the choice you’ll have is having your employer no longer provide you health care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And don’t take my word for it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The U.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Chamber of Commerce, which generally doesn’t support a lot of Democrats, said that this plan could lead to the unraveling of the employer-based health care system.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: All I want to do, if you’ve already got health care, is lower your costs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That includes you, Joe.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let’s stop there and go to another question.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And this one goes to Senator McCain.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator McCain, you believe Roe v.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Wade should be overturned.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator Obama, you believe it shouldn’t.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Could either of you ever nominate someone to the Supreme Court who disagrees with you on this issue?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I would never and have never in all the years I’ve been there imposed a litmus test on any nominee to the court.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s not appropriate to do.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: But you don’t want Roe v.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Wade to be overturned?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I thought it was a bad decision.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think there were a lot of decisions that were bad.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I think that decisions should rest in the hands of the states.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I’m a federalist.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And I believe strongly that we should have nominees to the United States Supreme Court based on their qualifications rather than any litmus test.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Now, let me say that there was a time a few years ago when the United States Senate was about to blow up.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Republicans wanted to have just a majority vote to confirm a judge and the Democrats were blocking in an unprecedented fashion.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: We got together seven Republicans, seven Democrats.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You were offered a chance to join.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: You chose not to because you were afraid of the appointment of, quote, “conservative judges.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: ” I voted for Justice Breyer and Justice Ginsburg.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Not because I agreed with their ideology, but because I thought they were qualified and that elections have consequences when presidents are nominated.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: This is a very important issue we’re talking about.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Senator Obama voted against Justice Breyer and Justice Roberts on the grounds that they didn’t meet his ideological standards.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: That’s not the way we should judge these nominees.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Elections have consequences.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: They should be judged on their qualifications.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And so that’s what I will do.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I will find the best people in the world — in the United States of America who have a history of strict adherence to the Constitution.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: And not legislating from the bench.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: But even if it was someone — even someone who had a history of being for abortion rights, you would consider them?

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I would consider anyone in their qualifications.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: I do not believe that someone who has supported Roe v.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: Wade that would be part of those qualifications.

speaker: John McCain
sentence_text: But I certainly would not impose any litmus test.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, I think it’s true that we shouldn’t apply a strict litmus test and the most important thing in any judge is their capacity to provide fairness and justice to the American people.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it is true that this is going to be, I think, one of the most consequential decisions of the next president.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is very likely that one of us will be making at least one and probably more than one appointments and Roe versus Wade probably hangs in the balance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now I would not provide a litmus test.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I am somebody who believes that Roe versus Wade was rightly decided.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that abortion is a very difficult issue and it is a moral issue and one that I think good people on both sides can disagree on.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what ultimately I believe is that women in consultation with their families, their doctors, their religious advisers, are in the best position to make this decision.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I think that the Constitution has a right to privacy in it that shouldn’t be subject to state referendum, any more than our First Amendment rights are subject to state referendum, any more than many of the other rights that we have should be subject to popular vote.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So this is going to be an important issue.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I will look for those judges who have an outstanding judicial record, who have the intellect, and who hopefully have a sense of what real-world folks are going through.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’ll just give you one quick example.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Senator McCain and I disagreed recently when the Supreme Court made it more difficult for a woman named Lilly Ledbetter to press her claim for pay discrimination.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: For years, she had been getting paid less than a man had been paid for doing the exact same job.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when she brought a suit, saying equal pay for equal work, the judges said, well, you know, it’s taken you too long to bring this lawsuit, even though she didn’t know about it until fairly recently.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We tried to overturn it in the Senate.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I supported that effort to provide better guidance to the courts; John McCain opposed it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that it’s important for judges to understand that if a woman is out there trying to raise a family, trying to support her family, and is being treated unfairly, then the court has to stand up, if nobody else will.

speaker: Barack Obama

speaker: Mitt Romney

sentence_text: I think it’s, frankly, not moral for my generation to keep spending massively more than we take in, knowing those burdens are going to be passed on to the next generation and they’re going to be paying the interest and the principal all their lives.

speaker: Mitt Romney

sentence_text: Well, mathematically, there are three ways that you can cut a deficit.

speaker: Mitt Romney

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And number is to grow the economy, because if more people work in a growing economy, they’re paying taxes, and you can get the job done that way.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I understand.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The problem with raising taxes is that it slows down the rate of growth.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And you could never quite get the job done.

sentence_text: I apologize, Mr.

sentence_text: I like it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Good.

speaker: Mitt Romney

sentence_text: Mr.

sentence_text: When I walked into the Oval Office, I had more than a trillion-dollar deficit greeting me.

sentence_text: So 77 government programs, everything from aircrafts that the Air Force had ordered but weren’t working very well, 18 government — 18 government programs for education that were well-intentioned, not weren’t helping kids learn, we went after medical fraud in Medicare and Medicaid very aggressively, more aggressively than ever before, and have saved tens of billions of dollars, $50 billion of waste taken out of the system.

sentence_text: And I worked with Democrats and Republicans to cut a trillion dollars out of our discretionary domestic budget.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s not how America was built.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Ultimately, we’re going to have to make some decisions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the magnitude of the tax cuts that you’re talking about, Governor, would end up resulting in severe hardship for people, but more importantly, would not help us grow.

sentence_text: As I indicated before, when you talk about shifting Medicaid to states, we’re talking about potentially a 30 — a 30 percent cut in Medicaid over time.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, you know, that may not seem like a big deal when it just is, you know, numbers on a sheet of paper, but if we’re talking about a family who’s got an autistic kid and is depending on that Medicaid, that’s a big problem.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And governors are creative.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There’s no doubt about it.

sentence_text: But they’re not creative enough to make up for 30 percent of revenue on something like Medicaid.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What ends up happening is some people end up not getting help.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I remember, as a governor, when this idea was floated by Tommy Thompson, the governors — Republican and Democrats — said, please let us do that.

sentence_text: We can care for our own poor in so much better and more effective a way than having the federal government tell us how to care for our poor.

sentence_text: So — so let’s state — one of the magnificent things about this country is the whole idea that states are the laboratories of democracy.

sentence_text: Let states do this.
