sentence_text: … people, right, not for current retirees.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: For — so if you’re — if you’re 54 or 55, you might want to listen ’cause this — this will affect you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The idea, which was originally presented by Congressman Ryan, your running mate, is that we would give a voucher to seniors and they could go out in the private marketplace and buy their own health insurance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The problem is that because the voucher wouldn’t necessarily keep up with health care inflation, it was estimated that this would cost the average senior about $6,000 a year.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, in fairness, what Governor Romney has now said is he’ll maintain traditional Medicare alongside it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But there’s still a problem, because what happens is, those insurance companies are pretty clever at figuring out who are the younger and healthier seniors.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They recruit them, leaving the older, sicker seniors in Medicare.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And every health care economist that looks at it says, over time, what’ll happen is the traditional Medicare system will collapse.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And then what you’ve got is folks like my grandmother at the mercy of the private insurance system precisely at the time when they are most in need of decent health care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So, I don’t think vouchers are the right way to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And this is not my own — only my opinion.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: AARP thinks that the — the savings that we obtained from Medicare bolster the system, lengthen the Medicare trust fund by eight years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Benefits were not affected at all.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And ironically, if you repeal Obamacare, and I have become fond of this term, “Obamacare,” if you repeal it, what happens is those seniors right away are going to be paying $600 more in prescription care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They’re now going to have to be paying copays for basic checkups that can keep them healthier.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the primary beneficiary of that repeal are insurance companies that are estimated to gain billions of dollars back when they aren’t making seniors any healthier.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I don’t think that’s the right approach when it comes to making sure that Medicare is stronger over the long term.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’ll talk about — specifically about health care in a moment.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But what — do you support the voucher system, Governor?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: What I support is no change for current retirees and near-retirees to Medicare.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the president supports taking $716 billion out of that program.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And what about the vouchers?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So that’s — that’s number one.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two is for people coming along that are young, what I do to make sure that we can keep Medicare in place for them is to allow them either to choose the current Medicare program or a private plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Their choice.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They get to choose — and they’ll have at least two plans that will be entirely at no cost to them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So they don’t have to pay additional money, no additional $6,000.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s not going to happen.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They’ll have at least two plans.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And by the way, if the government can be as efficient as the private sector and offer premiums that are as low as the private sector, people will be happy to get traditional Medicare or they’ll be able to get a private plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I know my own view is I’d rather have a private plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’d just assume not have the government telling me what kind of health care I get.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’d rather be able to have an insurance company.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: If I don’t like them, I can get rid of them and find a different insurance company.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But people make their own choice.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The other thing we have to do to save Medicare?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have to have the benefits high for those that are low income, but for higher income people, we’re going to have to lower some of the benefits.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have to make sure this program is there for the long term.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s the plan that I’ve put forward.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And, by the way the idea came not even from Paul Ryan or — or Senator Wyden, who’s the co-author of the bill with — with Paul Ryan in the Senate, but also it came from Bill — Bill Clinton’s chief of staff.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is an idea that’s been around a long time, which is saying, hey, let’s see if we can’t get competition into the Medicare world so that people can get the choice of different plans at lower cost, better quality.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I believe in competition.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Jim, if I — if I can just respond very quickly, first of all, every study has shown that Medicare has lower administrative costs than private insurance does, which is why seniors are generally pretty happy with it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And private insurers have to make a profit.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Nothing wrong with that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s what they do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so you’ve got higher administrative costs, plus profit on top of that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if you are going to save any money through what Governor Romney’s proposing, what has to happen is, is that the money has to come from somewhere.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when you move to a voucher system, you are putting seniors at the mercy of those insurance companies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And over time, if traditional Medicare has decayed or fallen apart, then they’re stuck.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And this is the reason why AARP has said that your plan would weaken Medicare substantially.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s why they were supportive of the approach that we took.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: One last point I want to make.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We do have to lower the cost of health care, not just in Medicare and Medicaid… LEHRER: Talk about that in a minute.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: … but — but — but overall.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s — that’s a big topic.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Can we — can we stay on Medicare?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Is that a — is that a separate topic?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Yeah, we’re going to — yeah, I want to get to it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’m sorry.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But all I want to do is go very quickly…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let’s get back to Medicare.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: … before we leave the economy…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let’s get back to Medicare.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The president said that the government can provide the service at lower cost and without a profit.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: If that’s the case, then it will always be the best product that people can purchase.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Wait a minute, Governor.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But my experience — my experience the private sector typically is able to provide a better product at a lower cost.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Can we — can the two of you agree that the voters have a choice — a clear choice between the two…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Absolutely.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: … of you on Medicare?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Absolutely.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Absolutely.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: So to finish quickly, briefly, on the economy, what is your view about the level of federal regulation of the economy right now?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Is there too much?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And in your case, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, is there — should there be more?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Beginning with you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: This is not a new two-minute segment to start.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And we’ll go for a few minutes, and then we’re going to go to health care, OK?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Regulation is essential.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You can’t have a free market work if you don’t have regulation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: As a businessperson, I had to have — I need to know the regulations.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I needed them there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You couldn’t have people opening up banks in their — in their garage and making loans.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I mean, you have to have regulations so that you can have an economy work.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Every free economy has good regulation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: At the same time, regulation can become excessive.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Is it excessive now, do you think?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: In some places, yes.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Other places, no.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Like where?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: No, it can become out of date.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And what’s happened with some of the legislation that’s been passed during the president’s term, you’ve seen regulation become excessive, and it’s hurt — it’s hurt the economy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let me give you an example.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Dodd-Frank was passed.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And it includes within it a number of provisions that I think has some unintended consequences that are harmful to the economy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: One is it designates a number of banks as too big to fail, and they’re effectively guaranteed by the federal government.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is the biggest kiss that’s been given to — to New York banks I’ve ever seen.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is an enormous boon for them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: There’ve been 122 community and small banks have closed since Dodd- Frank.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So there’s one example.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Here’s another.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: In Dodd-Frank…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you want to repeal Dodd-Frank?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, I would repeal and replace it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re not going to get rid of all regulation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You have to have regulation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And there are some parts of Dodd-Frank that make all the sense in the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You need transparency, you need to have leverage limits for…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Well, here’s a specific…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But let’s — let’s mention — let me mention the other one.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let’s talk…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: No, let’s not.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Let’s let him respond — let’s let him respond to this specific on Dodd-Frank and what the governor just said.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think this is a great example.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The reason we have been in such a enormous economic crisis was prompted by reckless behavior across the board.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, it wasn’t just on Wall Street.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You had loan officers were — that were giving loans and mortgages that really shouldn’t have been given, because the folks didn’t qualify.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You had people who were borrowing money to buy a house that they couldn’t afford.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You had credit agencies that were stamping these as A1 great investments when they weren’t.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But you also had banks making money hand over fist, churning out products that the bankers themselves didn’t even understand, in order to make big profits, but knowing that it made the entire system vulnerable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So what did we do?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We stepped in and had the toughest reforms on Wall Street since the 1930s.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We said you’ve got — banks, you’ve got to raise your capital requirements.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You can’t engage in some of this risky behavior that is putting Main Street at risk.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve going to make sure that you’ve got to have a living will so — so we can know how you’re going to wind things down if you make a bad bet so we don’t have other taxpayer bailouts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the meantime, by the way, we also made sure that all the help that we provided those banks was paid back every single dime, with interest.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, Governor Romney has said he wants to repeal Dodd-Frank.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, you know, I appreciate and it appears we’ve got some agreement that a marketplace to work has to have some regulation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But in the past, Governor Romney has said he just want to repeal Dodd- Frank, roll it back.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so the question is: Does anybody out there think that the big problem we had is that there was too much oversight and regulation of Wall Street?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because if you do, then Governor Romney is your candidate.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But that’s not what I believe.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Sorry, but that’s just not — that’s just not the facts.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Look, we have to have regulation on Wall Street.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s why I’d have regulation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But I wouldn’t designate five banks as too big to fail and give them a blank check.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s one of the unintended consequences of Dodd-Frank.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It wasn’t thought through properly.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to get rid of that provision because it’s killing regional and small banks.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They’re getting hurt.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let me mention another regulation in Dodd-Frank.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You say we were giving mortgages to people who weren’t qualified.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s exactly right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s one of the reasons for the great financial calamity we had.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And so Dodd-Frank correctly says we need to have qualified mortgages, and if you give a mortgage that’s not qualified, there are big penalties, except they didn’t ever go on and define what a qualified mortgage was.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s been two years.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We don’t know what a qualified mortgage is yet.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So banks are reluctant to make loans, mortgages.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Try and get a mortgage these days.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s hurt the housing market because Dodd-Frank didn’t anticipate putting in place the kinds of regulations you have to have.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s not that Dodd-Frank always was wrong with too much regulation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Sometimes they didn’t come out with a clear regulation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I will make sure we don’t hurt the functioning of our — of our marketplace and our business, because I want to bring back housing and get good jobs.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I think we have another clear difference between the two of you.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Now, let’s move to health care where I know there is a clear difference, and that has to do with the Affordable Care Act, Obamacare.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And it’s a two-minute new — new segment, and that means two minutes each.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And you go first, Governor Romney.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You want it repealed.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You want the Affordable Care Act repealed.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Why?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I sure do.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, in part, it comes, again, from my experience.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You know, I was in New Hampshire.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: A woman came to me and she said, look, I can’t afford insurance for myself or my son.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I met a couple in Appleton, Wisconsin, and they said, we’re thinking of dropping our insurance, we can’t afford it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the number of small businesses I’ve gone to that are saying they’re dropping insurance because they can’t afford it, the cost of health care is just prohibitive.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And — and we’ve got to deal with cost.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And, unfortunately, when — when — when you look at Obamacare, the Congressional Budget Office has said it will cost $2,500 a year more than traditional insurance.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So it’s adding to cost.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And as a matter of fact, when the president ran for office, he said that, by this year, he would have brought down the cost of insurance for each family by $2,500 a family.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Instead, it’s gone up by that amount.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So it’s expensive.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Expensive things hurt families.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So that’s one reason I don’t want it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Second reason, it cuts $716 billion from Medicare to pay for it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I want to put that money back in Medicare for our seniors.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number three, it puts in place an unelected board that’s going to tell people ultimately what kind of treatments they can have.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I don’t like that idea.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Fourth, there was a survey done of small businesses across the country, said, what’s been the effect of Obamacare on your hiring plans?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And three-quarters of them said it makes us less likely to hire people.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I just don’t know how the president could have come into office, facing 23 million people out of work, rising unemployment, an economic crisis at the — at the kitchen table, and spend his energy and passion for two years fighting for Obamacare instead of fighting for jobs for the American people.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It has killed jobs.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the best course for health care is to do what we did in my state: craft a plan at the state level that fits the needs of the state.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then let’s focus on getting the costs down for people, rather than raising it with the $2,500 additional premium.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President, the argument against repeal?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: OBAMA: Well, four years ago, when I was running for office, I was traveling around and having those same conversations that Governor Romney talks about.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And it wasn’t just that small businesses were seeing costs skyrocket and they couldn’t get affordable coverage even if they wanted to provide it to their employees.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: It wasn’t just that this was the biggest driver of our federal deficit, our overall health care costs, but it was families who were worried about going bankrupt if they got sick, millions of families, all across the country.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: If they had a pre-existing condition, they might not be able to get coverage at all.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: If they did have coverage, insurance companies might impose an arbitrary limit.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And so as a consequence, they’re paying their premiums, somebody gets really sick, lo and behold, they don’t have enough money to pay the bills, because the insurance companies say that they’ve hit the limit.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: So we did work on this, alongside working on jobs, because this is part of making sure that middle-class families are secure in this country.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And let me tell you exactly what Obamacare did.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Number one, if you’ve got health insurance, it doesn’t mean a government takeover.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You keep your own insurance.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: You keep your own doctor.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But it does say insurance companies can’t jerk you around.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: They can’t impose arbitrary lifetime limits.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: They have to let you keep your kid on their insurance — your insurance plan until you’re 26 years old.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And it also says that you’re going to have to get rebates if insurance companies are spending more on administrative costs and profits than they are on actual care.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Number two, if you don’t have health insurance, we’re essentially setting up a group plan that allows you to benefit from group rates that are typically 18 percent lower than if you’re out there trying to get insurance on the individual market.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Now, the last point I’d make before…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Two minutes — two minutes is up, sir.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: No, I think — I had five seconds before you interrupted me, was … … the irony is that we’ve seen this model work really well in Massachusetts, because Governor Romney did a good thing, working with Democrats in the state to set up what is essentially the identical model and as a consequence people are covered there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It hasn’t destroyed jobs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And as a consequence, we now have a system in which we have the opportunity to start bringing down costs, as opposed to just leaving millions of people out in the cold.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Your five seconds went away a long time ago.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, Governor.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor, tell — tell the president directly why you think what he just said is wrong about Obamacare?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, I did with my first statement.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: First of all, I like the way we did it in Massachusetts.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I like the fact that in my state, we had Republicans and Democrats come together and work together.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: What you did instead was to push through a plan without a single Republican vote.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: As a matter of fact, when Massachusetts did something quite extraordinary — elected a Republican senator to stop Obamacare, you pushed it through anyway.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So entirely on a partisan basis, instead of bringing America together and having a discussion on this important topic, you pushed through something that you and Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid thought was the best answer and drove it through.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: What we did in a legislature 87 percent Democrat, we worked together; 200 legislators in my legislature, only two voted against the plan by the time we were finished.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: What were some differences?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We didn’t raise taxes.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You’ve raised them by $1 trillion under Obamacare.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We didn’t cut Medicare.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Of course, we don’t have Medicare, but we didn’t cut Medicare by $716 billion.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We didn’t put in place a board that can tell people ultimately what treatments they’re going to receive.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We didn’t also do something that I think a number of people across this country recognize, which is put — put people in a position where they’re going to lose the insurance they had and they wanted.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Right now, the CBO says up to 20 million people will lose their insurance as Obamacare goes into effect next year.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And likewise, a study by McKinsey and Company of American businesses said 30 percent of them are anticipating dropping people from coverage.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So for those reasons, for the tax, for Medicare, for this board, and for people losing their insurance, this is why the American people don’t want Medicare — don’t want Obamacare.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s why Republicans said, do not do this, and the Republicans had — had the plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They put a plan out.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They put out a plan, a bipartisan plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It was swept aside.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I think something this big, this important has to be done on a bipartisan basis.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And we have to have a president who can reach across the aisle and fashion important legislation with the input from both parties.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor Romney said this has to be done on a bipartisan basis.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This was a bipartisan idea.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact, it was a Republican idea.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And Governor Romney at the beginning of this debate wrote and said what we did in Massachusetts could be a model for the nation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I agree that the Democratic legislators in Massachusetts might have given some advice to Republicans in Congress about how to cooperate, but the fact of the matter is, we used the same advisers, and they say it’s the same plan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It — when Governor Romney talks about this board, for example, unelected board that we’ve created, what this is, is a group of health care experts, doctors, et cetera, to figure out, how can we reduce the cost of care in the system overall?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because there — there are two ways of dealing with our health care crisis.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: One is to simply leave a whole bunch of people uninsured and let them fend for themselves, to let businesses figure out how long they can continue to pay premiums until finally they just give up, and their workers are no longer getting insured, and that’s been the trend line.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Or, alternatively, we can figure out, how do we make the cost of care more effective?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And there are ways of doing it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So at Cleveland Clinic, one of the best health care systems in the world, they actually provide great care cheaper than average.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the reason they do is because they do some smart things.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They — they say, if a patient’s coming in, let’s get all the doctors together at once, do one test instead of having the patient run around with 10 tests.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let’s make sure that we’re providing preventive care so we’re catching the onset of something like diabetes.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let’s — let’s pay providers on the basis of performance as opposed to on the basis of how many procedures they’ve — they’ve engaged in.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, so what this board does is basically identifies best practices and says, let’s use the purchasing power of Medicare and Medicaid to help to institutionalize all these good things that we do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the fact of the matter is that, when Obamacare is fully implemented, we’re going to be in a position to show that costs are going down.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And over the last two years, health care premiums have gone up — it’s true — but they’ve gone up slower than any time in the last 50 years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So we’re already beginning to see progress.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the meantime, folks out there with insurance, you’re already getting a rebate.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let me make one last point.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor Romney says, we should replace it, I’m just going to repeal it, but — but we can replace it with something.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But the problem is, he hasn’t described what exactly we’d replace it with, other than saying we’re going to leave it to the states.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But the fact of the matter is that some of the prescriptions that he’s offered, like letting you buy insurance across state lines, there’s no indication that that somehow is going to help somebody who’s got a pre-existing condition be able to finally buy insurance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact, it’s estimated that by repealing Obamacare, you’re looking at 50 million people losing health insurance…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Let’s…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: … at a time when it’s vitally important.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Let’s let the governor explain what you would do…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: … if Obamacare is repealed.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: How would you replace it?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, actually it’s — it’s — it’s a lengthy description.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But, number one, preexisting conditions are covered under my plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, young people are able to stay on their family plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s already offered in the private marketplace.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You don’t have to have the government mandate that for that to occur.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But let’s come back to something the president and I agree on, which is the key task we have in health care is to get the cost down so it’s more affordable for families.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then he has as a model for doing that a board of people at the government, an unelected board, appointed board, who are going to decide what kind of treatment you ought to have.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: In my opinion, the government is not effective in — in bringing down the cost of almost anything.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: As a matter of fact, free people and free enterprises trying to find ways to do things better are able to be more effective in bringing down the cost than the government will ever be.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Your example of the Cleveland Clinic is my case in point, along with several others I could describe.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is the private market.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: These are small — these are enterprises competing with each other, learning how to do better and better jobs.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I used to consult to businesses — excuse me, to hospitals and to health care providers.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I was astonished at the creativity and innovation that exists in the American people.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: In order to bring the cost of health care down, we don’t need to have a board of 15 people telling us what kinds of treatments we should have.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We instead need to put insurance plans, providers, hospitals, doctors on target such that they have an incentive, as you say, performance pay, for doing an excellent job, for keeping costs down, and that’s happening.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Innermountain Healthcare does it superbly well, Mayo Clinic is doing it superbly well, Cleveland Clinic, others.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But the right answer is not to have the federal government take over health care and start mandating to the providers across America, telling a patient and a doctor what kind of treatment they can have.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s the wrong way to go.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The private market and individual responsibility always work best.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let me just point out first of all this board that we’re talking about can’t make decisions about what treatments are given.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s explicitly prohibited in the law.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But let’s go back to what Governor Romney indicated, that under his plan, he would be able to cover people with preexisting conditions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, actually Governor, that isn’t what your plan does.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What your plan does is to duplicate what’s already the law, which says if you are out of health insurance for three months, then you can end up getting continuous coverage and an insurance company can’t deny you if you’ve — if it’s been under 90 days.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But that’s already the law and that doesn’t help the millions of people out there with preexisting conditions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There’s a reason why Governor Romney set up the plan that he did in Massachusetts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It wasn’t a government takeover of health care.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It was the largest expansion of private insurance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what it does say is that “insurers, you’ve got to take everybody.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” Now, that also means that you’ve got more customers.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But when — when Governor Romney says that he’ll replace it with something, but can’t detail how it will be in fact replaced and the reason he set up the system he did in Massachusetts was because there isn’t a better way of dealing with the preexisting conditions problem.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It just reminds me of, you know, he says that he’s going to close deductions and loopholes for his tax plan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how it’s going to be paid for, but we don’t know the details.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He says that he’s going to replace Dodd-Frank, Wall Street reform, but we don’t know exactly which ones.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He won’t tell us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He now says he’s going to replace Obamacare and ensure that all the good things that are in it are going to be in there and you don’t have to worry.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And at some point, I think the American people have to ask themselves, is the reason that Governor Romney is keeping all these plans to replace secret because they’re too good?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Is it — is it because that somehow middle-class families are going to benefit too much from them?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: No.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The reason is, is because, when we reform Wall Street, when we tackle the problem of pre-existing conditions, then, you know, these are tough problems and we’ve got to make choices.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the choices we’ve made have been ones that ultimately are benefiting middle-class families all across the country.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’re going to move to…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: No.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I — I have to respond to that.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: No, but…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Which is — which is my experience as a governor is if I come in and — and lay down a piece of legislation and say, “It’s my way or the highway,” I don’t get a lot done.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: What I do is the same way that Tip O’Neill and Ronald Reagan worked together some years ago.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: When Ronald Reagan ran for office, he laid out the principles that he was going to foster.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: He said he was going to lower tax rates.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: He said he was going to broaden the base.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You’ve said the same thing, you’re going to simplify the tax code, broaden the base.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Those are my principles.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I want to bring down the tax burden on middle-income families.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I’m going to work together with Congress to say, OK, what — what are the various ways we could bring down deductions, for instance?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: One way, for instance, would be to have a single number.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Make up a number, $25,000, $50,000.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Anybody can have deductions up to that amount.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then that number disappears for high-income people.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s one way one could do it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: One could follow Bowles-Simpson as a model and take deduction by deduction and make differences that way.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: There are alternatives to accomplish the objective I have, which is to bring down rates, broaden the base, simplify the code, and create incentives for growth.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And with regards to health care, you had remarkable details with regards to my pre-existing condition plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You obviously studied up on — on my plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: In fact, I do have a plan that deals with people with pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s part of my health care plan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And what we did in Massachusetts is a model for the nation state by state.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I said that at that time.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The federal government taking over health care for the entire nation and whisking aside the 10th Amendment, which gives states the rights for these kinds of things, is not the course for America to have a stronger, more vibrant economy.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: That is a terrific segue to our next segment, and is the role of government.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And — and let’s see.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Role of government.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And it is — you are first on this, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And the question is this.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you believe, both of you — but you had the first two minutes on this, Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President — do you believe there’s a fundamental difference between the two of you as to how you view the mission of the federal government?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, I definitely think there are differences.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And do you — yeah.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The first role of the federal government is to keep the American people safe.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s its most basic function.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And as commander-in-chief, that is something that I’ve worked on and thought about every single day that I’ve been in the Oval Office.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I also believe that government has the capacity, the federal government has the capacity to help open up opportunity and create ladders of opportunity and to create frameworks where the American people can succeed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Look, the genius of America is the free enterprise system and freedom and the fact that people can go out there and start a business, work on an idea, make their own decisions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But as Abraham Lincoln understood, there are also some things we do better together.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So, in the middle of the Civil War, Abraham Lincoln said, let’s help to finance the Transcontinental Railroad, let’s start the National Academy of Sciences, let’s start land grant colleges, because we want to give these gateways of opportunity for all Americans, because if all Americans are getting opportunity, we’re all going to be better off.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That doesn’t restrict people’s freedom.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That enhances it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so what I’ve tried to do as president is to apply those same principles.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when it comes to education what I’ve said is we’ve got to reform schools that are not working.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We use something called Race to the Top.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Wasn’t a top-down approach, Governor.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What we’ve said is to states, we’ll give you more money if you initiate reforms.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And as a consequence, you had 46 states around the country who have made a real difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what I’ve also said is let’s hire another 100,000 math and science teachers to make sure we maintain our technological lead and our people are skilled and able to succeed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And hard-pressed states right now can’t all do that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact we’ve seen layoffs of hundreds of thousands of teachers over the last several years, and Governor Romney doesn’t think we need more teachers.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I do, because I think that that is the kind of investment where the federal government can help.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It can’t do it all, but it can make a difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And as a consequence we’ll have a better trained workforce and that will create jobs because companies want to locate in places where we’ve got a skilled workforce.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Two minutes, Governor, on the role of government.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Your view?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, first, I love great schools.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Massachusetts, our schools are ranked number one of all 50 states.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the key to great schools, great teachers.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So I reject the idea that I don’t believe in great teachers or more teachers.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Every school district, every state should make that decision on their own.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The role of government: Look behind us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The role of government is to promote and protect the principles of those documents.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: First, life and liberty.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have a responsibility to protect the lives and liberties of our people, and that means a military second to none.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I do not believe in cutting our military.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I believe in maintaining the strength of America’s military.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Second, in that line that says we are endowed by our creator with our rights, I believe we must maintain our commitment to religious tolerance and freedom in this country.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That statement also says that we are endowed by our creator with the right to pursue happiness as we choose.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I interpret that as, one, making sure that those people who are less fortunate and can’t care for themselves are cared by — by one another.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re a nation that believes that we’re all children of the same god and we care for those that have difficulties, those that are elderly and have problems and challenges, those that are disabled.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We care for them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And we — we look for discovery and innovation, all these things desired out of the American heart to provide the pursuit of happiness for our citizens.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But we also believe in maintaining for individuals the right to pursue their dreams and not to have the government substitute itself for the rights of free individuals.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And what we’re seeing right now is, in my view, a — a trickle-down government approach, which has government thinking it can do a better job than free people pursuing their dreams.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And it’s not working.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the proof of that is 23 million people out of work.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The proof of that is 1 out of 6 people in poverty.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The proof of that is we’ve gone from 32 million on food stamps to 47 million on food stamps.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The proof of that is that 50 percent of college graduates this year can’t find work.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We know that the path we’re taking is not working.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s time for a new path.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Let’s go through some specifics in terms of what — how each of you views the role of government.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: How do — education.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Does the federal government have a responsibility to improve the quality of public education in America?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, the primary responsibility for education is — is, of course, at the state and local level.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But the federal government also can play a very important role.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I — and I agree with Secretary Arne Duncan, he’s — some ideas he’s put forward on Race to the Top, not all of them, but some of them I agree with and — and congratulate him for pursuing that.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The federal government can get local and — and state schools to do a better job.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: My own view, by the way, is I’ve added to that.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I happen to believe, I want the kids that are getting federal dollars from IDEA or Title I — these are disabled kids or — or — or poor kids or — or lower-income kids, rather, I want them to be able to go to the school of their choice.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So all federal funds, instead of going to the — to the state or to the school district, I’d have go, if you will, follow the child and let the parent and the child decide where to send their — their — their student.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: How do you see the federal government’s responsibility to, as I say, to improve the quality of public education in this country?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, as I’ve indicated, I think that it has a significant role to play.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Through our Race to the Top program, we’ve worked with Republican and Democratic governors to initiate major reforms, and they’re having an impact right now.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you think you have a difference with your views and — and those of Governor Romney on — about education and the federal government?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, this is where budgets matter, because budgets reflect choices.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So when Governor Romney indicates that he wants to cut taxes and potentially benefit folks like me and him, and to pay for it we’re having to initiate significant cuts in federal support for education, that makes a difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, his — his running mate, Congressman Ryan, put forward a budget that reflects many of the principles that Governor Romney’s talked about.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it wasn’t very detailed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This seems to be a trend.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But — but what it did do is to — if you extrapolated how much money we’re talking about, you’d look at cutting the education budget by up to 20 percent.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When it comes to community colleges, we are seeing great work done out there all over the country because we have the opportunity to train people for jobs that exist right now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And one of the things I suspect Governor Romney and I probably agree on is getting businesses to work with community colleges so that they’re setting up their training programs…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Do you — do you agree, Governor?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let me just finish the point.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The — where they’re partnering so that they’re designing training programs.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And people who are going through them know that there’s a job waiting for them if they complete it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That makes a big difference, but that requires some federal support.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Let me just say one final example.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When it comes to making college affordable, whether it’s two-year or four-year, one of the things that I did as president was we were sending $60 billion to banks and lenders as middlemen for the student loan program, even though the loans were guaranteed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So there was no risk for the banks or the lenders, but they were taking billions out of the system.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we said, “Why not cut out the middleman?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” And as a consequence, what we’ve been able to do is to provide millions more students assistance, lower or keep low interest rates on student loans.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And this is an example of where our priorities make a difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor Romney, I genuinely believe cares about education, but when he tells a student that, you know, “you should borrow money from your parents to go to college,” you know, that indicates the degree to which, you know, there may not be as much of a focus on the fact that folks like myself, folks like Michelle, kids probably who attend University of Denver, just don’t have that option.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And for us to be able to make sure that they’ve got that opportunity and they can walk through that door, that is vitally important not just to those kids.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s how we’re going to grow this economy over the long term.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’re running out of time, gentlemen.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: LEHRER: Governor?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: President, Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: President, you’re entitled as the president to your own airplane and to your own house, but not to your own facts.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: All right, I’m not going to cut education funding.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I don’t have any plan to cut education funding and — and grants that go to people going to college.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’m planning on to grow.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So I’m not planning on making changes there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But you make a very good point, which is that the place you put your money just makes a pretty clear indication of where your heart is.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You put $90 billion into — into green jobs.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I — look, I’m all in favor of green energy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: $90 billion, that would have — that would have hired 2 million teachers.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: $90 billion.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And these businesses, many of them have gone out of business, I think about half of them, of the ones have been invested in have gone out of business.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: A number of them happened to be owned by people who were contributors to your campaigns.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Look, the right course for America’s government, we were talking about the role of government, is not to become the economic player, picking winners and losers, telling people what kind of health treatment they can receive, taking over the health care system that has existed in this country for a long, long time and has produced the best health records in the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The right answer for government is say, How do we make the private sector become more efficient and more effective?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: How do we get schools to be more competitive?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let’s grade them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I propose we grade our schools so parents know which schools are succeeding and failing, so they can take their child to a — to a school that he’s being more successful.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I don’t want to cut our commitment to education.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I wanted to make it more effective and efficient.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And by the way, I’ve had that experience.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I don’t just talk about it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’ve been there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Massachusetts schools are ranked number one in the nation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is not because I didn’t have commitment to education.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s because I care about education for all of our kids.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right, gentlemen…

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Excuse me .

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Excuse me, sir.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: We’ve got — we’ve got — barely have three minutes left.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: I’m not going to grade the two of you and say your answers have been too long or I’ve done a poor job.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You’ve done a great job.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Oh, well, no.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But the fact is government — the role of government and governing, we’ve lost a pod in other words.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: So we only have three — three minutes left in the — in the debate before we go to your closing statements.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: And so I want to ask finally here, and remember, we’ve got three minutes total time here — and the question is this.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Many of the legislative functions of the federal government right now are in a state of paralysis as a result of partisan gridlock.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: If elected, in your case, if re-elected, in your case, what would you do about that?

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Governor?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Jim, I had the great experience — it didn’t seem like it at the time — of being elected in a state where my legislature was 87 percent Democrat.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And that meant I figured out from day one I had to get along and I had to work across the aisle to get anything done.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We drove our schools to be number one in the nation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We cut taxes 19 times.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: But what would you do as president?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We — as president, I will sit on day one — actually, the day after I get elected — I’ll sit down with leaders — the Democratic leaders, as well as Republican leaders, and continue — as we did in my state — we met every Monday for a couple hours, talked about the issues and the challenges in the — in the — in our state in that case.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have to work on a collaborative basis, not because we’re going to compromise our principle, but because there’s common ground.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the challenges America faces right now — look, the reason I’m in this race is there are people that are really hurting today in this country.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And we face — this deficit could crush the future generations.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: What’s happening in the Middle East, there are developments around the world that are of real concern.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And Republicans and Democrats both love America.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But we need to have leadership — leadership in Washington that will actually bring people together and get the job done and could not care less if — if it’s a Republican or a Democrat.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’ve done it before.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’ll do it again.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Lehrer
sentence_text: President?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, first of all, I think Governor Romney’s going to have a busy first day, because he’s also going to repeal Obamacare, which will not be very popular among Democrats as you’re sitting down with them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But, look, my philosophy has been, I will take ideas from anybody, Democrat or Republican, as long as they’re advancing the cause of making middle-class families stronger and giving ladders of opportunity to the middle class.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how we cut taxes for middle- class families and small businesses.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how we cut a trillion dollars of spending that wasn’t advancing that cause.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how we signed three trade deals into law that are helping us to double our exports and sell more American products around the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how we repealed “don’t ask/don’t tell.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” That’s how we ended the war in Iraq, as I promised, and that’s how we’re going to wind down the war in Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how we went after Al Qaida and bin Laden.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So we’ve — we’ve seen progress even under Republican control of the House of Representatives.

sentence_text: We don’t have to settle for 23 million people struggling to find a good job.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: If I become president, I’ll get America working again.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I will get us on track to a balanced budget.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The president hasn’t.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I will.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’ll make sure we can reform Medicare and Social Security to preserve them for coming — coming generations.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The president said he would.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: He didn’t.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: Governor…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’ll get our incomes up.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And by the way, I’ve done these things.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I served as governor and showed I could get them done.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: President, last two minutes belong to you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Barry, I think a lot of this campaign, maybe over the last four years, has been devoted to this nation that I think government creates jobs, that that somehow is the answer.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s not what I believe.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I believe that the free enterprise system is the greatest engine of prosperity the world’s ever known.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I believe in self-reliance and individual initiative and risk takers being rewarded.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I also believe that everybody should have a fair shot and everybody should do their fair share and everybody should play by the same rules, because that’s how our economy’s grown.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s how we built the world’s greatest middle class.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And — and that is part of what’s at stake in this election.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There’s a fundamentally different vision about how we move our country forward.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I believe Governor Romney is a good man.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Loves his family, cares about his faith.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I also believe that when he said behind closed doors that 47 percent of the country considered themselves victims who refuse personal responsibility, think about who he was talking about.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Folks on Social Security who’ve worked all their lives.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Veterans who’ve sacrificed for this country.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Students who are out there trying to hopefully advance their own dreams, but also this country’s dreams.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Soldiers who are overseas fighting for us right now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: People who are working hard every day, paying payroll tax, gas taxes, but don’t make enough income.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I want to fight for them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s what I’ve been doing for the last four years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because if they succeed, I believe the country succeeds.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When my grandfather fought in World War II and he came back and he got a G.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Bill and that allowed him to go to college, that wasn’t a handout.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That was something that advanced the entire country.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I want to make sure that the next generation has those same opportunities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s why I’m asking for your vote and that’s why I’m asking for another four years.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: President Obama, Governor Romney, thank you for being here tonight.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: On that note we have come to an end of this town hall debate.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: Our thanks to the participants for their time and to the people of Hofstra University for their hospitality.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: The next and final debate takes place Monday night at Lynn University in Boca Raton, Florida.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: Don’t forget to watch.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: Election Day is three weeks from today.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: Don’t forget to vote.

speaker: Crowley
sentence_text: Good night.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Good evening from the campus of Lynn University here in Boca Raton, Florida.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: This is the fourth and last debate of the 2012 campaign, brought to you by the Commission on Presidential Debates.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: This one’s on foreign policy.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’m Bob Schieffer of CBS News.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The questions are mine, and I have not shared them with the candidates or their aides.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The audience has taken a vow of silence — no applause, no reaction of any kind, except right now when we welcome President Barack Obama and Governor Mitt Romney.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Gentlemen, your campaigns have agreed to certain rules and they are simple.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: They’ve asked me to divide the evening into segments.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’ll pose a question at the beginning of each segment.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: You will each have two minutes to respond and then we will have a general discussion until we move to the next segment.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Tonight’s debate, as both of you know, comes on the 50th anniversary of the night that President Kennedy told the world that the Soviet Union had installed nuclear missiles in Cuba, perhaps the closest we’ve ever come to nuclear war.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And it is a sobering reminder that every president faces at some point an unexpected threat to our national security from abroad.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: So let’s begin.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The first segment is the challenge of a changing Middle East and the new face of terrorism.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’m going to put this into two segments so you’ll have two topic questions within this one segment on the subject.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The first question, and it concerns Libya.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The controversy over what happened there continues.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Four Americans are dead, including an American ambassador.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Questions remain.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What happened?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What caused it?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Was it spontaneous?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Was it an intelligence failure?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Was it a policy failure?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Was there an attempt to mislead people about what really happened?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor Romney, you said this was an example of an American policy in the Middle East that is unraveling before our very eyes.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’d like to hear each of you give your thoughts on that.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor Romney, you won the toss.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: You go first.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Thank you, Bob.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And thank you for agreeing to moderate this debate this evening.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Thank you to Lynn University for welcoming us here.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: President, it’s good to be with you again.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We were together at a humorous event a little earlier, and it’s nice to maybe funny this time, not on purpose.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’ll see what happens.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is obviously an area of great concern to the entire world, and to America in particular, which is to see a — a complete change in the — the structure and the — the environment in the Middle East.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: With the Arab Spring, came a great deal of hope that there would be a change towards more moderation, and opportunity for greater participation on the part of women in public life, and in economic life in the Middle East.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But instead, we’ve seen in nation after nation, a number of disturbing events.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Of course we see in Syria, 30,000 civilians having been killed by the military there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We see in — in Libya, an attack apparently by, I think we know now, by terrorists of some kind against — against our people there, four people dead.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Our hearts and — and minds go out to them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Mali has been taken over, the northern part of Mali by al-Qaeda type individuals.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have in — in Egypt, a Muslim Brotherhood president.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And so what we’re seeing is a pretty dramatic reversal in the kind of hopes we had for that region.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Of course the greatest threat of all is Iran, four years closer to a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And — and we’re going to have to recognize that we have to do as the president has done.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I congratulate him on — on taking out Osama bin Laden and going after the leadership in al-Qaeda.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But we can’t kill our way out of this mess.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re going to have to put in place a very comprehensive and robust strategy to help the — the world of Islam and other parts of the world, reject this radical violent extremism, which is — it’s certainly not on the run.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s certainly not hiding.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is a group that is now involved in 10 or 12 countries, and it presents an enormous threat to our friends, to the world, to America, long term, and we must have a comprehensive strategy to help reject this kind of extremism.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, my first job as commander in chief, Bob, is to keep the American people safe.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s what we’ve done over the last four years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We ended the war in Iraq, refocused our attention on those who actually killed us on 9/11.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And as a consequence, Al Qaeda’s core leadership has been decimated.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In addition, we’re now able to transition out of Afghanistan in a responsible way, making sure that Afghans take responsibility for their own security.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that allows us also to rebuild alliances and make friends around the world to combat future threats.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now with respect to Libya, as I indicated in the last debate, when we received that phone call, I immediately made sure that, number one, that we did everything we could to secure those Americans who were still in harm’s way; number two, that we would investigate exactly what happened, and number three, most importantly, that we would go after those who killed Americans and we would bring them to justice.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s exactly what we’re going to do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I think it’s important to step back and think about what happened in Libya.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Keep in mind that I and Americans took leadership in organizing an international coalition that made sure that we were able to, without putting troops on the ground at the cost of less than what we spent in two weeks in Iraq, liberate a country that had been under the yoke of dictatorship for 40 years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Got rid of a despot who had killed Americans and as a consequence, despite this tragedy, you had tens of thousands of Libyans after the events in Benghazi marching and saying America is our friend.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We stand with them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now that represents the opportunity we have to take advantage of.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, you know, Governor Romney, I’m glad that you agree that we have been successful in going after Al Qaida, but I have to tell you that, you know, your strategy previously has been one that has been all over the map and is not designed to keep Americans safe or to build on the opportunities that exist in the Middle East.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, my strategy is pretty straightforward, which is to go after the bad guys, to make sure we do our very best to interrupt them, to — to kill them, to take them out of the picture.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But my strategy is broader than that.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s — that’s important, of course.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But the key that we’re going to have to pursue is a — is a pathway to get the Muslim world to be able to reject extremism on its own.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We don’t want another Iraq, we don’t want another Afghanistan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s not the right course for us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The right course for us is to make sure that we go after the — the people who are leaders of these various anti-American groups and these — these jihadists, but also help the Muslim world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And how do we do that?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: A group of Arab scholars came together, organized by the U.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: , to look at how we can help the — the world reject these — these terrorists.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the answer they came up with was this: One, more economic development.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We should key our foreign aid, our direct foreign investment, and that of our friends, we should coordinate it to make sure that we — we push back and give them more economic development.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, better education.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number three, gender equality.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number four, the rule of law.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have to help these nations create civil societies.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But what’s been happening over the last couple of years is, as we’ve watched this tumult in the Middle East, this rising tide of chaos occur, you see Al Qaida rushing in, you see other jihadist groups rushing in.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And — and they’re throughout many nations in the Middle East.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s wonderful that Libya seems to be making some progress, despite this terrible tragedy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But next door, of course, we have Egypt.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Libya’s 6 million population; Egypt, 80 million population.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We want — we want to make sure that we’re seeing progress throughout the Middle East.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: With Mali now having North Mali taken over by Al Qaida; with Syria having Assad continuing to — to kill, to murder his own people, this is a region in tumult.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And, of course, Iran on the path to a nuclear weapon, we’ve got real .

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We’ll get to that, but let’s give the president a chance.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor Romney, I’m glad that you recognize that Al Qaida is a threat, because a few months ago when you were asked what’s the biggest geopolitical threat facing America, you said Russia, not Al Qaida; you said Russia, in the 1980s, they’re now calling to ask for their foreign policy back because, you know, the Cold War’s been over for 20 years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But Governor, when it comes to our foreign policy, you seem to want to import the foreign policies of the 1980s, just like the social policies of the 1950s and the economic policies of the 1920s.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You say that you’re not interested in duplicating what happened in Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But just a few weeks ago, you said you think we should have more troops in Iraq right now.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the — the challenge we have — I know you haven’t been in a position to actually execute foreign policy — but every time you’ve offered an opinion, you’ve been wrong.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You said we should have gone into Iraq, despite that fact that there were no weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You said that we should still have troops in Iraq to this day.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You indicated that we shouldn’t be passing nuclear treaties with Russia despite the fact that 71 senators, Democrats and Republicans, voted for it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You said that, first, we should not have a timeline in Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Then you said we should.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now you say maybe or it depends, which means not only were you wrong, but you were also confusing in sending mixed messages both to our troops and our allies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So, what — what we need to do with respect to the Middle East is strong, steady leadership, not wrong and reckless leadership that is all over the map.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And unfortunately, that’s the kind of opinions that you’ve offered throughout this campaign, and it is not a recipe for American strength, or keeping America safe over the long haul.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’m going to add a couple of minutes here to give you a chance to respond.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, of course I don’t concur with what the president said about my own record and the things that I’ve said.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They don’t happen to be accurate.

speaker: Mitt Romney
