sentence_text: But — but I can say this, that we’re talking about the Middle East and how to help the Middle East reject the kind of terrorism we’re seeing, and the rising tide of tumult and — and confusion.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And — and attacking me is not an agenda.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Attacking me is not talking about how we’re going to deal with the challenges that exist in the Middle East, and take advantage of the opportunity there, and stem the tide of this violence.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But I’ll respond to a couple of things that you mentioned.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: First of all, Russia I indicated is a geopolitical foe.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Not…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Excuse me.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s a geopolitical foe, and I said in the same — in the same paragraph I said, and Iran is the greatest national security threat we face.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Russia does continue to battle us in the U.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: time and time again.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I have clear eyes on this.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’m not going to wear rose-colored glasses when it comes to Russia, or Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Putin.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I’m certainly not going to say to him, I’ll give you more flexibility after the election.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: After the election, he’ll get more backbone.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, with regards to Iraq, you and I agreed I believe that there should be a status of forces agreement.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Oh you didn’t?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You didn’t want a status of…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What I would not have had done was left 10,000 troops in Iraq that would tie us down.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that certainly would not help us in the Middle East.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’m sorry, you actually — there was a — there was an effort on the part of the president to have a status of forces agreement, and I concurred in that, and said that we should have some number of troops that stayed on.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That was something I concurred with…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: …that your posture.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That was my posture as well.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You thought it should have been 5,000 troops…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: … I thought there should have been more troops, but you know what?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The answer was we got…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: … no troops through whatsoever.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This was just a few weeks ago that you indicated that we should still have troops in Iraq.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: No, I…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: …I’m sorry that’s a…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You — you…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: …that’s a — I indicated…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: …major speech.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: …I indicated that you failed to put in place a status…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: …of forces agreement at the end of the conflict that existed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor — here — here’s — here’s one thing…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: …here’s one thing I’ve learned as commander in chief.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let him answer…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You’ve got to be clear, both to our allies and our enemies, about where you stand and what you mean.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You just gave a speech a few weeks ago in which you said we should still have troops in Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That is not a recipe for making sure that we are taking advantage of the opportunities and meeting the challenges of the Middle East.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, it is absolutely true that we cannot just meet these challenges militarily.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so what I’ve done throughout my presidency and will continue to do is, number one, make sure that these countries are supporting our counterterrorism efforts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number two, make sure that they are standing by our interests in Israel’s security, because it is a true friend and our greatest ally in the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number three, we do have to make sure that we’re protecting religious minorities and women because these countries can’t develop unless all the population, not just half of it, is developing.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Number four, we do have to develop their economic — their economic capabilities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But number five, the other thing that we have to do is recognize that we can’t continue to do nation building in these regions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Part of American leadership is making sure that we’re doing nation building here at home.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That will help us maintain the kind of American leadership that we need.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let me interject the second topic question in this segment about the Middle East and so on, and that is, you both mentioned — alluded to this, and that is Syria.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The war in Syria has now spilled over into Lebanon.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We have, what, more than 100 people that were killed there in a bomb.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: There were demonstrations there, eight people dead.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President, it’s been more than a year since you saw — you told Assad he had to go.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Since then, 30,000 Syrians have died.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We’ve had 300,000 refugees.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The war goes on.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: He’s still there.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Should we reassess our policy and see if we can find a better way to influence events there?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Or is that even possible?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And you go first, sir.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What we’ve done is organize the international community, saying Assad has to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve mobilized sanctions against that government.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have made sure that they are isolated.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have provided humanitarian assistance and we are helping the opposition organize, and we’re particularly interested in making sure that we’re mobilizing the moderate forces inside of Syria.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But ultimately, Syrians are going to have to determine their own future.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so everything we’re doing, we’re doing in consultation with our partners in the region, including Israel which obviously has a huge interest in seeing what happens in Syria; coordinating with Turkey and other countries in the region that have a great interest in this.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This — what we’re seeing taking place in Syria is heartbreaking, and that’s why we are going to do everything we can to make sure that we are helping the opposition.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we also have to recognize that, you know, for us to get more entangled militarily in Syria is a serious step, and we have to do so making absolutely certain that we know who we are helping; that we’re not putting arms in the hands of folks who eventually could turn them against us or allies in the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I am confident that Assad’s days are numbered.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what we can’t do is to simply suggest that, as Governor Romney at times has suggested, that giving heavy weapons, for example, to the Syrian opposition is a simple proposition that would lead us to be safer over the long term.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: SCHIEFFER: Governor?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, let’s step back and talk about what’s happening in Syria and how important it is.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: First of all, 30,000 people being killed by their government is a humanitarian disaster.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Secondly, Syria is an opportunity for us because Syria plays an important role in the Middle East, particularly right now.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Syria is Iran’s only ally in the Arab world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s their route to the sea.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s the route for them to arm Hezbollah in Lebanon, which threatens, of course, our ally, Israel.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And so seeing Syria remove Assad is a very high priority for us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, seeing a — a replacement government being responsible people is critical for us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And finally, we don’t want to have military involvement there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We don’t want to get drawn into a military conflict.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And so the right course for us, is working through our partners and with our own resources, to identify responsible parties within Syria, organize them, bring them together in a — in a form of — if not government, a form of — of — of council that can take the lead in Syria.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then make sure they have the arms necessary to defend themselves.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We do need to make sure that they don’t have arms that get into the — the wrong hands.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Those arms could be used to hurt us down the road.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to make sure as well that we coordinate this effort with our allies, and particularly with — with Israel.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But the Saudi’s and the Qatari, and — and the Turks are all very concerned about this.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They’re willing to work with us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to have a very effective leadership effort in Syria, making sure that the — the insurgent there are armed and that the insurgents that become armed, are people who will be the responsible parties.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Recognize — I believe that Assad must go.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I believe he will go.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But I believe — we want to make sure that we have the relationships of friendship with the people that take his place, steps that in the years to come we see Syria as a — as a friend, and Syria as a responsible party in the Middle East.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This — this is a critical opportunity for America.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And what I’m afraid of is we’ve watched over the past year or so, first the president saying, well we’ll let the U.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: deal with it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And Assad — excuse me, Kofi Annan came in and said we’re going to try to have a ceasefire.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That didn’t work.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Then it went to the Russians and said, let’s see if you can do something.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We should be playing the leadership role there, not on the ground with military.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: …by the leadership role.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are playing the leadership role.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We organized the Friends of Syria.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We are mobilizing humanitarian support, and support for the opposition.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we are making sure that those we help are those who will be friends of ours in the long term and friends of our allies in the region over the long term.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But going back to Libya — because this is an example of how we make choices.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When we went in to Libya, and we were able to immediately stop the massacre there, because of the unique circumstances and the coalition that we had helped to organize.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We also had to make sure that Moammar Gadhafi didn’t stay there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And to the governor’s credit, you supported us going into Libya and the coalition that we organized.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But when it came time to making sure that Gadhafi did not stay in power, that he was captured, Governor, your suggestion was that this was mission creep, that this was mission muddle.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Imagine if we had pulled out at that point.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, Moammar Gadhafi had more American blood on his hands than any individual other than Osama bin Laden.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so we were going to make sure that we finished the job.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s part of the reason why the Libyans stand with us.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we did so in a careful, thoughtful way, making certain that we knew who we were dealing with, that those forces of moderation on the ground were ones that we could work with, and we have to take the same kind of steady, thoughtful leadership when it comes to Syria.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s exactly what we’re doing.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor, can I just ask you, would you go beyond what the administration would do, like for example, would you put in no-fly zones over Syria?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I don’t want to have our military involved in Syria.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I don’t think there is a necessity to put our military in Syria at this stage.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I don’t anticipate that in the future.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: As I indicated, our objectives are to replace Assad and to have in place a new government which is friendly to us, a responsible government, if possible.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I want to make sure they get armed and they have the arms necessary to defend themselves, but also to remove — to remove Assad.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But I do not want to see a military involvement on the part of our — of our troops.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Well —

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And this isn’t — this isn’t going to be necessary.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We — we have, with our partners in the region, we have sufficient resources to support those groups.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But look, this has been going on for a year.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is a time — this should have been a time for American leadership.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We should have taken a leading role, not militarily, but a leading role organizationally, governmentally to bring together the parties; to find responsible parties.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: As you hear from intelligence sources even today, the — the insurgents are highly disparate.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They haven’t come together.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They haven’t formed a unity group, a council of some kind.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That needs to happen.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: America can help that happen.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And we need to make sure they have the arms they need to carry out the very important role which is getting rid of Assad.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Can we get a quick response, Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President, because I want to…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, I’ll — I’ll be very quick.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: What you just heard Governor Romney said is he doesn’t have different ideas.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s because we’re doing exactly what we should be doing to try to promote a moderate Syrian leadership and a — an effective transition so that we get Assad out.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s the kind of leadership we’ve shown.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s the kind of leadership we’ll continue to show.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: May I ask you, you know, during the Egyptian turmoil, there came a point when you said it was time for President Mubarak to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Right.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Some in your administration thought perhaps we should have waited a while on that.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Do you have any regrets about that?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: No, I don’t, because I think that America has to stand with democracy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The notion that we would have tanks run over those young people who were in Tahrir Square, that is not the kind of American leadership that John F.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Kennedy talked about 50 years ago.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what I’ve also said is that now that you have a democratically elected government in Egypt, that they have to make sure that they take responsibility for protecting religious minorities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we have put significant pressure on them to make sure they’re doing that; to recognize the rights of women, which is critical throughout the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: These countries can’t develop if young women are not given the kind of education that they need.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They have to abide by their treaty with Israel.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That is a red line for us, because not only is Israel’s security at stake, but our security is at stake if that unravels.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They have to make sure that they’re cooperating with us when it comes to counterterrorism.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we will help them with respect to developing their own economy, because ultimately what’s going to make the Egyptian revolution successful for the people of Egypt, but also for the world, is if those young people who gathered there are seeing opportunities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Their aspirations are similar to young people’s here.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They want jobs, they want to be able to make sure their kids are going to a good school.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They want to make sure that they have a roof over their heads and that they have the prospects of a better life in the future.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so one of the things that we’ve been doing is, is, for example, organizing entrepreneurship conferences with these Egyptians to give them a sense of how they can start rebuilding their economy in a way that’s noncorrupt, that’s transparent.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what is also important for us to understand is, is that for America to be successful in this region there’s some things that we’re going to have to do here at home as well.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, one of the challenges over the last decade is we’ve done experiments in nation building in places like Iraq and Afghanistan and we’ve neglected, for example, developing our own economy, our own energy sectors, our own education system.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it’s very hard for us to project leadership around the world when we’re not doing what we need to do…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor Romney, I want to hear your response to that, but I would just ask you, would you have stuck with Mubarak?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: No.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I believe, as the president indicated, and said at the time that I supported his — his action there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I felt that — I wish we’d have had a better vision of the future.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I wish that, looking back at the beginning of the president’s term and even further back than that, that we’d have recognized that there was a growing energy and passion for freedom in that part of the world, and that we would have worked more aggressively with our friend and with other friends in the region to have them make the transition towards a more representative form of government, such that it didn’t explode in the way that it did.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But once it exploded, I felt the same as the president did, which is these freedom voices and the streets of Egypt, where the people who were speaking of our principles and the President Mubarak had done things which were unimaginable and the idea of him crushing his people was not something that we could possibly support.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let me step back and talk about what I think our mission has to be in the Middle East and even more broadly, because our purpose is to make sure the world is more — is peaceful.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We want a peaceful planet.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We want people to be able to enjoy their lives and know they’re going to have a bright and prosperous future, not be at war.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s our purpose.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the mantle of leadership for the — promoting the principles of peace has fallen to America.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We didn’t ask for it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But it’s an honor that we have it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But for us to be able to promote those principles of peace requires us to be strong.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And that begins with a strong economy here at home.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Unfortunately, the economy is not stronger.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: When the — when the president of Iraq — excuse me, of Iran, Ahmadinejad, says that our debt makes us not a great country, that’s a frightening thing.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Former chief of the — Joint Chiefs of Staff said that — Admiral Mullen said that our debt is the biggest national security threat we face.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This — we have weakened our economy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need a strong economy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to have as well a strong military.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Our military is second to none in the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re blessed with terrific soldiers, and extraordinary technology and intelligence.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But the idea of a trillion dollar in cuts through sequestration and budget cuts to the military would change that.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to have strong allies.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Our association and connection with our allies is essential to America’s strength.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re the great nation that has allies, 42 allies and friends around the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And, finally, we have to stand by our principles.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And if we’re strong in each of those things, American influence will grow.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But unfortunately, in nowhere in the world is America’s influence will grow.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But unfortunately, in — nowhere in the world is America’s influence greater today than it was four years ago.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And that’s because we’ve become weaker in each of those four…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: …you’re going to get a chance to respond to that, because that’s a perfect segue into our next segment, and that is, what is America’s role in the world?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And that is the question.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What do each of you see as our role in the world, and I believe, Governor Romney, it’s your chance to go first.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well I — I absolutely believe that America has a — a responsibility, and the privilege of helping defend freedom and promote the principles that — that make the world more peaceful.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And those principles include human rights, human dignity, free enterprise, freedom of expression, elections.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Because when there are elections, people tend to vote for peace.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They don’t vote for war.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So we want to promote those principles around the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We recognize that there are places of conflict in the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We want to end those conflicts to the extent humanly possible.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But in order to be able to fulfill our role in the world, America must be strong.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: America must lead.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And for that to happen, we have to strengthen our economy here at home.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You can’t have 23 million people struggling to get a job.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You can’t have an economy that over the last three years keeps slowing down its growth rate.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You can’t have kids coming out of college, half of them can’t find a job today, or a job that’s commensurate with their college degree.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have to get our economy going.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And our military, we’ve got to strengthen our military long-term.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We don’t know what the world is going to throw at us down the road.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We — we make decisions today in the military that — that will confront challenges we can’t imagine.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: In the 2000 debates, there was no mention of terrorism, for instance.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And a year later, 9/11 happened.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So, we have to make decisions based upon uncertainty, and that means a strong military.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I will not cut our military budget.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have to also stand by our allies.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I — I think the tension that existed between Israel and the United States was very unfortunate.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I think also that pulling our missile defense program out of Poland in the way we did was also unfortunate in terms of, if you will, disrupting the relationship in some ways that existed between us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then, of course, with regards to standing for our principles, when — when the students took to the streets in Tehran and the people there protested, the Green Revolution occurred, for the president to be silent I thought was an enormous mistake.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have to stand for our principles, stand for our allies, stand for a strong military and stand for a stronger economy.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: America remains the one indispensable nation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the world needs a strong America, and it is stronger now than when I came into office.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because we ended the war in Iraq, we were able to refocus our attention on not only the terrorist threat, but also beginning a transition process in Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It also allowed us to refocus on alliances and relationships that had been neglected for a decade.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And Governor Romney, our alliances have never been stronger, in Asia, in Europe, in Africa, with Israel, where we have unprecedented military and intelligence cooperation, including dealing with the Iranian threat.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what we also have been able to do is position ourselves so we can start rebuilding America, and that’s what my plan does.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Making sure that we’re bringing manufacturing back to our shores so that we’re creating jobs here, as we’ve done with the auto industry, not rewarding companies that are shipping jobs overseas.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Making sure that we’ve got the best education system in the world, including retraining our workers for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Doing everything we can to control our own energy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve cut our oil imports to the lowest level in two decades because we’ve developed oil and natural gas.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But we also have to develop clean energy technologies that will allow us to cut our exports in half by 2020.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s the kind of leadership that we need to show.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we’ve got to make sure that we reduce our deficit.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Unfortunately, Governor Romney’s plan doesn’t do it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve got to do it in a responsible way by cutting out spending we don’t need, but also asking the wealthiest to pay a little bit more.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That way we can invest in the research and technology that’s always kept us at the cutting edge.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, Governor Romney has taken a different approach throughout this campaign.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Both at home and abroad, he has proposed wrong and reckless policies.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He’s praised George Bush as a good economic steward and Dick Cheney as somebody who’s — who shows great wisdom and judgment.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And taking us back to those kinds of strategies that got us into this mess are not the way that we are going to maintain leadership in the 21st century.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor Romney, “wrong and reckless” policies?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’ve got a policy for the future and agenda for the future.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And when it comes to our economy here at home, I know what it takes to create 12 million new jobs and rising take-home pay.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And what we’ve seen over the last four years is something I don’t want to see over the next four years.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The president said by now we’d be a 5.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: 4 percent unemployment.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re 9 million jobs short of that.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I will get America working again and see rising take-home pay again, and I’ll do it with five simple steps.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number one, we are going to have North American energy independence.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re going to do it by taking full advantage of oil, coal, gas, nuclear and our renewables.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, we’re going to increase our trade.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Trade grows about 12 percent year.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It doubles about every — every five or so years.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We can do better than that, particularly in Latin America.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The opportunities for us in Latin America we have just not taken advantage of fully.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: As a matter of fact, Latin America’s economy is almost as big as the economy of China.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re all focused on China.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Latin America is a huge opportunity for us — time zone, language opportunities.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number three, we’re going to have to have training programs that work for our workers and schools that finally put the parents and the teachers and the kids first, and the teachers’ unions going to have to go behind.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then we’re going to have to get to a balanced budget.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We can’t expect entrepreneurs and businesses large and small to take their life savings or their company’s money and invest in America if they think we’re headed to the road to Greece.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And that’s where we’re going right now unless we finally get off this spending and borrowing binge.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I’ll get us on track to a balanced budget.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And finally, number five, we’ve got to champion small business.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Small business is where jobs come from.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Two-thirds of our jobs come from small businesses.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: New business formation is down to the lowest level in 30 years under this administration.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I want to bring it back and get back good jobs and rising take-home pay.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, let’s talk about what we need to compete.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: First of all, Governor Romney talks about small businesses.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But, Governor, when you were in Massachusetts, small businesses development ranked about 48th, I think out of 50 states in Massachusetts, because the policies that you are promoting actually don’t help small businesses.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the way you define small businesses includes folks at the very top.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they include you and me.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s not the kind of small business promotion we need.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But let’s take an example that we know is going to make a difference in the 21st century and that’s our education policy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We didn’t have a lot of chance to talk about this in the last debate.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, under my leadership, what we’ve done is reformed education, working with governors, 46 states.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’ve seen progress and gains in schools that were having a terrible time.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they’re starting to finally make progress.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what I now want to do is to hire more teachers, especially in math and science, because we know that we’ve fallen behind when it comes to math and science.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And those teachers can make a difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, Governor Romney, when you were asked by teachers whether or not this would help the economy grow, you said this isn’t going to help the economy grow.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When you were asked about reduced class sizes, you said class sizes don’t make a difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I tell you, if you talk to teachers, they will tell you it does make a difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if we’ve got math teachers who are able to provide the kind of support that they need for our kids, that’s what’s going to determine whether or not the new businesses are created here.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Companies are going to locate here depending on whether we’ve got the most highly skilled workforce.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the kinds of budget proposals that you’ve put forward, when we don’t ask either you or me to pay a dime more in terms of reducing the deficit, but instead we slash support for education, that’s undermining our long-term competitiveness.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That is not good for America’s position in the world, and the world notices.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let me get back to foreign policy.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Can I just get back…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well — well, I need to speak a moment…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: … if you’ll let me, Bob, just about education…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: … because I’m — I’m so proud of the state that I had the chance to be governor of.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have every two years tests that look at how well our kids are doing.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Fourth graders and eighth graders are tested in English and math.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: While I was governor, I was proud that our fourth graders came out number one of all 50 states in English, and then also in math.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And our eighth graders number one in English and also in math.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: First time one state had been number one in all four measures.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: How did we do that?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, Republicans and Democrats came together on a bipartisan basis to put in place education principles that focused on having great teachers in the classroom.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Ten years earlier…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And that was — that was — that was what allowed us to become the number one state in the nation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But that was 10 years before you took office.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then you cut education spending when you came into office.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The first — the first — the first — and we kept our schools number one in the nation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They’re still number one today.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the principles that we put in place, we also gave kids not just a graduation exam that determined whether they were up to the skills needed to — to be able compete, but also if they graduated the quarter of their class, they got a four-year tuition- free ride at any Massachusetts public institution of higher learning.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That happened before you came into office.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That was actually mine, actually, Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: President.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You got that fact wrong.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let me get — I want to try to shift it, because we have heard some of this in the other debates.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor, you say you want a bigger military.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: You want a bigger Navy.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: You don’t want to cut defense spending.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What I want to ask you — we were talking about financial problems in this country.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Where are you going to get the money?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, let’s come back and talk about the military, but all the way — all the way through.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: First of all, I’m going through from the very beginning — we’re going to cut about 5 percent of the discretionary budget, excluding military.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s number one.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: But can you do this without driving deeper…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The good news is .

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’d be happy to have you take a look.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Come on our website.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You look at how we get to a balanced budget within eight to 10 years.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We do it by getting — by reducing spending in a whole series of programs.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: By the way, number one I get rid of is Obamacare.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: There are a number of things that sound good, but frankly, we just can’t afford them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And that one doesn’t sound good and it’s not affordable.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So I’d get rid of that one from day one.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: To the extent humanly possible, we get that out.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We take program after program that we don’t absolutely have to have, and we get rid of them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, we take some programs that we are doing to keep, like Medicaid, which is a program for the poor; we’ll take that healthcare program for the poor and we give it to the states to run because states run these programs more efficiently.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: As a governor, I thought please, give me this program.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I can run this more efficiently than the federal government and states, by the way, are proving it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: States like Arizona, Rhode Island have taken these — these Medicaid dollars; have shown they can run these programs more cost-effectively.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I want to do those two things and get this — get this to a balanced budget with eight — eight to 10 years.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But the military — let’s get back to the military, though.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: SCHIEFFER: That’s what I’m trying…

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He should have answered the first question.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Look, Governor Romney’s called for $5 trillion of tax cuts that he says he’s going to pay for by closing deductions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, the math doesn’t work, but he continues to claim that he’s going to do it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: He then wants to spend another $2 trillion on military spending that our military is not asking for.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Now, keep in mind that our military spending has gone up every single year that I’ve been in office.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We spend more on our military than the next 10 countries combined; China, Russia, France, the United Kingdom, you name it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The next 10.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And what I did was work with our joint chiefs of staff to think about, what are we going to need in the future to make sure that we are safe?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that’s the budget that we’ve put forward.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But, what you can’t do is spend $2 trillion in additional military spending that the military is not asking for, $5 trillion on tax cuts.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You say that you’re going to pay for it by closing loopholes and deductions, without naming what those loopholes and deductions are.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And then somehow you’re also going to deal with the deficit that we’ve already got.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The math simply doesn’t work.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But when it comes to our military, what we have to think about is not, you know just budgets, we’ve got to think about capabilities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We need to be thinking about cyber security.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We need to be talking about space.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s exactly what our budget does, but it’s driven by strategy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s not driven by politics.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s not driven by members of Congress, and what they would like to see.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s driven by, what are we going to need to keep the American people safe?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s exactly what our budget does, and it also then allows us to reduce our deficit, which is a significant national security concern.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because we’ve got to make sure that our economy is strong at home so that we can project military power overseas.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’m pleased that I’ve balanced budgets.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I was on the world of business for 25 years.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: If you didn’t balance your budget, you went out of business.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I went into the Olympics that was out of balance, and we got it on balance, and made a success there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I had the chance to be governor of a state.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Four years in a row, Democrats and Republicans came together to balance the budget.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We cut taxes 19 times and balanced our budget.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The president hasn’t balanced a budget yet.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I expect to have the opportunity to do so myself.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’m going to be able to balance the budget.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let’s talk about military spending, and that’s this.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Our Navy is old — excuse me, our Navy is smaller now than at any time since 1917.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The Navy said they needed 313 ships to carry out their mission.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re now at under 285.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re headed down to the low 200s if we go through a sequestration.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s unacceptable to me.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I want to make sure that we have the ships that are required by our Navy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Our Air Force is older and smaller than at any time since it was founded in 1947.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’ve changed for the first time since FDR — since FDR we had the — we’ve always had the strategy of saying we could fight in two conflicts at once.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Now we’re changing to one conflict.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Look, this, in my view, is the highest responsibility of the President of the United States, which is to maintain the safety of the American people.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I will not cut our military budget by a trillion dollars, which is a combination of the budget cuts the president has, as well as the sequestration cuts.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That, in my view, is making — is making our future less certain and less secure.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Bob, I just need to comment on this.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: First of all, the sequester is not something that I’ve proposed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is something that Congress has proposed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It will not happen.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The budget that we are talking about is not reducing our military spending.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is maintaining it.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But I think Governor Romney maybe hasn’t spent enough time looking at how our military works.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You mentioned the Navy, for example, and that we have fewer ships than we did in 1916.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, Governor, we also have fewer horses and bayonets, because the nature of our military’s changed.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have these things called aircraft carriers, where planes land on them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We have these ships that go underwater, nuclear submarines.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so the question is not a game of Battleship, where we’re counting slips.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s what are our capabilities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And so when I sit down with the Secretary of the Navy and the Joint Chiefs of Staff, we determine how are we going to be best able to meet all of our defense needs in a way that also keeps faith with our troops, that also makes sure that our veterans have the kind of support that they need when they come home.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that is not reflected in the kind of budget that you’re putting forward because it just doesn’t work.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And, you know, we visited the website quite a bit and it still doesn’t work.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: A lot to cover.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: I’d like — I’d like to move to the next segment: red lines, Israel and Iran.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Would either of you — and you’ll have two minutes — and, President Obama, you have the first go at this one — would either of you be willing to declare that an attack on Israel is an attack on the United States, which, of course, is the same promise that we give to our close allies like Japan.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And if you made such a declaration, would not that deter Iran?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: It’s certainly deterred the Soviet Union for a long, long time when we made that — we made — we made that promise to our allies.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: First of all, Israel is a true friend.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It is our greatest ally in the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if Israel is attacked, America will stand with Israel.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I’ve made that clear throughout my presidency.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: So you’re — you’re saying we’ve already made that declaration.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I will stand with Israel if they are attacked.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And this is the reason why, working with Israel, we have created the strongest military and intelligence cooperation between our two countries in history.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In fact, this week we’ll be carrying out the largest military exercise with Israel in history, this very week.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But to the issue of Iran, as long as I’m president of the United States Iran will not get a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I made that clear when I came into office.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We then organized the strongest coalition and the strongest sanctions against Iran in history, and it is crippling their economy.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Their currency has dropped 80 percent.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Their oil production has plunged to the lowest level since they were fighting a war with Iraq 20 years ago.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So their economy is in a shambles.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the reason we did this is because a nuclear Iran is a threat to our national security, and it is a threat to Israel’s national security.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We cannot afford to have a nuclear arms race in the most volatile region of the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Iran is a state sponsor of terrorism.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And for them to be able to provide nuclear technology to non-state actors, that’s unacceptable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they have said that they want to see Israel wiped off the map.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So the work that we’ve done with respect to sanctions now offers Iran a choice.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They can take the diplomatic route and end their nuclear program or they will have to face a united world and a United States president, me, who said we’re not going to take any options off the table.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The disagreement I have with Governor Romney is that, during the course of this campaign, he’s often talked as if we should take premature military action.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I think that would be a mistake, because when I’ve sent young men and women into harm’s way, I always understand that that is the last resort, not the first resort.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Two minutes.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, first of all, I want to underscore the same point the president mad,e which is that if I’m President of the United States, when I’m President of the United States, we will stand with Israel.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And if Israel is attacked, we have their back, not just diplomatically, not just culturally, but militarily.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s number one.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, with regards to Iran and the threat of Iran, there’s no question but that a nuclear Iran, a nuclear-capable Iran is unacceptable to America.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It presents a threat not only to our friends but ultimately a threat to us to have Iran have nuclear material, nuclear weapons that could be used against us or used to be threatening to us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It is also essential for us to understand what our mission is in Iran, and that is to dissuade Iran from having a nuclear weapon through peaceful and diplomatic means.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And crippling sanctions are something I called for five years ago, when I was in Israel, speaking at the Herzliya Conference.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I laid out seven steps, crippling sanctions were number one.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And they do work.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You’re seeing it right now in the economy.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It’s absolutely the right thing to do, to have crippling sanctions.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I would have put them in place earlier.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But it’s good that we have them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, something I would add today is I would tighten those sanctions.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I would say that ships that carry Iranian oil, can’t come into our ports.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I imagine the E.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: would agree with us as well.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Not only ships couldn’t, but I’d say companies that are moving their oil can’t, people who are trading in their oil can’t.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I would tighten those sanctions further.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Secondly, I’d take on diplomatic isolation efforts.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I’d make sure that Ahmadinejad is indicted under the Genocide Convention.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: His words amount to genocide incitation.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I would indict him for it.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I would also make sure that their diplomats are treated like the pariah they are around the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The same way we treated the apartheid diplomats of South Africa.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to increase pressure time, and time again on Iran because anything other than a — a — a solution to this, which says — which stops this — this nuclear folly of theirs, is unacceptable to America.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And of course, a military action is the last resort.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: It is something one would only – only consider if all of the other avenues had been — had been tried to their full extent.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let me ask both of you, there — as you know, there are reports that Iran and the United States a part of an international group, have agreed in principle to talks about Iran’s nuclear program.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What is the deal, if there are such talks?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What is the deal that you would accept, Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Well, first of all those are reports in the newspaper.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They are not true.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But our goal is to get Iran to recognize it needs to give up its nuclear program and abide by the U.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: resolutions that have been in place.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because they have the opportunity to reenter the community of nations, and we would welcome that.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There — there are people in Iran who have the same aspirations as people all around the world for a better life.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we hope that their leadership takes the right decision, but the deal we’ll accept is they end their nuclear program.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s very straightforward.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I’m glad that Governor Romney agrees with the steps that we’re taking.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, there have been times, Governor, frankly, during the course of this campaign, where it sounded like you thought that you’d do the same things we did, but you’d say them louder and somehow that — that would make a difference.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it turns out that the work involved in setting up these crippling sanctions is painstaking.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s meticulous.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We started from the day we got into office.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the reason is was so important — and this is a testament to how we’ve restored American credibility and strength around the world — is we had to make sure that all the countries participated, even countries like Russia and China.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Because if it’s just us that are imposing sanctions — we’ve had sanctions in place a long time.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: It’s because we got everybody to agree that Iran is seeing so much pressure.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we’ve got to maintain that pressure.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There is a deal to be had, and that is that they abide by the rules that have already been established.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: They convince the international community they are not pursuing a nuclear program.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: There are inspections that are very intrusive.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But over time, what they can do is regain credibility.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the meantime, though, we’re not going to let up the pressure until we have clear evidence that that takes place.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And one last thing — just — just to make this point.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The clock is ticking.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We’re not going to allow Iran to perpetually engage in negotiations that lead nowhere.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I’ve been very clear to them.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, because of the intelligence coordination that we do with a range of countries, including Israel, we have a sense of when they would get breakout capacity, which means that we would not be able to intervene in time to stop their nuclear program.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that clock is ticking.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we’re going to make sure that if they do not meet the demands of the international community, then we are going to take all options necessary to make sure they don’t have a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I think from the very beginning, one of the challenges we’ve had with Iran is that they have looked at this administration, and felt that the administration was not as strong as it needed to be.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I think they saw weakness where they had expected to find American strength.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I say that because from the very beginning, the president in his campaign four years ago, said he would meet with all the world’s worst actors in his first year, he’d sit down with Chavez and Kim Jong-il, with Castro and President Ahmadinejad of Iran.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I think they looked and thought, well, that’s an unusual honor to receive from the President of the United States.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then the president began what I have called an apology tour, of going to various nations in the Middle East and criticizing America.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I think they looked at that and saw weakness.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Then when there were dissidents in the streets of Tehran, a Green Revolution, holding signs saying, is America with us, the president was silent.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I think they noticed that as well.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I think that when the president said he was going to create daylight between ourselves and Israel, that they noticed that as well.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: All of these things suggested, I think, to the Iranian mullahs that, hey, you know, we can keep on pushing along here, we can keep talks going on, we’re just going to keep on spinning centrifuges.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Now there are some 10,000 centrifuges spinning uranium, preparing to create a nuclear threat to the United States and to the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s unacceptable for us, and it’s essential for a president to show strength from the very beginning, to make it very clear what is acceptable and not acceptable.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And an Iranian nuclear program is not acceptable to us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They must not develop nuclear capability.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And the way to make sure they understand that is by having, from the very beginning, the tightest sanctions possible.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They need to be tightened.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Our diplomatic isolation needs to be tougher.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to indict Ahmadinejad.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We need to put the pressure on them as hard as we possibly can, because if we do that, we won’t have to take the military action.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Bob, let me just respond.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Nothing Governor Romney just said is true, starting with this notion of me apologizing.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: This has been probably the biggest whopper that’s been told during the course of this campaign.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And every fact checker and every reporter who’s looked at it, Governor, has said this is not true.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when it comes to tightening sanctions, look, as I said before, we’ve put in the toughest, most crippling sanctions ever.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the fact is, while we were coordinating an international coalition to make sure these sanctions were effective, you were still invested in a Chinese state oil company that was doing business with the Iranian oil sector.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So I’ll let the American people decide, judge, who’s going to be more effective and more credible when it comes to imposing crippling sanctions.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And with respect to our attitude about the Iranian revolution, I was very clear about the murderous activities that had taken place and that was contrary to international law and everything that civilized people stand for.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And — and so the strength that we have shown in Iran is shown by the fact that we’ve been able to mobilize the world.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When I came into office, the world was divided.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Iran was resurgent.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Iran is at its weakest point, economically, strategically, militarily, then since — then in many years.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we are going to continue to keep the pressure on to make sure that they do not get a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That’s in America’s national interest and that will be the case so long as I’m president.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re four years closer to a nuclear Iran.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’re four years closer to a nuclear Iran.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And — and — we should not have wasted these four years to the extent they — they continue to be able to spin these centrifuges and get that much closer.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: That’s number one.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Number two, Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: President, the reason I call it an apology tour is because you went to the Middle East and you flew to Egypt and to Saudi Arabia and to Turkey and Iraq.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And by the way, you skipped Israel, our closest friend in the region, but you went to the other nations.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And by the way, they noticed that you skipped Israel.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And then in those nations, and on Arabic TV, you said that America had been dismissive and derisive.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You said that on occasion America had dictated to other nations.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: President, America has not dictated to other nations.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We have freed other nations from dictators.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Bob, let me — let me respond.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: If we’re going to talk about trips that we’ve taken — when I was a candidate for office, first trip I took was to visit our troops.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And when I went to Israel as a candidate, I didn’t take donors.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I didn’t attend fundraisers.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I went to Yad Beshef , the Holocaust museum there, to remind myself the nature of evil and why our bond with Israel will be unbreakable.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And then I went down to the border towns of Storok , which had experienced missiles raining dowm from Hamas.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I saw families there who showed me there where missiles had come down near their children’s bedrooms.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I was reminded of what that would mean if those were my kids.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Which is why as president, we funded an Iron Dome program to stop those missiles.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: So that’s how I’ve used my travels, when I travel to Israel and when I travel to the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the — the central question at this point is going to be: Who is going to be credible to all parties involved?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they can look at my track record, whether it’s Iran sanctions, whether it’s dealing with counterterrorism, whether it’s supporting democracy, whether it’s supporting women’s rights, whether it’s supporting religious minorities.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And they can say that the President of the United States and the United States of America has stood on the right side of history.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And that kind of credibility is precisely why we’ve been able to show leadership on a wide range of issues facing the world right now.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: What if — what if the prime minister of Israel called you on the phone and said, “Our bombers are on the way.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We’re going to bomb Iran.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: ” What do you —

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Bob, let’s not go into hypotheticals of that nature.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Our relationship with Israel, my relationship with the prime minister of Israel is such that we would not get a call saying our bombers are on the way, or their fighters are on the way.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: This is the kind of thing that would have been discussed and thoroughly evaluated well before that kind of —

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: So you’d say it just wouldn’t happen?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: That’s —

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: OK.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Let’s see what —

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But let me — let me come back — we can come back.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Let’s come back to what the president was speaking about, which is what’s happening in the world and the president’s statement that things are going so well.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Look, I look at what’s happening around the world, and i see Iran four years closer to a bomb.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I see the Middle East with a rising tide of violence, chaos, tumult.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I see jihadists continuing to spread, whether they’re rising or just about the same level, hard to precisely measure, but it’s clear they’re there.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They’re very strong.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I see Syria with 30,000 civilians dead, Assad still in power.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I see our trade deficit with China, larger than it’s — growing larger every year, as a matter of fact.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I look around the world and I don’t feel that you see North Korea, continuing to export their nuclear technology, Russia said they’re not going to follow Nunn-Lugar any more.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They’re back away from a nuclear proliferation treaty that we had with them.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I look around the world, I don’t see our influence growing around the world.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I see our influence receding, in part because of the failure of the president to deal with our economic challenges at home; in part because of our withdrawal from our commitment to our military in the way I think it ought to be; in part because of the — the — the turmoil with Israel.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I mean, the president received a letter from 38 Democrat senators saying the tensions with Israel were a real problem.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They asked him, please repair the tension — Democrat senators — please repair the tension…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: … the damage in his — in his own party.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Governor, the problem is, is that on a whole range of issues, whether it’s the Middle East, whether it’s Afghanistan, whether it’s Iraq, whether it’s now Iran, you’ve been all over the map.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: I mean, I’m — I’m pleased that you now are endorsing our policy of applying diplomatic pressure and potentially having bilateral discussions with the Iranians to end their nuclear program.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But just a few years ago you said that’s something you’d never do.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the same way that you initially opposed a timetable in Afghanistan, now you’re for it, although it depends.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: In the same way that you say you would have ended the war in Iraq, but recently gave a speech saying that we should have 20,000 more folks in there.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: The same way that you said that it was mission creep to go after Gadhafi.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When it comes to going after Osama bin Laden, you said, well, any president would make that call.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But when you were a candidate in 2008, as I was, and I said if I got bin Laden in our sights I would take that shot, you said we shouldn’t move heaven and earth to get one man.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And you said we should ask Pakistan for permission.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And if we had asked Pakistan permission, we would not have gotten him.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And it was worth moving heaven and earth to get him.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: You know, after we killed bin Laden I was at ground zero for a memorial and talked to a young women who was four years old when 9/11 happened.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And the last conversation she had with her father was him calling from the twin towers, saying “Peyton , I love you and I will always watch over you.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” And for the next decade, she was haunted by that conversation.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And she said to me, “You know, by finally getting bin Laden, that brought some closure to me.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: ” And when we do things like that — when we bring those who have harmed us to justice, that sends a message to the world and it tells Peyton that we did not forget her father.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And I make that point because that’s the kind of clarity of leadership, and those decisions are not always popular.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: Those decisions generally — generally are not poll-tested.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And even some in my own party, including my current vice president, had the same critique as you did.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: But what the American people understand is that I look at what we need to get done to keep the American people safe and to move our interests forward, and I make those decisions.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: All right, let’s go.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And that leads us — this takes us right to the next segment, Governor, America’s longest war, Afghanistan and Pakistan…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Bob…

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Governor, you get to go first.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: You can’t — but you can’t have the president just lay out a whole series of items without giving me a chance to respond.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: With respect, sir, you had laid out quite a program…

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, that’s probably true.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: We’ll give you — we’ll catch up.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: The United States is scheduled to turn over responsibility for security in Afghanistan to the Afghan government in 2014.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: At that point, we will withdraw our combat troops, leave a smaller force of Americans, if I understand our policy, in Afghanistan for training purposes.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: It seems to me the key question here is: What do you do if the deadline arrives and it is obvious the Afghans are unable to handle their security?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Do we still leave?

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: And I believe, Governor Romney, you go first?

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: Well, we’re going to be finished by 2014, and when I’m president, we’ll make sure we bring our troops out by the end of 2014.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The commanders and the generals there are on track to do so.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: We’ve seen progress over the past several years.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: The surge has been successful and the training program is proceeding apace.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: There are now a large number of Afghan Security Forces, 350,000 that are ready to step in to provide security and we’re going to be able to make that transition by the end of 2014.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So our troops will come home at that point.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: I can tell you at the same time, that we will make sure that we look at what’s happening in Pakistan, and recognize that what’s happening in Pakistan is going to have a major impact on the success in Afghanistan.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I say that because I know a lot of people that feel like we should just brush our hands and walk away.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And I don’t mean you, Mr.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: President, but some people in the — in our nation feel that Pakistan is being nice to us, and that we should walk away fro mthem.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: But Pakistan is important to the region, to the world and to us, because Pakistan has 100 nuclear warheads and they’re rushing to build a lot more.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They’ll have more than Great Britain sometime in the — in the relatively near future.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: They also have the Haqqani Network and the Taliban existent within their country.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And so a Pakistan that falls apart, becomes a failed state, would be of extraordinary danger to Afghanistan and to us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And so we’re going to have to remain helpful in encouraging Pakistan to move towards a more stable government and rebuild the relationship with us.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: And that means that our aid that we provide to Pakistan is going to have to be conditioned upon certain benchmarks being met.

speaker: Mitt Romney
sentence_text: So for me, I look at this as both a need to help move Pakistan in the right direction, and also to get Afghanistan to be ready, and they will be ready by the end of 2014.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: Mr.

speaker: Schieffer
sentence_text: President?

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: When I came into office, we were still bogged down in Iraq and Afghanistan had been drifting for a decade.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: We ended the war in Iraq, refocused our attention on Afghanistan, and we did deliver a surge of troops.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: That was facilitated in part because we had ended the war in Iraq.

speaker: Barack Obama
sentence_text: And we are now in a position where we have met many of the objectives that got us there in the first place.

speaker: Barack Obama
